**Subject: New Process for Booking Meeting Rooms, Starting Monday, December 1**

Hi team,

To reduce double-bookings and make sure everyone can find a room when they need one, we're introducing a new process for booking meeting rooms. It takes effect on **Monday, December 1**.

**What's changing**

1. **All bookings go through the shared calendar.** Reserve rooms only through the room calendars in Outlook/Google Calendar. Add the room as a "resource" when you create your meeting invite. Verbal bookings, sticky notes, and whiteboard sign-ups will no longer count.
2. **Book up to four weeks in advance.** This gives everyone a fair chance at popular rooms.
3. **Two-hour limit for standard bookings.** If you need a room for longer, such as for a workshop or all-day session, please email [Office Manager Name] for approval.
4. **Check in within 10 minutes.** If no one checks in on the room panel (or accepts the booking) within 10 minutes of the start time, the room will be released automatically for others to use.
5. **Cancel if your plans change.** If your meeting is cancelled or moved, please delete the room booking right away so the space is freed up.

**Room etiquette reminders**

- Leave the room as you found it: wipe the whiteboards, take your trash, and reset the chairs.
- Wrap up on time so the next group can start promptly.
- Report any equipment issues (screens, video conferencing, etc.) to [IT/Facilities contact].

**Need help?**

A short guide on adding rooms to calendar invites is attached. If you have questions or run into problems, contact [Name] at [contact details].

Thanks for your cooperation. These changes should make finding a space much easier for all of us.

Best regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Title]

Subject: It's been way too long!

Hi Sam,

I was clearing out an old box of books last weekend and found my battered copy of *Introduction to Macroeconomics*, the one with your doodles all over the margins from those 9 a.m. lectures we barely survived. I laughed out loud, then realized it's been five years since we last saw each other. Five years! I'm not sure how that happened, but I didn't want to let it go any longer without saying hello.

I've been thinking about you a lot lately and wondering how you're doing. Are you still in the city, or did you finally make the move to the coast you always talked about? Are you still playing guitar? I still remember those late nights in the common room when you'd play the same three songs over and over and we'd all sing along badly.

As for me, life has been full of changes. I moved twice, switched jobs last year (for the better, thankfully), and took up running, which would have shocked our university selves, who considered walking to the library a workout. I've also gotten pretty good at cooking, so you'd finally get a decent meal if you visited, instead of the instant noodles we lived on.

I miss our conversations. You always had a way of making everything feel a bit lighter, even during exam season when we were running on coffee and panic. I've made good friends since then, but there's something about the people who knew you at twenty that can't be replaced.

I'd love to catch up properly, whether that's a long phone call, a video chat, or ideally meeting in person if we can work it out. I'd be happy to travel your way, or you're always welcome here. The guest room is ready and waiting.

No pressure to write back a novel. Even a few lines would make my day. I just wanted you to know I'm thinking of you and hope life has been kind to you.

Take care, and talk soon (I mean it this time!).

Warmly,
Alex

P.S. I'm keeping the textbook. Your doodle of our professor as a dinosaur is too good to throw away.

Subject: Next month's pick? I have a suggestion

Hi everyone,

I hope you're all doing well and that the last few chapters of this month's book weren't too painful for anyone still catching up! I really enjoyed our last discussion. It's always fun to see how differently we all read the same story.

I'd like to suggest *The Remains of the Day* by Kazuo Ishiguro for next month. It's a quiet, beautifully written novel about an English butler looking back on his decades of service as he takes a road trip across the countryside. On the surface it's a gentle story, but underneath it's about loyalty, regret, and the things we leave unsaid. I think it would make for a really rich conversation, especially about how much we can trust a narrator who isn't always honest with himself.

It's also on the shorter side (around 250 pages), which seems like a kindness with the holidays coming up. Most libraries should have copies, and it's easy to find secondhand too.

Of course, I'm happy to go with whatever the group prefers. If anyone has another title in mind, throw it out there and we can vote.

Looking forward to seeing you all soon. I'll bring the snacks!

Warmly,
[Your name]

Subject: Wedding photos (finally!) + a few stories from the big day

Hi everyone,

I promised I'd send these weeks ago, and here they are at last! I've put the full album in a shared folder (link below), but I attached a few favorites so you don't have to click through all 400 to get the highlights.

**[Link to shared album]**

Some stories from the day:

**The rain that wasn't.** The forecast called for an 80% chance of thunderstorms, and we spent the whole morning watching the sky like it owed us money. The caterers had the tents half up, and Aunt Ruth was handing out umbrellas like party favors. Then, about twenty minutes before the ceremony, the clouds just... parted. Photo #3 is the golden-hour light we got instead. I still don't quite believe it.

**The ring bearer's big moment.** Little Theo (age four, very serious about his job) made it halfway down the aisle before deciding the ring pillow would work better as a hat. He wore it proudly the rest of the way. Nobody could keep a straight face, including the officiant. Photo #7 captures it perfectly. We may frame that one.

**The vows.** I won't try to retell them because I'd get them wrong and get teary again. But when they got to the line about "choosing you on the boring Tuesdays, too," you could hear half the guests sniffling. Photo #12 is right at that moment. Look closely and you'll spot Grandpa Joe dabbing his eyes with his tie.

**The dance floor.** Things got wild. There was a full-on conga line by 9 p.m., a surprisingly competitive limbo contest (Photo #18, which shows Marcus going *very* low, and yes, he pulled something), and at least three people who swore they don't dance and then didn't sit down for two hours. The DJ played the Cha Cha Slide twice by popular demand.

**The late-night snack.** Around 11, they brought out trays of tiny grilled cheese sandwiches and tomato soup shooters, and I'm fairly sure that was the highlight of the evening for some guests. I ate four. No regrets.

**The send-off.** Everyone lined up with sparklers as the happy couple ran out to the car. Photo #24 is a little blurry, but I love it anyway because it shows exactly how it felt: chaotic, glowing, and full of joy.

It was one of those days that reminds you how lucky we are to have the people we have. I wish every one of you could have been there, and for those who were, thank you for making it so much fun.

If you have photos of your own, please send them my way or add them to the shared folder! I'd love to see the day from everyone's angle.

Hugs,
[Your name]

P.S. If anyone found a single silver earring shaped like a leaf near the dessert table, it belongs to my cousin Lena, and she would be forever grateful.

Subject: My new flat!

Dear Grandma and Grandpa,

I hope you're both keeping well and that the garden is surviving the colder weather. I've finally finished unpacking the last of the boxes, so I wanted to write and tell you all about my new flat.

It's on the second floor of an old red-brick building on a quiet street, just a few minutes' walk from the high street. There's no lift, so I'm getting plenty of exercise carrying the shopping up. Grandpa, I can already hear you saying it'll do me good!

The living room is my favourite part. It has a big bay window that lets in lots of morning light, and I've put my reading chair right in front of it with the blue knitted blanket you made me, Grandma. It looks perfect there. There's also a small fireplace. It doesn't work any more, but I've lined the mantelpiece with candles and the photo of us all from last summer.

The kitchen is small but cosy. There's just enough room for a little table for two by the window, and I've already made your shepherd's pie recipe twice. It wasn't quite as good as yours, but it was close! From the sink I can see the trees in the back garden, which are turning lovely shades of orange and gold at the moment.

My bedroom is at the back, so it's nice and quiet at night. The bathroom is a bit old-fashioned, with a proper claw-foot bath, which I absolutely love after a long day.

The neighbours seem friendly too. The lady downstairs, Margaret, brought me a tin of homemade biscuits on my first day. She reminds me a bit of you, Grandma.

You'll both have to come and visit once I've got the place properly sorted. I'll make sure there are plenty of cushions on the sofa, and I promise to have the kettle on as soon as you arrive.

Give my love to everyone, and I'll ring you on Sunday as usual.

Lots of love and big hugs,

[Your name]

Pulling works for dogs because it gets them where they want to go. The fix is to make sure it never does.

**Stop when the lead goes tight.** The moment there's tension, freeze. Don't yank, just become a tree. When your dog eases off and the lead slackens (even slightly), say "yes" and carry on walking. Forward movement becomes the reward for a loose lead.

**Reward position.** Carry small, tasty treats and reward your dog often for being beside you. Early on, reward every few steps. Gradually stretch it out.

**Change direction.** If your dog surges ahead, turn and walk the other way. They'll learn to keep an eye on you.

**Start somewhere boring.** Practise in your hallway or garden before tackling a busy street full of smells and squirrels. Distractions make it much harder.

**Burn some energy first.** A quick game of fetch before a training walk can take the edge off.

**Consider equipment.** A front-clip harness can reduce pulling while you train. Avoid choke or prong collars, which cause discomfort without teaching anything.

Be consistent. If pulling *sometimes* works, your dog will keep trying it. Expect a few weeks of patience.

You should sand it first. Paint doesn't stick well to a glossy surface. Without some "tooth" to grip, new paint can peel, chip, or scratch off easily, especially on high-traffic areas like doors, trim, and skirting boards.

Here's the basic process:

1. **Clean**: Wash the surface with sugar soap or a degreaser to remove grease, dirt, and fingerprints. Rinse and let it dry.
2. **Sand**: Lightly scuff the surface with 120–180 grit sandpaper or a sanding sponge. You're not trying to remove the paint, just dull the shine. Wipe off the dust with a damp or tack cloth.
3. **Prime**: Use a bonding or adhesion primer, especially if you're switching from oil-based gloss to water-based paint. Water-based paint over oil-based gloss without primer is a common cause of peeling.
4. **Paint**: Apply your topcoat.

**Alternatives:** Liquid deglosser or "sanding-free" bonding primers can work if sanding isn't practical, but a light scuff-sand is still the most reliable.

**Caution:** If your home was built before the late 1970s, test for lead paint before sanding. Lead test kits are inexpensive.

Ten minutes of prep saves you from redoing the whole job later.

I was terrified of motorways for years after passing my test, so I get it. What actually worked for me was building up in really small steps rather than trying to force myself onto the M25 at rush hour.

Start with a quiet stretch at an off-peak time, like early Sunday morning. Go one junction, come off, turn round, come back. That's it. Do that a few times until it feels boring, then go two junctions, and so on.

Joining was the bit that scared me most. The thing nobody told me is that you need to get your speed up on the slip road. Matching the traffic makes merging so much easier than creeping on at 45.

Stay in the left lane as long as you like. You don't have to overtake anyone. Lorries are fine to sit behind if you leave a decent gap.

If you can afford it, book a couple of motorway lessons with an instructor. Having someone calm next to you with dual controls takes a lot of the panic out.

And honestly, it does get easier. I drive them every week now without thinking about it.

You can, but it's not the best choice for initial seasoning.

**Why olive oil isn't ideal:**
- **Low smoke point:** Extra virgin olive oil smokes around 350–410°F (175–210°C). Seasoning works best when oil is heated past its smoke point so it polymerizes into a hard coating. Olive oil gets there, but it tends to produce a softer, sometimes sticky finish.
- **Flavor and residue:** It can leave a slightly gummy layer that flakes or turns rancid over time.

**Better options:**
- Vegetable shortening (Crisco)
- Canola or vegetable oil
- Grapeseed oil
- Flaxseed oil (very hard finish, but can flake if applied too thick)

**How to season properly:**
1. Clean and fully dry the pan (heat it on the stove to drive off moisture).
2. Rub on a *very thin* layer of oil, then wipe off as much as you can. It should look almost dry.
3. Bake upside down at 450–500°F (230–260°C) for an hour.
4. Let it cool in the oven. Repeat 3–5 times.

**That said:** cooking with olive oil in an already-seasoned pan is perfectly fine. Regular cooking builds seasoning naturally regardless of the oil.

The trick is to treat herbs according to whether they're tender or hardy.

**Tender herbs** (basil, parsley, cilantro, mint, dill, tarragon): Treat them like cut flowers. Trim the stem ends, stand them in a jar with an inch or two of water, and loosely cover the tops with a plastic bag. Refrigerate everything except basil, which turns black in the cold. Keep basil on the counter, out of direct sun. Change the water every couple of days.

**Hardy herbs** (rosemary, thyme, sage, oregano, chives): Wrap them loosely in a slightly damp paper towel, then put them in a zip-top bag or airtight container in the fridge. Moderate humidity is the goal. Too wet and they rot, too dry and they shrivel.

**General tips:**
- Don't wash herbs until you're ready to use them. Excess moisture speeds decay.
- Remove any yellowing or slimy leaves right away so they don't spoil the rest.
- For long-term storage, chop the herbs and freeze them in ice cube trays covered with olive oil or water. They're perfect for dropping into soups and sauces.

Stored this way, most herbs last one to two weeks, and hardy herbs often last longer.

Start with the easiest methods and escalate as needed:

1. **Rubber band trick:** Place a wide rubber band flat over the screw head, then press your screwdriver firmly into it and turn slowly. The rubber fills the stripped gaps and adds grip.

2. **Bigger or different bit:** Try a slightly larger Phillips bit, or tap a Torx bit snugly into the head with a hammer. Apply strong downward pressure while turning.

3. **Pliers:** If the head sticks up at all, grab it with locking pliers (Vise-Grips) and twist counterclockwise.

4. **Cut a new slot:** Use a Dremel or hacksaw to cut a straight slot across the head, then use a flathead screwdriver.

5. **Screw extractor:** The most reliable fix. Drill a small pilot hole in the screw head, then insert the extractor (reverse-threaded) and turn counterclockwise with a drill on reverse. It bites in as it turns and backs the screw out. Kits are cheap at any hardware store.

6. **Drill it out:** As a last resort, drill through the head until it pops off, then remove the shaft with pliers.

**Tip:** A drop of penetrating oil (like WD-40) can help loosen rusted or stuck screws. To prevent future stripping, use the correct bit size and keep firm pressure.

It depends on your goal and the type of exercise:

**Strength (heavy weights, 1–6 reps):** Rest 2–5 minutes. Lifting near your max taxes your nervous system and depletes short-term energy stores (ATP/creatine phosphate), which take a few minutes to replenish. Cutting rest short here usually means fewer reps and less weight on later sets.

**Muscle growth (6–15 reps):** Rest 1.5–3 minutes. Older advice pushed short rests (60 seconds) for "more pump," but research suggests longer rests let you maintain more total volume, which drives hypertrophy better.

**Muscular endurance (15+ reps, lighter loads):** Rest 30–90 seconds.

**Exercise type matters too:** Big compound lifts like squats, deadlifts, and bench press need more recovery than isolation moves like curls or lateral raises. You might rest 3–4 minutes after heavy squats but only 60–90 seconds between sets of curls.

**Practical rule:** Rest until you feel ready to perform the next set with good form and close to the same reps. If you're consistently failing early, rest longer. If you're pressed for time, use supersets (alternating non-competing muscle groups) to stay efficient without sacrificing recovery.

Fungus gnats are almost always a moisture problem. The adults lay eggs in the top inch or two of damp potting soil, and the larvae feed on fungi and decaying organic matter there. If your soil stays consistently wet, you're running a nursery for them.

Common causes:

- **Overwatering.** This is the big one. Most houseplants prefer the top layer to dry out between waterings.
- **Peat-heavy or organic-rich mixes.** These hold moisture and provide food for larvae.
- **Poor drainage.** Pots without holes, or saucers left full of water.
- **New soil or plants.** Bagged potting mix often arrives already infested.

How to break the cycle:

1. Let the top 1–2 inches of soil dry fully before watering. Bottom-watering helps keep the surface dry.
2. Put up yellow sticky traps to catch adults and monitor numbers.
3. Treat the larvae with BTI (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis), sold as "Mosquito Bits" or Gnatrol. Soak it in water and use that water on your plants for a few weeks.
4. Optionally, top-dress with sand or fine grit to discourage egg-laying.

Their life cycle is about 3–4 weeks, so stay consistent for at least a month.

I did Spanish and Japanese at the same time a few years back and it worked fine, mostly because they're so different my brain never mixed them up. A friend tried Spanish and Portuguese together and it was a mess. She'd start a sentence in one and finish it in the other. Close languages bleed into each other, especially early on.

Couple of things that helped me:

- Get one to a basic level first if you can. Even a few months of a head start makes a difference, because then you're not a total beginner at two things at once.
- Keep them separate. I did Japanese in the mornings and Spanish at night, and used different apps and notebooks. Sounds silly but it helped.
- Be honest about time. Two languages means each one moves slower. If you've got 30 minutes a day, splitting it in half might just leave you stuck in beginner territory forever with both.

If you're doing it for fun and you're not in a hurry, go for it. If you need one of them for a trip or a job, focus on that one first.

**Fit comes first.** A great deal on the wrong size is no deal. Know your frame size (check manufacturer charts using your height and inseam) and test ride before paying.

**Inspect the frame carefully.**
- *Aluminum/steel:* Look for cracks near welds, dents, and rust (especially inside steel tubes).
- *Carbon:* Check for cracks, chips, or soft spots. Tap gently with a coin; a dull thud instead of a crisp click can indicate hidden damage. Ask if it's ever been crashed.

**Check the drivetrain.** Use a chain checker for stretch. Look for "shark-fin" worn cassette and chainring teeth. Shift through all gears; it should be smooth and quiet.

**Wheels.** Spin them to check for wobble. Squeeze spokes for loose ones. Rim brake? Check for concave, worn braking surfaces. Wiggle the wheel side-to-side for hub play.

**Brakes and headset.** Brakes should engage firmly. Lock the front brake and rock the bike; clunking means a loose headset.

**Ask questions.** Service history, receipts, why they're selling. A proof of purchase also helps confirm it isn't stolen. Check the serial number on Bike Index.

Budget a bit extra for new tires, cables, or a tune-up.

It's moisture migration. When bread comes out of the oven, the crust is dry and the crumb inside is full of water. As the loaf sits, that moisture moves outward from the wet interior to the dry exterior until things even out. The crust absorbs the water and loses its crispness. Humidity in the air speeds this up.

Storage makes it worse. Plastic bags or airtight containers trap that escaping moisture right against the crust, so it softens within hours.

**What helps:**

- **Cool completely on a wire rack** before storing, so steam can escape from all sides.
- **Store in paper or cloth**, not plastic. A paper bag or a linen bread bag lets the loaf breathe. Cut-side down on a board works too.
- **Bake a bit longer or darker.** A well-developed crust holds up better. Some bakers turn off the oven and leave the loaf inside with the door cracked for 5–10 minutes to dry it further.
- **Re-crisp before serving.** 5–10 minutes in a 180–200°C (350–400°F) oven brings the crust right back.

Softening is normal and unavoidable over time, especially for lean breads like baguettes. That's why they're traditionally eaten the same day.

It's moisture migration. When bread comes out of the oven, the crust is very dry and the crumb inside is still full of water. As the loaf cools and sits, that moisture moves outward from the moist interior toward the dry exterior until the two even out. The crust absorbs it and loses its crispness. Humidity in the air speeds this up, since the dry crust also pulls moisture from its surroundings.

Storage makes a big difference. Sealing a loaf in a plastic bag traps the escaping moisture right against the crust, so it softens within hours. A paper bag, a linen bread bag, or simply leaving the loaf cut side down on a board lets some of that moisture escape, keeping the crust firmer for longer.

Baking choices help too. A longer bake drives off more water, giving a thicker, drier crust that holds up better. Some bakers leave the loaf in the switched-off oven with the door cracked for ten minutes at the end. Letting it cool fully on a wire rack before storing also prevents condensation.

If the crust has already gone soft, a few minutes in a hot oven will crisp it right back up.

For a single week of lessons, renting is almost always the smarter choice. Most surf schools include a wetsuit in the lesson price, so check with yours first before spending anything. If it isn't included, rental shops near popular surf spots usually charge somewhere between $10 and $20 a day, which adds up to far less than a decent new suit.

Buying makes sense if you already know you'll keep surfing after the week ends. A good wetsuit costs anywhere from $150 to $400 or more, and fit matters a lot. As a beginner you may not yet know what thickness suits your local water temperature or which brand fits your body well. Renting gives you a chance to figure that out.

There are a few reasons you might lean toward buying anyway. Some people dislike wearing a suit that dozens of others have worn, and rental suits can be worn out, smelly or poorly sized. If you have an unusual body shape and struggle to find a good fit, owning one could be worth it.

My suggestion is to rent for the week, pay attention to what you like, and buy later if surfing becomes a regular habit.

A ZZ plant (*Zamioculcas zamiifolia*) is hard to beat as a first plant for a dark flat. It tolerates low light better than almost anything else, stores water in its thick rhizomes, and actually prefers being forgotten. Water it only when the soil is completely dry, roughly every 2–4 weeks, and less in winter. Overwatering is the only reliable way to kill it.

Close runners-up:

- **Snake plant (*Sansevieria/Dracaena trifasciata*)**: similarly drought-tolerant, upright, and happy in dim corners.
- **Pothos (*Epipremnum aureum*)**: a trailing vine that copes with low light and droops visibly when thirsty, which makes it forgiving for beginners.
- **Cast iron plant (*Aspidistra elatior*)**: lives up to its name in gloomy hallways.

A few tips:

1. "Low light" still means *some* light. A spot within a few metres of any window is better than an interior room with none. If you have no natural light at all, a cheap LED grow bulb in a regular lamp works well.
2. Plants in low light grow slowly and use less water, so water less than you think.
3. Use a pot with drainage holes.

Note that ZZ plants and pothos are toxic if eaten, so keep them away from curious pets.

The biggest mistake is starting too big. Most people quit because they set out to write a page a day and it becomes a chore. Here's what works:

**1. Make it tiny.** Commit to one sentence a day. That's it. Some days you'll write more, but the bar is low enough that you'll never skip because it feels like too much.

**2. Attach it to an existing habit.** Journal right after brushing your teeth, with your morning coffee, or when you get into bed. A consistent trigger beats willpower.

**3. Use prompts when you're stuck.** Try "What's on my mind right now?", "One thing that went well today," or "What am I avoiding?" A blank page is intimidating; a question isn't.

**4. Drop the perfectionism.** Nobody's grading it. Bullet points, misspellings, and half-thoughts are fine. Write like nobody will ever read it, because nobody will.

**5. Keep it visible and easy.** Leave the notebook on your pillow, or pin a notes app to your home screen. Friction kills habits.

**6. Don't break the chain twice.** Missing a day is normal. Missing two in a row is how habits die, so just get back to it.

After a month, reread your old entries. Seeing how far you've come is the best motivation to keep going.

Almost always it's the base image, not your app.

If your Dockerfile starts with something like `FROM node` or `FROM python`, you're pulling in a full Debian install with compilers, headers, man pages, and a bunch of other stuff you'll never use at runtime. That alone can be close to a gig. Run `docker history yourimage` and you'll probably see one fat layer at the bottom and your app as a tiny sliver on top.

Things that usually help, roughly in order of payoff:

1. Switch to a slim or alpine variant (`python:3.12-slim`, `node:20-alpine`). Alpine can cause headaches with some native Python packages because of musl, so slim is often the safer bet.

2. Use a multi-stage build. Do your compiling and dependency installs in one stage, then copy just the finished output into a clean, small final image. For Go or Rust you can sometimes end up on `distroless` or even `scratch` and get the image down to a few MB.

3. Add a `.dockerignore`. People get bitten by `COPY . .` dragging in `node_modules`, `.git`, test data, or that 400 MB CSV sitting in the project folder.

4. Clean up package manager caches in the same `RUN` line that installs things. Deleting them in a later layer doesn't shrink anything, because the earlier layer still holds the files.

`dive` is a nice tool for poking around layers if you want to see exactly where the bloat is.

It depends on your system, but here's how to decide.

**Auto-increment integers** are the sensible default for a single-database application:
- Compact (4–8 bytes), so indexes stay small and fast.
- Sequential inserts keep B-tree indexes tidy, with minimal page splits.
- Easy to read, debug, and type into a query.

Downsides: they leak information (`/orders/1042` reveals volume and invites enumeration), and they require the database to assign them, which complicates merging data, sharding, or creating records offline.

**UUIDs** shine when IDs must be generated independently:
- Clients, multiple services, or replicas can create IDs without coordination.
- Non-guessable, so they're safer to expose in URLs.
- Merging datasets never causes collisions.

Downsides: 16 bytes (worse if stored as a 36-char string), and random UUIDv4 values scatter inserts across the index, hurting write performance and cache locality on large tables.

**The modern middle ground:** use **UUIDv7** (or ULID). It's time-ordered, so inserts stay roughly sequential like auto-increment, while keeping UUIDs' decentralized generation. Store it in a native `uuid`/binary column, not text.

Another common pattern is to use an internal auto-increment key for joins plus a separate public UUID column for external exposure.

**Rule of thumb:** a monolith with one database can use auto-increment. Distributed systems, offline clients, or public-facing IDs call for UUIDv7.

The usual culprit is that cron runs your job in a very different environment from your interactive shell.

**1. PATH is minimal.** Cron typically uses something like `/usr/bin:/bin`. Commands in `/usr/local/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, or anything your `.bashrc` adds won't be found. Use absolute paths, or set `PATH=` at the top of your crontab.

**2. No profile is loaded.** Your `.bashrc` and `.profile` aren't sourced, so environment variables, aliases, virtualenvs, nvm, and conda setups don't exist.

**3. The working directory is different.** Cron usually starts in your home directory, so relative paths like `./data.csv` break. Use absolute paths or `cd` explicitly first.

**4. The shell is different.** Cron defaults to `/bin/sh`, not bash, so bash-only syntax can fail silently.

**5. `%` is special.** In a crontab line, an unescaped `%` becomes a newline. This often breaks `date +%Y-%m-%d`. Escape it as `\%`.

**6. Permissions and user.** Check whether it's in the right user's crontab, whether the script is executable, and whether it needs a display or SSH agent it can't reach.

**How to debug:** Redirect output so you can see the actual error by appending `>> /tmp/job.log 2>&1` to the line. Also check the system log (`grep CRON /var/log/syslog` or `journalctl -u cron`). Nine times out of ten, the log shows "command not found" or "no such file."

For a small app, default to REST unless you have a specific reason not to.

**Choose REST when:**
- Your data model is simple and maps cleanly to resources (users, posts, orders).
- You have one client, or clients that need roughly the same data.
- You want HTTP caching, CDNs, and browser tooling to just work.
- You want the smallest learning curve. Every framework, host, and developer already knows REST.

**Choose GraphQL when:**
- Clients need very different shapes of the same data (e.g., a mobile app wants a slim payload, a dashboard wants deeply nested records).
- You're making many round trips to assemble one screen, and it's actually hurting performance.
- Your frontend team iterates quickly and is constantly asking for new endpoint variations.
- You're aggregating several backends behind one API.

**Costs of GraphQL to weigh:**
- Extra setup: schema, resolvers, a client library.
- Caching is harder because most requests are POSTs to a single endpoint.
- You must guard against N+1 queries (use a dataloader) and expensive nested queries (depth/complexity limits).

**Practical heuristic:** Start with REST. If you later find yourself building endpoints like `/posts-with-authors-and-comments-lite`, that's the signal GraphQL would pay off. Migrating a small app is cheap. Over-engineering one up front usually isn't.

An index doesn't guarantee a faster query. Several things can make it slower:

**1. Low selectivity.** If your WHERE clause matches a large share of rows (say, 20% or more), using the index means jumping back and forth between the index and the table for every match. Random I/O like that can cost more than a single sequential scan of the whole table. The optimizer usually knows this, but only if it has good information.

**2. Stale statistics.** The planner chooses its plan from table statistics. If those are outdated, it may think the index is selective when it isn't. Run `ANALYZE` (PostgreSQL), `ANALYZE TABLE` (MySQL), or update statistics (SQL Server), then retest.

**3. Missing columns.** If the query needs columns that aren't in the index, every match requires an extra lookup into the table. A covering index, one that includes all the columns the query needs, avoids this.

**4. Wrong column order.** In a composite index on (a, b), a filter on `b` alone can't use the index efficiently.

**5. Write overhead.** If the slow part is INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, that's expected. Every index must be maintained on each write.

**6. Caching effects.** Your "before" timing may have run with warm caches and your "after" with cold ones. Repeat each measurement several times.

**What to do:** run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (or your database's equivalent) on both versions and compare estimated versus actual row counts. A large mismatch usually points to the cause.

**Probably yes, especially if one person or one small team owns all three.**

For a handful of small services, a monorepo usually removes more friction than it adds:

- **Atomic changes.** If service A's API changes and service B consumes it, you update both in one commit and one PR. With separate repos, you coordinate versions, merge order, and "which commit works with which."
- **Shared code is easy.** Common types, config, or utilities live in a folder instead of a published package you have to version and release.
- **One set of tooling.** One CI config, one linter setup, one place to search, one clone for new contributors.

The usual monorepo pain points (slow CI, huge checkouts, complex build tools like Bazel or Nx) mostly appear at scale. With three small services, you can just run each service's tests when its directory changes. Most CI systems support path filters.

**Consider separate repos if:**

- Different teams own the services and want independent release cadences or access control.
- The services use very different stacks and share nothing.
- You plan to open-source one of them separately.

A practical layout:

```
services/a/
services/b/
services/c/
shared/
```

Start there. Splitting a repo later is straightforward with `git filter-repo`. Merging scattered repos back together, and untangling their version-compatibility history, is usually more painful.

The most common cause is **file permissions**. OpenSSH silently ignores your key if the server-side files are too open. On the server, your home directory must not be group- or world-writable. The `~/.ssh` directory should be `700`, and `authorized_keys` should be `600`. Everything should be owned by your user. Check the server's auth log (often `/var/log/auth.log` or `journalctl -u sshd`) for messages like "bad ownership or modes."

Other likely culprits:

- **Wrong file or wrong user.** The public key must be in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` of the account you're logging into. Watch for typos, a missing "s" in the filename, or a key broken across multiple lines when pasted.
- **Client isn't offering the key.** If the key isn't in a default location, SSH won't try it. Specify it with `-i` or an `IdentityFile` entry in `~/.ssh/config`. If you have many keys loaded in an agent, the server may hit its max-tries limit before reaching the right one.
- **Server config.** `PubkeyAuthentication` may be disabled, or `AuthorizedKeysFile` may point somewhere else.
- **Key type rejected.** Newer OpenSSH versions disable old `ssh-rsa` (SHA-1) signatures. Generate an Ed25519 key instead.
- **SELinux.** On RHEL-like systems, wrong security contexts on `~/.ssh` block access. Running `restorecon` fixes it.

**Best diagnostic:** connect with `ssh -v` and see which keys are offered and how the server responds.

Nine times out of ten this is permissions. sshd is picky: if your home directory, `~/.ssh`, or `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the server is writable by anyone other than you, it silently ignores the key and falls back to password auth. You want `~/.ssh` at 700 and `authorized_keys` at 600, and your home dir shouldn't be group-writable either. This bites people constantly after copying files around as root.

If that's fine, check these:

- **Wrong key being offered.** Your client might be trying a different key than the one you installed. Run `ssh -v user@host` and read the output. It tells you exactly which keys it tried and what the server said back. Honestly, start here, it saves a lot of guessing.
- **Key pasted badly.** The public key has to be one single line in `authorized_keys`. Line breaks from a copy-paste will break it. `ssh-copy-id` avoids this.
- **Wrong user or wrong file.** You added it to root's authorized_keys but you're logging in as yourself, or vice versa.
- **Server config.** Check that `PubkeyAuthentication` isn't set to no in `sshd_config`, and that `AuthorizedKeysFile` points where you think it does.
- **It's actually asking for your passphrase**, not your password. Read the prompt carefully. If so, that's normal; use ssh-agent.

The server's auth log (`/var/log/auth.log` or `journalctl -u sshd`) will usually just tell you the reason outright.

**Authentication** answers *"Who are you?"*
**Authorisation** answers *"What are you allowed to do?"*

Authentication is the process of verifying identity. The user proves they are who they claim to be, typically with a password, a one-time code, a fingerprint, a client certificate, or a token issued by an identity provider. If it fails, the system doesn't know who you are, and the usual response is **401 Unauthorized** (confusingly named; it really means "unauthenticated").

Authorisation happens *after* identity is established. The system checks whether that identity has permission to perform the requested action on the requested resource. This is often done through roles, access control lists, scopes, or policy rules. If it fails, the system knows who you are but refuses the action, and the usual response is **403 Forbidden**.

An analogy: at an airport, showing your passport at security is authentication. Your boarding pass determining which plane you may board, and whether you can enter the business lounge, is authorisation.

In practice:

- **Login form, OAuth/OpenID Connect sign-in, MFA** are authentication.
- **"Only admins can delete users", "users can edit only their own posts", OAuth scopes** are authorisation.

They're frequently implemented together, but keeping them conceptually separate makes security logic clearer: first establish identity reliably, then evaluate permissions for every protected operation.

Authentication is the process of establishing who someone is. Authorisation is the process of deciding what that person is allowed to do. They usually happen in that order: the system first confirms your identity, then checks whether that identity has permission for the action you are attempting.

A useful analogy is an office building. Showing your ID badge at the front desk is authentication, because it proves you are the employee you claim to be. Whether that badge then opens the server room door is authorisation, because being a genuine employee does not automatically grant access to every room.

In software, authentication typically involves passwords, one-time codes, biometrics, certificates or a login through a provider such as Google. The result is usually a session or a token that represents the verified user. Authorisation then uses that identity, often alongside roles, groups or specific permissions, to decide whether a request should succeed. For example, a logged-in user may be allowed to read a document but not delete it.

HTTP status codes reflect the distinction, somewhat confusingly. A 401 Unauthorized response actually means the request lacks valid authentication, while 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you lack permission.

Keeping the two concepts separate in your design makes systems easier to reason about and secure, since a flaw in either one can expose data independently of the other.

# duration

A small, dependency-free library for parsing [ISO 8601 durations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Durations) such as `P3Y6M4DT12H30M5S` or `PT1.5H` into structured values you can actually work with.

ISO 8601 durations show up everywhere: API responses, calendar feeds, video metadata, configuration files. They are compact and unambiguous, but they are awkward to handle by hand. Regex-based one-liners tend to break on fractional values, week designators, or edge cases like `P0D`. This library handles the full format correctly and stays out of your way.

## Features

- **Complete format support.** Handles years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, and seconds, including fractional components (`PT0.5S`, `P1,5D`).
- **Strict by default.** Malformed input like `P`, `PT`, `P1H`, or `P1M2Y` is rejected with a clear error message that points to the problem, so it is never silently misread.
- **Lossless.** Components are kept exactly as written. `P1M` stays "one month" and is never approximated as 30 days.
- **Round-trippable.** Parsed durations can be serialized back to canonical ISO 8601 strings.
- **Tiny.** No runtime dependencies and a minimal API surface.

## Quick example

```js
import { parse } from "duration";

const d = parse("P1DT2H30M");
// { years: 0, months: 0, weeks: 0, days: 1, hours: 2, minutes: 30, seconds: 0 }

d.toString(); // "P1DT2H30M"
```

## What it doesn't do

Durations that use calendar units (years, months, days) have no fixed length. A month can be 28 to 31 days, and a day can be 23 or 25 hours across a DST change. Converting them to a total number of seconds requires a reference date and time zone. This library deliberately leaves that step to you or your date library of choice, rather than guessing.

## Configuring Retries

Transient failures such as dropped connections, timeouts, and temporary server errors are common in networked systems. The client can automatically retry failed requests according to a configurable retry policy.

Retries are **disabled by default**. You must opt in by supplying a `RetryPolicy`.

### Quick Start

```python
from httpclient import Client, RetryPolicy

client = Client(
    base_url="https://api.example.com",
    retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
)

response = client.get("/users/42")
```

With this configuration, a failed request is attempted up to three times in total: the initial attempt plus two retries. The client uses exponential backoff between attempts.

### Retry Policy Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_attempts` | `int` | `1` | Total number of attempts, including the first. `1` disables retries. |
| `backoff` | `Backoff` | `ExponentialBackoff()` | Strategy that determines the delay between attempts. |
| `retry_on_status` | `set[int]` | `{429, 502, 503, 504}` | HTTP status codes that trigger a retry. |
| `retry_on_exceptions` | `tuple[type, ...]` | `(ConnectError, ReadTimeout)` | Exception types that trigger a retry. |
| `retry_methods` | `set[str]` | `{"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "PUT", "DELETE"}` | HTTP methods eligible for retry. |
| `respect_retry_after` | `bool` | `True` | Honor the `Retry-After` response header when present. |
| `max_retry_after` | `float` | `60.0` | Upper bound, in seconds, on any delay taken from `Retry-After`. |
| `total_timeout` | `float \| None` | `None` | Maximum wall-clock time, in seconds, across all attempts. |

### Backoff Strategies

#### Exponential backoff (default)

```python
from httpclient import ExponentialBackoff

RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=5,
    backoff=ExponentialBackoff(
        initial=0.5,     # delay before the first retry, in seconds
        multiplier=2.0,  # factor applied after each attempt
        max_delay=30.0,  # cap on any single delay
        jitter=True,     # randomize delays to avoid synchronized retries
    ),
)
```

The resulting delays before jitter are 0.5s, 1s, 2s, and 4s.

When `jitter=True`, the client uses "full jitter." Each delay is a random value between `0` and the computed delay. Keep jitter enabled when many clients may fail at the same moment, so their retries don't hit the server all at once.

#### Constant backoff

```python
from httpclient import ConstantBackoff

RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4, backoff=ConstantBackoff(delay=1.0))
```

#### Custom backoff

You can pass any callable that accepts the attempt number (starting at `1`) and returns a delay in seconds:

```python
def fibonacci_backoff(attempt: int) -> float:
    a, b = 0.5, 0.5
    for _ in range(attempt - 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return min(a, 20.0)

RetryPolicy(max_attempts=6, backoff=fibonacci_backoff)
```

### Idempotency and Non-Idempotent Methods

By default, the client does not retry `POST` and `PATCH` requests. Repeating these methods can cause duplicate side effects, such as charging a customer twice.

To retry these methods safely, send an idempotency key that your server recognizes, and add the method to `retry_methods`:

```python
policy = RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=3,
    retry_methods={"GET", "PUT", "DELETE", "POST"},
)

client.post(
    "/payments",
    json={"amount": 1000},
    headers={"Idempotency-Key": "a1b2c3d4"},
    retry=policy,
)
```

> **Warning:** Only enable retries for `POST` or `PATCH` if the server guarantees idempotent handling. Otherwise a request that succeeded on the server, but whose response was lost in transit, will be executed again.

### Per-Request Overrides

A policy set on the `Client` applies to every request. To override it for a single call, pass `retry`:

```python
# Disable retries for this call only
client.get("/health", retry=None)

# Use a more aggressive policy for this call
client.get("/reports/large", retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=8, total_timeout=120))
```

### Honoring `Retry-After`

When a `429` or `503` response includes a `Retry-After` header, the client waits for the specified duration instead of the computed backoff. The header may be given in seconds or as an HTTP date. The wait is capped at `max_retry_after`. If the server requests a longer delay than the cap allows, the client stops retrying and returns the response.

### Observing Retries

Use the `on_retry` hook to log or record metrics for each retry:

```python
import logging

log = logging.getLogger("httpclient")

def log_retry(request, attempt, delay, error=None, response=None):
    reason = error or f"HTTP {response.status_code}"
    log.warning("Retrying %s %s (attempt %d) in %.2fs: %s",
                request.method, request.url, attempt, delay, reason)

RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, on_retry=log_retry)
```

### When Retries Are Exhausted

When retries run out, the client returns or raises the outcome of the **final** attempt:

- If the last attempt received a response, that response is returned. Call `response.raise_for_status()` if you want an exception for error statuses.
- If the last attempt raised an exception, the client raises `RetryError`. The original exception is available as `RetryError.last_exception`, and the full list of attempts is available as `RetryError.attempts`.

```python
from httpclient import RetryError

try:
    client.get("/flaky")
except RetryError as e:
    print(f"Gave up after {len(e.attempts)} attempts: {e.last_exception}")
```

### Best Practices

- **Keep `max_attempts` small.** Three to five attempts is usually enough. More attempts can amplify load on a struggling service.
- **Always set a `total_timeout`** for user-facing requests, so retries can't exceed your latency budget.
- **Keep jitter enabled** in distributed systems.
- **Avoid retrying at multiple layers.** If a proxy or SDK above this client also retries, the number of attempts multiplies.
- **Don't retry `4xx` errors** other than `408` and `429`. They usually indicate a problem with the request itself, and sending it again won't fix it.

## Job queue backing up

**How you'll know:** queue depth alert fires (>5k pending for 10+ min), or someone in #support says emails/exports are "stuck."

**First, figure out if it's us or a dependency.**

Look at the queue dashboard. Is the processed rate flat, or did it drop to zero?

- **Dropped to zero:** workers are probably dead or wedged. Check `kubectl get pods -l app=worker`. If they're crashlooping, look at the logs before you restart anything. Restarting a crashloop just hides the reason.
- **Still processing, just slow:** usually a downstream thing. Check whether Postgres is pegged or a third-party API (Stripe, SendGrid) is timing out. Their status pages are bookmarked in the team folder.

**Things that usually fix it:**

1. Scale workers up: `kubectl scale deploy/worker --replicas=12` (normal is 4). Don't go past 16 or you'll starve the DB of connections. We learned that one the hard way.
2. If one job type is hogging everything (it's almost always `report_export`), pause it: `./bin/queue pause report_export`. Customers can wait an hour for a CSV. They can't wait on password resets.
3. If there's a poison job that keeps failing and retrying, find it in the dead-letter view and kill it. Write down the job ID so someone can look at it later.

**Don't:**
- Flush the queue. Ever. Not even if it's "just the low priority stuff."
- Restart Redis. You will lose things.

**After:** scale back down once depth is under 500, unpause anything you paused, and drop a short note in #incidents saying what happened and what you did. It doesn't need to be a full writeup unless it lasted over an hour or customers noticed.

If you're stuck after 20 min, page whoever's secondary. Nobody's going to be annoyed.

Deploys at our company follow a continuous delivery model built on our main branch. Once your pull request has been approved by at least one reviewer and all CI checks pass (unit tests, integration tests, linting, and security scans), you can merge it into `main`, which automatically triggers a build and deploys the change to our staging environment within about ten minutes. Take the time to verify your change in staging, since this is where you'll catch issues that didn't surface in tests, and keep an eye on the #deploys Slack channel, where the pipeline posts status updates. Production deploys go out on a scheduled train several times a day, bundling everything that has landed in staging; if you need to ship urgently outside the train, you can request a hotfix deploy from the on-call engineer. Every production release is rolled out gradually (starting with a small percentage of traffic) and monitored against our error-rate and latency dashboards, with automatic rollback if key metrics regress. If something goes wrong after your change ships, don't panic: post in #deploys, loop in on-call, and remember that a quick rollback is always preferable to a rushed fix-forward. *(Note: adjust the specifics, such as channel names, timing, approval requirements, and rollout percentages, to match your team's actual pipeline.)*

I went to Pittsburgh for a friend's wedding expecting a tired old steel town, and I left kind of in love with it. Nobody told me how dramatic the geography is. The city is wedged between rivers and steep hills, so you keep turning a corner and suddenly there's a skyline view or a set of public stairs climbing up a hillside between houses. Riding the Duquesne Incline up Mount Washington at dusk was easily the best twenty minutes of the trip, and it cost less than a coffee.

The neighborhoods surprised me too. Each one feels like its own little town, with bakeries, dive bars, and people who will absolutely stop and give you directions plus their opinion on where to get pierogies. I went in thinking I'd fill a free afternoon and ended up wishing I'd stayed an extra three days. If it's not on your list, it probably should be.

I think a big part of it is that streaming made music feel weightless. You have access to basically everything ever recorded, but it's all just tiles on a screen you scroll past. A record pushes back against that. You have to pick one, pull it out of the sleeve, set it on the platter, and flip it halfway through. That little bit of effort makes you actually listen to an album front to back instead of skipping around, and a lot of people (myself included) missed that without realizing it.

There's also the ownership side. When a song can vanish from your streaming library overnight because of some licensing dispute, having a physical copy you can hold, with big cover art and liner notes, feels meaningful. Whether it "sounds better" is endlessly debatable, but I don't think sound quality is really what's driving the revival. It's the ritual and the tangibility.

I think the answer depends a lot on what you mean by "happen." Robotaxis are already running without safety drivers in a handful of cities, and I'd bet that footprint expands a lot over the next decade, especially in warm, well-mapped metro areas with good roads. But that's a long way from the version most people picture, where you can buy a car that drives itself anywhere, in any weather, while you nap in the back. Snow, rural roads with faded lines, construction zones, and the endless weird edge cases are still really hard, and the liability and regulatory questions move slower than the tech does.

So my guess is that in ten years autonomous ride-hailing and freight on certain highway corridors will be normal and kind of boring, while personally owned cars will mostly have very good driver assistance rather than true self-driving. It'll feel less like a revolution and more like one of those things that quietly spread city by city until one day you realize you haven't thought about it in a while.

This hit close to home. I spent six years on a med-surg floor before I realized the exhaustion I felt wasn't something a weekend off could fix. It's the constant short-staffing, the charting that eats your breaks, and the guilt of feeling like you never gave a patient enough time. People outside the profession don't always get that burnout isn't about being weak or not loving the job. Often it's because you care so much and the system keeps asking for more than any one person can give.

What helped me was finally talking honestly with coworkers and realizing I wasn't alone, then setting harder boundaries around extra shifts. I also eventually moved to a unit with better ratios. That isn't possible for everyone, I know. If you're in the thick of it right now, please be gentle with yourself and reach out to someone, whether that's a colleague, a therapist, or your employee assistance program. You deserve care too.

I've been on both sides of this and honestly I think whiteboard puzzles mostly test whether you've ground through enough leetcode in the last month. The best engineer I ever hired totally froze on a graph traversal question, and we almost passed on her. What saved it was a coworker who said "let's just have her walk us through something she built" and she spent 40 minutes explaining a caching layer she'd designed, tradeoffs and all. Learned more from that than from any puzzle.

That said I don't think they're totally useless. If someone can't write a loop or reason about why their solution is slow, that's worth knowing. I just think the bar should be "can you code and think out loud," not "can you invent Dijkstra's on the spot while three people stare at you."

Bought a 2017 Civic from a private seller last spring and honestly it went better than I expected, mostly because I didn't trust my own judgment. I paid a local independent mechanic about $120 for a pre-purchase inspection and he found a slow oil leak from the valve cover gasket and brake pads that were nearly gone. Neither was a dealbreaker, but I used his written estimate to knock $600 off the asking price, so the inspection more than paid for itself.

My biggest advice: run the VIN through a history report, ask for maintenance records, and don't let anyone rush you. The seller was fine waiting a day for the inspection. The one before him who insisted "someone else is coming at 5" was the car I'm glad I walked away from.
