**Two Days at the Coast and I Still Have Sand in My Car**

So we finally did it. After talking about it since basically March, Jen and I packed up the car Friday after work and drove out to the coast. We got there way later than planned because of an accident on the highway, and I'm pretty sure we ate gas station taquitos for dinner. No regrets.

Saturday morning was cold. Like, actually cold. I don't know why I keep forgetting that the ocean in November isn't the ocean in July. I brought one hoodie. One. Jen let me borrow her flannel, which was about two sizes too small, and I wore it all day anyway.

We walked the beach for probably three hours. Found a bunch of sand dollars, most of them broken, and one perfect one that I wrapped in a napkin and then promptly sat on in the car. So that's gone.

The best part was this tiny chowder place near the pier. No sign, just a chalkboard out front that said OPEN in letters that were mostly smudged. The guy behind the counter talked to us for twenty minutes about his dog. The chowder was honestly the best I've ever had, and I'm not just saying that because I was freezing.

Sunday we slept in, got coffee, watched the waves for a while, and drove home slow.

I don't know. Sometimes you just need to stand somewhere loud and windy and feel small for a bit. Already want to go back.

I almost canceled my first therapy appointment three times. The first time, I told myself I was too busy. The second time, I convinced myself my problems weren't serious enough to take up someone's hour. The third time, I just sat in my car outside the building, staring at the door and wondering what I would even say.

I went in anyway. I'm still a little surprised by that.

The office was smaller than I expected, with a plant in the corner that looked like it was thriving more than I was. My therapist asked me why I was there, and I gave her the polished version: stress at work, trouble sleeping, nothing dramatic. She nodded and waited. That silence did something to me. Within ten minutes I was talking about things I hadn't said out loud in years, and I was crying in front of a stranger, which I had promised myself I would not do.

Here's what I didn't expect. Nobody fixed me that day. There was no breakthrough moment, no perfect insight that rearranged my life. I mostly just felt tired when I walked out. But I also felt lighter, like I had set down a bag I didn't realize I'd been carrying.

I've been going for six weeks now. Some sessions feel productive and some feel like I'm going in circles. I'm learning that both are part of it.

If you've been thinking about starting, this is your sign. You don't need a crisis to deserve help. Sometimes it's enough to be tired of carrying things alone.

**The 7:42 and Me**

Every weekday morning, I stand on Platform 2 with a coffee that's slightly too hot and a book I probably won't read. The 7:42 arrives, usually on time, sometimes not, and I've made peace with both outcomes.

I didn't always love this commute. When I first started taking the train, I treated it as dead time, forty minutes to be endured between home and work. I'd scroll through my phone, check emails I couldn't answer yet, and arrive at the office already frazzled.

Somewhere along the way, that changed. Maybe it was the morning the fog lay so thick over the river that the whole valley looked like it was holding its breath. Maybe it was the older gentleman who sits three rows ahead and solves the crossword in pen, never once hesitating. I started paying attention.

Now the train feels like a small, moving room that belongs to no one and everyone. There's the student who sleeps against the window, the nurse heading home from a night shift, the couple who share one pair of earbuds. We never speak, but we know each other in a quiet way. When someone is missing for a week, I notice.

The commute has become my buffer, a space between who I am at home and who I need to be at work. I watch the fields turn from green to gold to frost-white as the seasons pass. I think. Sometimes I don't think at all.

Tomorrow the 7:42 will come again. I'll be there, coffee in hand, ready.

# The Week Portugal Tried to Break Me

I'd been planning this trip for eleven months. Spreadsheets. Color-coded itineraries. A packing list so thorough it had its own packing list. Lisbon, then the Algarve, then a few lazy days in Porto drinking wine I couldn't pronounce.

The universe, it turns out, does not care about spreadsheets.

It started at the airport, where my suitcase decided to take its own holiday, apparently to Frankfurt. I arrived in Lisbon with the clothes I was wearing and a phone charger. The airline assured me it would arrive "within forty-eight hours." It arrived on day six.

Then came the heatwave. Thirty-nine degrees, in a borrowed shirt from a souvenir shop that said *I ♥ SARDINES* in glittery letters. I wore it for three days. I now have a complicated relationship with sardines.

In the Algarve, I got food poisoning from a seafood stew I'd been told was "the best on the coast." Maybe it was. I'll never know, because I spent the next thirty-six hours becoming intimately familiar with my rental's bathroom tiles. They were lovely tiles, at least. Hand-painted.

By Porto, I'd given up on the itinerary entirely. And that's when something strange happened. I sat by the river with no plan, ate bread and cheese, and watched the light turn gold over the rooftops. A stranger shared his wine with me. We talked for hours.

It was the best evening of the whole trip.

I still make spreadsheets. But now I leave a column blank.

# Should Extracurricular Activities Be Mandatory?

Every afternoon when the final bell rings, students scatter in different directions. Some head to soccer practice, rehearsals, or robotics club, while others go straight home. Many educators argue that schools should require every student to join at least one extracurricular activity. Although the idea sounds appealing, making extracurricular activities mandatory would do more harm than good.

First, students already have heavy workloads. Between classes, homework, and studying for tests, many teenagers feel overwhelmed. According to surveys by the American Psychological Association, teens report stress levels during the school year that rival those of adults. Adding another required commitment would leave less time for rest, family, and simply being young. An activity meant to enrich students' lives could easily become one more source of pressure.

Second, many students have responsibilities outside of school that a mandate would ignore. Some work part-time jobs to help support their families. Others care for younger siblings while their parents work. For these students, staying after school is not a matter of preference but of possibility. A mandatory policy would unfairly punish them for circumstances beyond their control.

Third, forcing participation defeats the purpose of extracurricular activities. These activities are valuable precisely because students choose them out of genuine interest. A student who loves painting will put real effort into art club, but a student forced to join the chess club just to meet a requirement will likely show up, watch the clock, and leave. Required enthusiasm is not enthusiasm at all.

Supporters of mandatory activities argue that they help students build teamwork, leadership, and friendships. These benefits are real. However, schools can encourage participation without requiring it. They can hold activity fairs, offer a wider variety of clubs, provide transportation, and reduce fees so that every student has the opportunity to join.

In conclusion, extracurricular activities are a wonderful part of school life, but they should remain a choice. Respecting students' time, responsibilities, and interests will lead to more meaningful participation than any requirement ever could. The best way to get students involved is to invite them, not force them.

# The Case for Car-Free Cities

For more than a century, the automobile has shaped how cities are built. Wide roads, sprawling parking lots, and congested highways have become normal parts of urban life. However, as cities face growing problems with pollution, traffic, and public health, it is time to rethink this model. Cities should move toward becoming car-free because doing so would improve the environment, make residents healthier, and create more livable communities.

First, car-free cities would greatly reduce pollution. Transportation is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, and private cars produce much of it. Exhaust fumes also contain harmful pollutants that worsen air quality and contribute to asthma and other respiratory illnesses. Cities that have limited car use, such as Oslo and parts of Paris, have seen measurable drops in air pollution. Replacing cars with public transit, bicycles, and walking would help cities fight climate change and protect the air their residents breathe.

Second, removing cars would encourage healthier lifestyles. When people walk or cycle to school, work, or shops, they build physical activity into their daily routines. This can lower rates of obesity, heart disease, and stress. Car-free streets are also safer. Traffic accidents kill and injure millions of people worldwide every year, and pedestrians and cyclists are especially vulnerable. Fewer cars mean fewer collisions and safer streets for children and the elderly.

Finally, car-free cities would be more pleasant places to live. Roads and parking take up enormous amounts of urban space. Without cars, that land could become parks, playgrounds, outdoor cafés, and housing. Streets would be quieter, and neighbors would be more likely to meet and interact, which strengthens community bonds.

Critics argue that cars are necessary for convenience, deliveries, and people with disabilities. These concerns are valid, but they can be addressed. Exceptions can be made for emergency vehicles, delivery vans, and accessible transport, while improved public transit can make travel easy for everyone.

In conclusion, car-free cities offer a cleaner, healthier, and more welcoming future. By reducing our dependence on cars, we can build cities designed for people rather than vehicles. It is a change worth making.

**Why Community Service Should Be Required for High School Graduation**

Every year, millions of students graduate from high school with strong grades and impressive test scores, yet many have never spent an afternoon helping someone in need. Schools teach students how to solve equations and analyze literature, but they often neglect one of the most important lessons of all: how to be an active, caring member of a community. For this reason, high schools should require students to complete community service before graduating.

First, community service teaches skills that classrooms cannot. When students volunteer at a food bank, tutor younger children, or help clean up a local park, they learn teamwork, responsibility, and communication. These are the same skills employers and colleges look for. A student who has organized a clothing drive has practiced leadership in a way that no textbook can provide. Service turns abstract lessons into real-world experience.

Second, community service builds empathy and broadens perspective. Many teenagers live in a bubble, surrounded by people who share their background and circumstances. Volunteering at a homeless shelter or a nursing home exposes them to people whose lives are very different from their own. This experience helps students understand social problems not as distant headlines but as real challenges faced by real people. Students who develop empathy are more likely to become thoughtful citizens and compassionate adults.

Critics argue that required service is a contradiction, because true volunteering should be voluntary. They worry that forcing students to serve will make them resentful. However, schools already require many things students might not choose on their own, such as physical education and foreign languages, because these subjects have lasting value. Furthermore, studies show that students who are introduced to service often continue volunteering long after the requirement ends. Sometimes people need a push to discover something meaningful.

Finally, communities themselves benefit. Schools, libraries, shelters, and environmental groups often struggle with limited staff and funding. Thousands of student volunteers can make a significant difference in the services these organizations provide.

Community service gives students valuable skills, deeper understanding, and a sense of purpose, while strengthening the communities around them. Requiring it is not a burden. It is an investment in better citizens and a better society.

**Should Extracurricular Activities Be Graded?**

Extracurricular activities such as sports teams, drama clubs, debate societies, and volunteer groups are an important part of school life. Some educators argue that students should receive grades for these activities to reward effort and encourage participation. However, grading extracurricular activities would do more harm than good, because it would destroy the voluntary spirit that makes them valuable, add unnecessary pressure, and create unfair comparisons between students.

First, the main purpose of extracurricular activities is to let students explore their interests freely. A student joins the chess club because she loves chess, not because she needs a good mark. Once a grade is attached, the activity becomes another obligation. Psychologists call this the "overjustification effect": when people are rewarded externally for something they already enjoy, their natural motivation often decreases. Grading would turn passion into homework.

Second, students already face heavy academic pressure. Tests, assignments, and exams fill their schedules and cause stress. Extracurricular activities are one of the few places where young people can relax, make mistakes, and grow without fear of failure. If a missed goal in a football match or a forgotten line in a school play could lower a student's average, many would avoid trying new things altogether. Instead of building confidence, grading would build anxiety.

Third, grading extracurriculars would be deeply unfair. How can a teacher fairly compare a talented violinist with a beginner who is learning bravely? Should a student be punished for lacking natural athletic ability? Furthermore, not all students have equal access to these activities. Some must work part-time jobs or care for younger siblings after school. Grading participation would disadvantage these students for circumstances beyond their control.

Supporters of grading claim it would make students take activities more seriously. Yet there are better ways to recognize commitment, such as certificates, awards, or written feedback in a portfolio. These methods celebrate achievement without turning hobbies into competitions.

In conclusion, extracurricular activities should remain ungraded. Their true value lies in freedom, enjoyment, and personal growth. Schools should encourage participation through support and recognition, not through marks. Let students play, create, and explore simply because they want to.

**Should Students Choose Their Own Classes?**

Every year, students across the country sit in classrooms wondering why they have to learn a subject they will never use. This frustration raises an important question: should students be allowed to choose their own classes? Students should have significant freedom to select their courses, but that freedom should work within a framework of core requirements.

The strongest argument for student choice is motivation. People work harder when they care about what they are doing. A student who loves biology will likely pour more effort into an advanced science course than into a required class that feels pointless to them. When students pick their own paths, they take ownership of their education. That ownership builds responsibility and independence, skills they will need in college and in their careers.

Choice also helps students discover who they are. High school is a time to explore interests, and elective courses such as computer programming, creative writing, or music theory can spark passions that shape a person's future. A rigid schedule leaves little room for that kind of discovery.

However, complete freedom would be a mistake. Teenagers do not always know what they will need later in life. A student who avoids math might later discover that their dream career requires it. Core subjects like English, mathematics, science, and history give everyone a foundation of knowledge and critical thinking that a functioning society depends on. Without requirements, some students might choose only easy classes and graduate unprepared.

The best solution is balance. Schools should require a set of essential courses while giving students wide choice in electives and in how they meet certain requirements. This approach respects students' interests while ensuring they gain the skills they need.

In the end, education works best when students are partners in their own learning. Giving them a meaningful voice in their schedules, guided by thoughtful requirements, prepares them both to succeed and to enjoy the journey.

**Learning from Home: A Choice Worth Offering**

For most of the history of education, learning meant sitting in a classroom. Today, technology makes it possible for students to attend classes from their kitchen tables. While online learning is not perfect for everyone, students should be allowed to take classes online from home because it offers flexibility, expands opportunities, and prepares them for the modern world.

First, online classes give students flexibility that traditional schools cannot. Some students have health problems, family responsibilities, or part-time jobs that make a fixed school schedule difficult. Others live far from school and spend hours commuting each day. Online learning allows these students to keep up with their education without sacrificing other important parts of their lives. For a student recovering from an illness, for example, an online option could mean the difference between falling behind and graduating on time.

Second, online learning expands access to courses. A small rural school may not offer advanced classes like computer science, Mandarin, or AP Physics. Through online programs, students anywhere can study subjects their local school cannot provide. This helps level the playing field between students in wealthy districts and those in communities with fewer resources.

Finally, learning online builds skills students will need later in life. Many colleges offer online courses, and more and more jobs involve remote work. Students who learn to manage their time, communicate through digital tools, and stay motivated without constant supervision are developing valuable independence.

Critics argue that online students miss out on social interaction and may struggle without a teacher present. These concerns are real, which is why online learning should be a choice rather than a requirement. Students who thrive in person can stay in the classroom, while those who benefit from learning at home can do so.

In the end, education should fit the needs of each student. Allowing online classes from home gives students the freedom to learn in the way that works best for them.

The Best Age to Start a Career

People love to ask teenagers what they want to be when they grow up, as if there's a deadline coming. When I was twelve I wanted to be a marine biologist. At fifteen it was architecture. Now I honestly don't know, and I've started to think that's fine. If you ask me, there isn't one perfect age to start a career, but the mid-twenties is probably closer to right than eighteen.

My uncle is a good example of why. He went straight into an electrician apprenticeship after high school because his dad told him it was the smart move. It was, financially. He was making decent money at twenty while his friends were taking out loans. But by thirty he was miserable. He told me once that he never actually chose the job; it just happened to him. He eventually went back to school for nursing and says he's happier now, even though he started over with a lot less money and a lot more stress.

On the other hand, my neighbor knew she wanted to be a vet since she was about six. She volunteered at animal shelters all through high school and went right into pre-vet. For her, waiting would have been a waste of time.

So I guess the real answer depends on whether you actually know yourself yet. Most eighteen-year-olds don't. I don't. A few years of trying different jobs, taking classes, or even just working somewhere boring can teach you what you can't stand, which is useful information.

The problem is that waiting costs money, and not everyone can afford to wander around figuring things out. That's a real issue. But if you have the option, I think it's better to start a little late on the right path than early on the wrong one. My uncle would probably agree.

There's a shoebox in my closet that has moved with me through five apartments. It's a Nike box, size ten, though I have never owned a pair of shoes that came in it. I think it belonged to my brother. Inside are letters, maybe sixty of them, held together in loose bundles by rubber bands that have mostly gone brittle and snapped.

I don't read them often. Once a year, maybe, usually when I'm supposed to be packing or cleaning and need an excuse to sit on the floor for an hour. There's a run of letters from my grandmother, written on onionskin paper because she believed airmail stationery was the only proper kind, even for a letter traveling forty miles. There are three from a girl I knew the summer I was seventeen, and those are embarrassing in a way that's almost pleasant now. There's one from my father, the only one he ever wrote me, sent during my first semester of college. It's mostly about the car insurance.

I've wondered why I keep them. They don't contain much information. My grandmother wrote about the weather and the neighbors and what she'd made for dinner. Nobody's going to learn anything from them. If the box disappeared tomorrow, my life would go on exactly as before.

But I think that's sort of the point. A letter is proof that someone sat down, on a specific afternoon, and thought about you long enough to fill a page. My grandmother's handwriting got shakier over the years, and you can watch it happen if you read them in order. Near the end she started double-checking her spelling with little corrections above the line. That isn't in any photograph of her. It's only there.

And my father's letter, the one about car insurance. He signs it "Love, Dad," which he never said out loud, not once that I can remember. I used to think the letter was a disappointment. Now I think he just didn't know what else to put in the middle.

Texts and emails don't do this, or I haven't found a way to make them. They sit on a server somewhere and I could search them in two seconds, which somehow makes them weigh less. You can't find a coffee ring on an email, or a word crossed out three times.

So the box stays. I'll probably move it again in a few years, tape the lid shut, write LETTERS on the side in marker, and carry it myself so the movers don't drop it.

**The Quiet Architecture of Lists**

I have kept lists for as long as I can remember. Grocery lists on the backs of envelopes, reading lists in the margins of notebooks, lists of things to say before a difficult conversation, lists of things I wish I had said after. If someone were to gather every list I have ever written, they would have a stranger and truer biography than any diary could offer.

The obvious purpose of a list is practical. It remembers so that I do not have to. Milk, stamps, call the dentist. The mind, relieved of its clerical duties, is free to wander. But I have come to suspect that the practical purpose is only the surface of the habit, and that something more interesting lies beneath it.

A list is an act of ordering. When I sit down to write one, I am taking the shapeless fog of obligation and desire that hangs over a day and pressing it into a column. The fog does not disappear, but it acquires edges. Ten tasks written down are almost always less frightening than ten tasks circling unspoken in the head. In this sense, the list is a small argument against chaos, a way of insisting that the world, or at least my portion of it, can be understood.

There is also the pleasure of the line drawn through a finished item. It is a minor pleasure, almost embarrassing to admit, yet it is real. I have occasionally caught myself adding a task I had already completed simply to have the satisfaction of crossing it out. This tells me that lists are not only about what must be done but about the need to feel that something has been done, that the day was not lost.

Yet lists can deceive. They flatten everything to the same weight. "Buy batteries" sits beside "forgive my brother," each given a single line, a single bullet point. The list cannot tell me which matters more. It records but does not judge, and I must remember to supply the judgment myself.

Perhaps the most revealing lists are the ones never finished: the long-abandoned inventories of places to visit, skills to learn, letters to write. They are monuments to hope rather than records of achievement. I keep them anyway. A list, after all, is a modest form of faith, the belief that there will be a tomorrow in which these things might still be done.

# The Moving Theatre

There is no better seat for watching humanity than the one beside a rain-streaked bus window. On public transport we are thrown together with strangers in a way that daily life rarely allows. For twenty minutes we share air, space, and a destination we may not have in common. Few of us notice that we are, at the same time, an audience and a cast.

Consider the morning train. It has its own quiet choreography: the businessman folding his newspaper into precise quarters, the student mouthing vocabulary words under her breath, the nurse whose eyes close the moment she sits, as if her body has been waiting all night for permission. None of them perform for anyone, and that is what makes them worth watching. They are unguarded and briefly themselves, unaware that a stranger is quietly composing their biographies.

That is the private game of the observant commuter. We invent lives. The elderly man clutching a bouquet must be visiting his wife, or perhaps an old flame he has finally gathered the courage to call. The teenager staring hard at his phone has just received news, good or terrible, and we will never know which. These fictions say as much about us as about them. We project our own hopes and anxieties onto faces that cannot correct us.

Yet people-watching on a bus is not merely voyeurism. It is a kind of moral education. When a young mother struggles with a pram and three passengers rise at once to help, we witness ordinary kindness without ceremony. When someone is rude to the driver, we feel a collective wince, a silent agreement about how people ought to behave. Public transport reminds us that we belong to a society, not just to a household or an office.

There is humility in it too. Sitting among strangers, we realise how small our own preoccupations are. The deadline that consumed our morning shrinks beside the evident grief of the woman across the aisle, or the giddy joy of a couple who cannot stop laughing at a private joke. Everyone carries a full and complicated life, and for a moment we glimpse the sheer number of them.

Then the doors open, the stories scatter onto the platform, and the characters vanish into the city. We step off too, perhaps unaware that someone, somewhere in the carriage, was watching us and wondering who we might be.

**The Vanishing Hand**

I found my grandmother's recipe cards last winter, tucked into a tin that once held butter cookies. The recipes themselves were unremarkable: pound cake, pickled beets, a casserole involving canned soup. The handwriting stopped me. Her loops leaned rightward as if hurrying toward the next ingredient. Her capital *T* had a flourish she must have practiced as a girl. On one card a grease stain had blurred the word "nutmeg," and I could almost see her kitchen, her elbow knocking the bottle, her shrug. No typed document could have carried that much of her.

Handwriting is fading, and most of us barely notice. Schools have trimmed cursive from their curricula. Signatures have shrunk into scribbles on touchscreens. Many adults now go weeks without writing anything longer than a grocery list. The case for letting it go is reasonable. Typing is faster, more legible, easier to search and share. Why grieve a tool when better tools exist?

But handwriting was never only a tool. It was a trace of the body. Every written word carried the pressure of a particular wrist, the tremor of a particular mood. A love letter written in haste looked different from one composed slowly over an evening, and the recipient could read both the words and the weather behind them. Typed text flattens that. A font belongs to everyone, so it belongs to no one.

There is also something about the pace of the pen. Writing by hand is slow enough that thought must keep up with it, or rather, that the hand must wait for thought. Researchers have suggested that students who take notes by hand remember more, perhaps because they cannot transcribe everything and must decide what matters. I suspect the same is true outside the classroom. When I journal on paper, I write less, and I mean more of it.

I don't want to romanticize the past. Penmanship was once drilled with rulers and reprimands, and left-handed children were forced to write against their nature. Clear typed text has opened doors for people whose hands don't cooperate. Progress has real gifts.

Still, I worry about what we lose when a skill becomes optional and then obsolete. Our descendants may inherit our digital archives, vast and searchable, and find nothing in them that looks like us. No hurried slant, no blotted nutmeg.

So I've started writing letters again, badly at first. My hand cramps. My lines wander. But each envelope I send carries a small, imperfect proof that someone was here.

**In Praise of Doing Nothing**

There is a particular afternoon I remember from childhood. I lay on the grass behind my grandmother's house and watched clouds for what felt like hours. Nobody asked me to do anything. I had no goal, no plan, no sense that time was being spent or wasted. I simply existed, and the sky moved above me. I have spent much of my adult life trying, without much luck, to return to that afternoon.

We live in a culture that treats idleness as a kind of moral failure. To be busy is to be important. To be idle is to be lazy, unmotivated, or somehow behind. When someone asks how we are, we often answer "busy" with a certain pride, as if exhaustion were proof of a life well lived. Even our leisure has become productive. We read books to improve ourselves, exercise to optimize our bodies, and take vacations that require detailed itineraries. Rest itself has become another task to complete.

Yet some of the most meaningful moments of my life have come from doing nothing at all. Ideas I struggled with for weeks have arrived, fully formed, while I stared out a train window. Old grief has softened during long walks with no destination. Conversations with friends, aimless and wandering, have taught me more about them than any planned activity ever could. The mind, it seems, needs empty space in order to work. It needs room to drift, to make strange connections, to notice what it would otherwise ignore.

Bertrand Russell once argued that a great deal of harm is done in the world by the belief that work is virtuous. I think he was onto something. When we never pause, we lose the chance to ask whether our efforts are pointed in the right direction. We keep running without checking the map. Idleness offers that check. It lets us step back and see our lives from a little distance.

Of course, idleness is a privilege. Many people cannot afford to stop, and romanticizing rest can ring hollow to someone working two jobs. But perhaps that is exactly why it matters. A society that valued idleness might arrange itself so that more people could enjoy it.

I am trying, slowly, to relearn the art of doing nothing. Some days I sit on a bench and resist the urge to reach for my phone. It is harder than it sounds. But occasionally, for a moment, the clouds move, and I am a child again on the grass.

Dear Kenji,

Thank you so much for your last letter and the photos of the cherry blossoms in Kyoto. They were beautiful! You asked me to tell you about where I live, so here it goes.

My town is called Millbrook, and it sits in a green valley surrounded by rolling hills. About twelve thousand people live here, so it's small enough that you often bump into someone you know at the grocery store. A slow, winding river runs right through the middle of town, and in summer, families gather on its banks for picnics and fishing.

The heart of Millbrook is Main Street, lined with old brick buildings that are over a hundred years old. My favorite spot is a tiny bakery called Rosie's, where they make cinnamon rolls the size of your hand. Every Saturday morning, there's a farmers' market in the town square, with fresh vegetables, honey, and homemade jam.

Autumn is the best season here. The maple trees turn brilliant shades of red and orange, and the whole town celebrates with a harvest festival featuring hayrides, apple cider, and a pumpkin-carving contest. Winters are cold and snowy, which means sledding on Miller's Hill!

It's not an exciting city like Tokyo, but it feels like home. I think you would enjoy the quiet pace and friendly faces.

What is your neighborhood like? I'd love to hear more about your daily life.

Your friend,
Sam

The book was about carp. Teddy hadn't wanted a book about carp, but the one on sharks was out again, had been out since September, and Mrs. Oyelaran at the desk said carp were basically sharks if you squinted. She said that kind of thing a lot.

He read it on the bus home, or held it open anyway, while Kyle Brandt two seats up tried to flick a sunflower seed into Jenna Moss's hood. Page 41 had a diagram of a carp's insides that looked like a bag of groceries. Page 42 had the envelope.

It was the thin blue kind his grandmother used for writing to her sister in Gdańsk, with red and blue stripes along the edge. It wasn't sealed. Somebody had used it as a bookmark and forgotten, he figured, except there was a letter inside, two pages folded in thirds, and the handwriting went all the way to the edges like whoever wrote it was afraid of running out of room.

*Dear R.*, it started. *I know you said not to write here.*

Elias Marrow aged his paper in tea the color of river silt, then baked it in the oven his landlady believed he used for bread. He had not baked bread in eleven years. The kitchen smelled permanently of scorched linen and iron gall ink, and the neighbors had stopped asking.

Tonight's commission lay pinned beneath four brass weights: a coastline that did not exist. A Flemish collector wanted a lost Ortelius variant, the kind of thing rumored in auction catalogues and never actually seen. He had paid half in advance. Elias had spent three weeks inventing a peninsula south of Patagonia, a crooked thumb of land studded with Latin names, a sea monster coiled in the margin with its tail curling into the compass rose.

The trick, he had learned long ago, was not to copy. Copies were caught. The trick was to make mistakes the old cartographers would have made, to believe what they believed. He drew rivers running the wrong way. He placed a kingdom of giants where the sailors' gossip said it should be. He let his hand tremble slightly on the coast, the way a man's hand trembles when he is guessing.

He dipped the pen and began the final inscription in the cartouche: *Terra Nondum Cognita*. Land not yet known.

The ink took to the paper oddly. It spread, then drew back, as if the sheet were breathing. Elias frowned and set the pen down.

Along the edge of his invented peninsula, in a hand he did not recognize, a small word had appeared that he was certain he had not written. It was tidy and brown, as if it had been there for four hundred years.

*Here.*

Outside, the rain stopped all at once. Somewhere below his window, faint and impossible in a city two hundred miles from any coast, he heard the sound of surf.

The clock on the table ticked louder than it had any right to.

Mira Okafor had played four hundred and twelve tournament games, and she had never once noticed the sound of a chess clock until this afternoon, in the back room of the Hotel Ambassador, with the air conditioning broken and a man named Viktor Desh breathing through his mouth across the board from her. Each tick seemed to land somewhere behind her left eye.

She was fifteen. Desh was fifty-three and had been a grandmaster since before her parents met. He had shaken her hand at the start without looking at her face, the way you might shake hands with a waiter.

Now he was thinking. He had been thinking for twenty-two minutes.

Mira knew why. Eleven moves ago she had given up her knight for two pawns and nothing else, nothing visible, and Desh had taken it with a small, private smile, as if he'd found a coin on the sidewalk. Only now, with his king pinned against the edge of the board and her rook sliding into the open file, was he beginning to understand that the knight had never been a gift. It had been a door, and he had walked through it.

She did not look at him. Her coach, Mr. Albescu, had told her years ago that you never look at your opponent when you're winning. *Let them suffer privately,* he'd said. *It's the only kindness you can offer.*

So she looked at her hands instead. There was a smear of blue ink on her thumb from the scoresheet. There was a scab on her knuckle from the fence behind her apartment building. Ordinary hands. Nothing in them that explained anything.

Desh reached out, hesitated, and pulled his hand back.

Somewhere behind her, a spectator coughed. The clock ticked. And Mira realized, with a cold drop in her stomach, that she wasn't sure she wanted to win.

Harold Pemberton had been dead for eleven years, and in all that time he had frightened exactly one person, and that was only because she'd tripped over the cat.

He'd taken credit for it anyway. A ghost had to have something.

The problem, as far as Harold could tell, was that nobody had ever explained the rules. One moment he'd been reaching for the top shelf of the pantry, a stepladder wobbling beneath him, and the next he'd been standing in the same pantry looking down at himself with the distinct feeling that he had made a terrible mistake regarding the stepladder. There had been no orientation. No pamphlet. No elderly spirit in a powdered wig to take him aside and say, *Now then, lad, here's how you rattle a chain.*

He didn't even have a chain. He'd checked.

What he had was a cardigan, the brown one with the leather elbow patches, and a pair of reading glasses perpetually pushed up on his forehead, because that was where they'd been when he died. He had tried moaning. It came out as a sort of apologetic throat-clearing, like a man trying to get a waiter's attention. He had tried flickering the lights, and managed it once, but the new family had simply called an electrician, who replaced a fuse and charged them ninety pounds. Harold had felt so guilty about the ninety pounds that he'd stopped trying the lights altogether.

The new family were called the Okonkwos, and they had lived in his house for four months. There was a mother, a father, a teenage son who wore headphones even in the shower, and a girl of about seven named Ada, who Harold suspected could see him.

He suspected this because, on Tuesday morning, she had looked straight at him over her cereal and said, "You're standing in the toaster."

**Flooding Closes Main Road as Heavy Rain Swamps Low-Lying Areas**

A stretch of Riverside Road remained closed Tuesday afternoon after overnight downpours sent floodwater across the route, forcing commuters onto lengthy detours and prompting warnings from local officials.

The closure runs between the Mill Lane junction and the Hartwell Bridge roundabout, where water reached depths of more than two feet in places. County highway crews set up barriers shortly after 5 a.m., and police turned back several motorists who attempted to drive through.

"We understand it's frustrating, but this water is deeper and faster than it looks," said Sgt. Dana Whitfield of the county police. "It only takes a few inches of moving water to sweep a car off the road. Please don't risk it."

More than three inches of rain fell in less than 12 hours, according to the regional weather service, overwhelming drainage systems and pushing the nearby Callow Brook over its banks.

Traffic was diverted through Station Street and Old Farm Road, adding up to 20 minutes to journeys during the morning rush. Two school bus routes were also rerouted, and Riverside Primary School opened an hour late.

Residents along the road reported water in gardens and garages, though no homes were believed to have been flooded internally. Sandbags were made available at the community center on Elm Street.

Highway officials said the road would stay closed until the water recedes and crews can inspect the surface for damage. Further showers are forecast for Wednesday, and a flood watch remains in effect through Thursday morning.

**Library's new seed scheme lets gardeners borrow, grow and give back**

Gardeners in Ashworth can now pick up seeds alongside their paperbacks, after the town library launched a free seed lending scheme this week.

The idea is simple. Members take a packet or two of seeds, grow them at home, then return some of the seeds from their own plants at the end of the season so someone else can have a go next year.

Librarian Carol Mitchell said the scheme started after a chat with a regular. "One of our members kept bringing in bags of runner bean seeds she'd saved and asking if anyone wanted them," she said. "We thought, why not make it official?"

The collection is kept in an old wooden card catalogue near the front desk, which Carol rescued from storage. Drawers are labelled by type: beans, tomatoes, herbs, flowers and "odds and ends."

About 40 varieties are on offer so far, most donated by the Ashworth Allotment Society. They include a purple-podded pea that society chairman Ron Hale says his family has grown since the 1950s.

"It'd be a shame for it to die out with me," he said. "Better it goes round the town."

Nobody will be fined if their crop fails. "Slugs happen," Carol said. "Just come back and try again."

Seeds are available to anyone with a library card. The library is also holding a free seed-saving workshop on Saturday 28 November at 10.30am. Places are limited, so call ahead to book.

**Millbrook Plant to Close, Cutting 200 Jobs**

MILLBROOK — Harlan Precision Components will close its Route 9 manufacturing plant at the end of February, eliminating about 200 jobs. The plant has been one of the town's largest employers for more than four decades.

Company officials told workers Tuesday morning. In a written statement, Harlan cited "sustained declines in demand and rising operational costs." The statement said production will move to the company's facility in Tennessee.

"We recognize the profound impact this decision has on our employees, their families and the Millbrook community," the statement read. The company said affected workers will receive severance packages and job placement help. Some may be offered transfers.

Outside the plant gates, workers described shock and frustration.

"I've been here twenty-two years," said machinist Dale Kowalski, 54. "My father worked here before me. Nobody saw this coming, not this fast."

The plant opened in 1981. It makes metal fittings for the automotive and agricultural industries. At its peak in the late 1990s it employed nearly 600 people.

Mayor Linda Ortega called the news "a heavy blow" to the town. She said local officials are working with the county workforce development board to set up an employment resource center for displaced workers.

"These are skilled, dedicated people," Ortega said. "We are going to do everything we can to keep them working and keep them in Millbrook."

Nearby businesses also expect to feel the loss. Several restaurants and shops along Main Street depend on the plant's workers.

A job fair for affected employees is tentatively planned for January at the Millbrook Community Center.

Birdwatchers flocked to Riverside Park this week after a rare painted bunting was spotted near the duck pond on Monday morning. The small, vividly colored songbird is typically found in the southern United States and Mexico, making its appearance here a surprise to local experts.

Margaret Ellison, a retired schoolteacher who walks in the park daily, was the first to notice the bird. "I saw a flash of blue, red and green in the shrubs and thought I was imagining things," she said. "I've never seen anything like it in all my years coming here."

Ellison snapped a photo on her phone and shared it with the Riverside Audubon Society, which confirmed the sighting within hours. By Tuesday, dozens of enthusiasts had gathered along the walking paths with binoculars and long-lens cameras, hoping to catch a glimpse.

Dr. Samuel Ortiz, an ornithologist at the state university, said the bird was likely blown off course during its fall migration. "Strong winds from recent storms can push birds hundreds of miles from their usual routes," he explained. "It's uncommon, but it does happen."

Ortiz encouraged visitors to keep their distance and avoid using recorded bird calls, which can stress the animal. Park officials have placed temporary signs near the pond asking guests to stay on marked trails.

The bunting has remained in the area for three days, feeding on seeds near the eastern edge of the pond. Experts say it may continue its journey south at any time, so those hoping to see it are advised to visit soon.

# What to Do If Your Home Is Flooded

Flooding can cause serious damage to your home and risks to your health. Follow this guidance to stay safe and begin recovery.

## Stay Safe First

- **Do not return home** until local authorities say it is safe.
- **Avoid floodwater.** It may be contaminated with sewage, chemicals or debris, and can hide sharp objects or open drains.
- **Never walk or drive through moving water.** Just 15 cm (6 inches) of fast-flowing water can knock you off your feet.
- **Switch off electricity and gas** at the mains if it is safe to do so. Do not touch electrical equipment while standing in water.

## When You Return

- Wear waterproof boots, rubber gloves and a face mask.
- Check for structural damage before entering. If in doubt, stay out.
- Open windows and doors to ventilate the property.
- Have gas and electrical systems inspected by a qualified professional before use.

## Protect Your Health

- Wash hands thoroughly with soap and clean water after contact with floodwater.
- Throw away any food, including sealed items, that has touched floodwater.
- Boil tap water until your water supplier confirms it is safe.
- Seek medical advice if you develop vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or an infected wound.

## Begin Recovery

- **Contact your insurer** as soon as possible.
- **Photograph all damage** before cleaning or removing items.
- Keep receipts for any emergency repairs or accommodation.
- Contact your local council for support with waste collection and temporary housing.

For further help, call the Floodline or visit your local authority's website.

# Applying for a Small Business Growth Grant

The Small Business Growth Grant supports local businesses that want to expand, hire staff, or improve their operations. Grants of up to $25,000 are available, and you do not need to pay them back.

## Who can apply

You may be eligible if your business:

- Is independently owned and operated
- Employs fewer than 50 people
- Has been trading for at least 12 months
- Is registered and based within the state
- Has no outstanding tax debts

Charities, franchises, and businesses that previously received this grant in the past three years are not eligible.

## What the grant can fund

Grants can cover equipment, technology upgrades, staff training, marketing, and minor building improvements. They cannot cover rent, wages, debt repayments, or costs you have already paid.

## How to apply

1. **Check your eligibility** using the online self-assessment tool.
2. **Prepare your documents.** You will need your business registration number, your most recent financial statements, and quotes for the items you want to fund.
3. **Complete the application form** through our online portal. You can save your progress and return later.
4. **Submit before the deadline.** Late applications will not be accepted.

## What happens next

We will acknowledge your application within five working days. An assessment panel reviews all applications, and we aim to notify you of the outcome within eight weeks. Successful applicants must sign a funding agreement and provide a short progress report within 12 months.

## Need help?

Call our Business Support Line on 1800 555 0199, Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm, or visit a regional service center.

# Getting a Fishing Licence

## Who needs a licence

You need a fishing licence if you are 16 or older and want to fish in any river, lake, canal or reservoir. Children under 16 can fish without one, but they must follow all local rules on catch limits and closed seasons.

If you fish at sea from the shore or a boat, you do not usually need a licence. Check local byelaws first, as some areas have their own requirements.

## Types of licence

We offer three options:

- **1-day licence**: good for a single trip or trying the sport for the first time.
- **8-day licence**: suits a short holiday or a week of fishing.
- **12-month licence**: the best value if you fish regularly.

Discounts are available for people aged 66 and over, and for holders of a Blue Badge or those receiving certain disability benefits.

## How to apply

The quickest way is online. You will need:

- your full name, date of birth and address
- a debit or credit card
- your Blue Badge or benefit details, if you are claiming a discount

Your licence will be valid from the date and time you choose. You can also buy a licence by phone on 0300 123 4567, Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm.

## While you are fishing

Carry your licence or licence number with you at all times. Our officers carry out regular checks, and fishing without a valid licence can lead to a fine of up to £2,500.

A licence does not give you the right to fish anywhere. You must also have permission from whoever owns the fishing rights.

I bought this cordless vacuum last spring to replace a bulky corded upright, and six months in, I'm mostly thrilled. Suction is strong on hardwood and handles our medium-pile rug well, though thick carpet takes a couple of extra passes. The real win is convenience: it hangs on the wall charger, so I grab it for quick cleanups several times a week instead of dreading a big weekly session.

Battery life has held up better than expected. I still get around 35 minutes on standard mode, maybe five minutes less than when new. Boost mode drains it in under ten, so I save that for stubborn spots.

**Two stars. I really wanted to love this one.**

I picked up *The Salt Orchard* after three friends swore it'd wreck me emotionally. It didn't. It barely bruised me.

The first fifty pages are gorgeous, I'll admit that. The prose is lush, the coastal town feels lived-in, and Mara's grief over her brother is handled with real care. Then the plot just... stalls. We get chapter after chapter of her walking the beach, remembering things, and staring at the lighthouse. I started skimming. I never skim.

The big twist? I guessed it on page 90. Honestly, I was hoping I'd be wrong.

What frustrates me most is the potential. There's a brilliant 250-page novel buried inside this 480-page one. An editor with sharp scissors could've saved it.

I finished it on a delayed train out of Leeds, which is probably the only reason I finished it at all. Lovely sentences, though. Shame about the story.

I picked up Stardew Valley over the holidays because my sister wouldn't stop talking about it. I figured I'd play an hour, maybe two. Instead, I lost most of winter break to turnips.

It's not flashy. The graphics are simple, the music's gentle, and nothing really explodes. But that's the point. You plant crops, fix up a run-down farm, and slowly get to know the townspeople, who turn out to be weirder and sadder and funnier than you'd expect.

What got me was how it never rushes you. Missed a festival? There's always next year. Forgot to water the cauliflower? Oh well.

My one complaint: fishing. The minigame's brutal at first, and I nearly quit over a single stubborn catfish.

Still, I'd recommend it to anyone who needs to unwind. I played most of it wrapped in a blanket on my parents' couch, cocoa going cold beside me. Honestly? Perfect.

Five stars.

★★★★☆ Finally, a grinder that doesn't sound like a jet engine

I'd been using a cheap blade grinder for years and honestly didn't think it mattered much. It does. The first cup I made with this burr grinder tasted noticeably smoother, less bitter, and I could actually pick out the chocolatey notes the bag promised.

Setup took maybe five minutes. There are 40 grind settings, which felt like overkill at first, but I've settled on 14 for my pour-over and 6 when my sister visits and insists on espresso. It's quieter than I expected, too. I can grind beans at 6 a.m. without waking my roommate, which is a big win.

Downsides? The static is real. Grounds cling to the catch cup and scatter a bit when you tap it out. A quick spritz of water on the beans helps. Cleaning the burrs is also fiddly.

Still, for the price, I'm happy. Would buy again.

★★★★☆ A Journey Worth Taking

I visited "Eternal Sands: Treasures of Ancient Egypt" last Saturday and left genuinely impressed. The exhibition winds through dimly lit galleries arranged chronologically, from the Old Kingdom to the Ptolemaic era, which makes the vast timeline surprisingly easy to follow.

The highlight is undoubtedly the painted coffin of a Theban priestess, its colors still vivid after nearly three thousand years. Nearby, a case of tiny faience amulets rewards close inspection, so take your time there. The interactive hieroglyph station was a hit with my kids, who spent twenty minutes spelling their names.

My only complaints: the audio guide costs extra and felt thin on detail, and the final room was crowded enough that I couldn't linger. Weekday mornings are probably your best bet.

Overall, it's a thoughtful, beautifully curated show that balances spectacle with scholarship. Highly recommended for families and history buffs alike.

Not at all. Bringing your own food is the whole point of a potluck. Everyone contributes a dish, so you're doing exactly what's expected. The only difference is that you'll make sure at least one option is safe for you.

A few tips to make it smooth:

- **Bring enough to share.** Make a full dish, not a single portion. That way it's a contribution, not a private meal, and others with similar restrictions may appreciate it.
- **Label it.** A small card listing ingredients or "free of nuts, dairy, gluten" helps other guests with allergies too.
- **Serve yourself first.** Shared serving spoons travel between dishes, so grab your portion before cross-contamination happens.
- **Give the host a heads-up.** A quick message like "I have a shellfish allergy, so I'll bring something I know is safe" is courteous and avoids awkward questions.
- **Skip the explanations if you want.** You don't owe anyone a detailed medical history. "I have allergies" is enough.

Most hosts would much rather you eat safely than go hungry or end up in the ER. Bringing a dish you can enjoy is considerate, not rude.

Yellowing lower leaves on tomatoes is very common, and there are a few usual causes:

**1. Natural aging.** As plants grow, they shed older bottom leaves that get shaded out. If it's just a few leaves and the plant otherwise looks healthy, don't worry.

**2. Nitrogen deficiency.** Nitrogen is mobile, so plants pull it from older leaves to feed new growth. Uniform yellowing that moves upward suggests feeding with a balanced fertilizer or compost.

**3. Watering issues.** Both overwatering (soggy roots can't absorb nutrients) and inconsistent watering cause yellowing. Aim for deep, regular watering and well-draining soil.

**4. Fungal disease.** Yellow leaves with brown spots or concentric rings point to **early blight**. Yellow patches with gray-brown spots may be **Septoria leaf spot**. Yellowing on one side of a leaf or stem can signal **Fusarium or Verticillium wilt**.

**What to do:**
- Remove affected lower leaves (and dispose of them, not in compost if diseased).
- Prune leaves touching the soil to prevent splash-borne spores.
- Mulch around the base.
- Water at the soil, not the foliage, preferably in the morning.
- Rotate tomato planting spots yearly.

If spots appear, a copper or chlorothalonil fungicide can help slow spread.

Motorway anxiety is really common, and the good news is it usually responds well to gradual exposure. Here's what helped me and others I know:

**Start small.** Pick a quiet stretch at an off-peak time, like early Sunday morning, and drive just one junction. Come off, take a breath, and do it again. Build up distance over several sessions.

**Take a confident passenger.** Having someone calm beside you makes a huge difference, especially for the first few trips.

**Consider a motorway lesson.** Many driving instructors offer refresher sessions specifically for this. In the UK, Pass Plus covers motorway driving too.

**Know the mechanics.** Most fear centres on joining. Use the slip road to match the speed of traffic, check your mirrors and blind spot early, and merge smoothly. Once you're on, stay in the left lane as long as you like. Nobody will mind.

Mushy rice usually comes down to a few common culprits:

**1. Too much water.** This is the big one. For long-grain white rice, try 1 part rice to 1.5 parts water, not the 1:2 ratio printed on many packages. Different varieties need different amounts, so adjust as you go.

**2. Not rinsing.** Surface starch turns gummy when cooked. Rinse the rice in cold water, swishing it around, until the water runs mostly clear.

**3. Stirring.** Stirring breaks the grains and releases more starch. Once the lid is on, leave it alone.

**4. Lifting the lid.** Rice cooks largely by steam. Peeking lets it escape and throws off the timing, which often leads people to add more water.

**5. Skipping the rest.** After cooking, take the pot off the heat and let it sit covered for 10 minutes. This lets moisture redistribute evenly. Then fluff with a fork.

**6. Heat too high.** Bring it to a boil, then drop it to the lowest simmer.

If you still struggle, a cheap rice cooker takes the guesswork out entirely.

Scratching is normal cat behavior. It keeps claws healthy, stretches muscles, and marks territory, so the goal is to redirect it, not stop it.

**Give them a better option.** Get a sturdy scratching post that's tall enough for your cat to stretch out fully and heavy enough not to wobble. Sisal rope is a favorite texture. Some cats prefer horizontal scratchers (cardboard), so try both.

**Location matters.** Put the post right next to the sofa at first, since that's where your cat already wants to scratch. You can move it gradually later.

**Make the post attractive.** Rub catnip or silvervine on it, dangle toys near it, and reward your cat with treats or praise when they use it.

**Make the sofa unappealing.** Cover the favorite spots with double-sided tape, a throw blanket, or plastic sofa guards. Cats dislike sticky surfaces.

**Trim their claws** every couple of weeks to reduce damage. Soft nail caps (like Soft Paws) are another humane option.

**Avoid punishment.** Yelling or spraying water just makes cats anxious and teaches them to scratch when you're not around. Never declaw; it's an amputation and causes lasting pain.

With consistency, most cats switch within a few weeks.

Procrastination on a thesis usually isn't laziness. It's avoidance. The project feels huge, vague, and tied to your sense of competence, so your brain dodges it. The fix is to make it smaller, clearer, and less loaded.

**Shrink the task.** "Work on thesis" is impossible to start. "Write 200 words on the limitations of my sample" is not. Each evening, write down the very next concrete action for tomorrow.

**Lower the bar.** Give yourself permission to write badly. A rough draft you can edit beats a perfect paragraph that lives only in your head.

**Use short, fixed sessions.** Try 25–50 minutes with your phone in another room. Starting is the hardest part, and a timer makes starting cheap.

**Same time, same place.** Routine removes the daily decision about *whether* to work.

**Track output, not hours.** Log words written or sections finished. Visible progress builds momentum.

**Create external accountability.** Send your advisor or a friend weekly updates, or join a writing group. Deadlines other people can see work far better than private ones.

**Watch for deeper issues.** If you're stuck because you don't know what to do next, that's a supervision problem, so ask for help. If it's persistent dread, consider talking to a counselor.

There are a few easy ways to check:

**1. The float test (most popular)**
Fill a bowl with cold water and gently place the egg in it:
- **Sinks and lies flat:** very fresh.
- **Sinks but stands on one end:** older but still fine to eat. Use it soon, ideally for baking or hard-boiling.
- **Floats:** likely old. As eggs age, moisture evaporates through the shell and the air cell inside grows. A floating egg isn't automatically spoiled, but it's past its prime, so check it carefully or toss it.

**2. The sniff test (most reliable)**
Crack the egg into a separate bowl before adding it to anything. A bad egg has an unmistakable sulfur or rotten smell. If it smells off, throw it out.

**3. Visual check**
Look for a slimy or powdery shell (possible bacteria or mold) and pink, green, or iridescent discoloration inside. A runny, spreading white just means the egg is older, not necessarily bad.

**4. Check the date**
Refrigerated eggs often stay good 3–5 weeks past the pack date, and frequently beyond the "sell-by" date.

**Bottom line:** When in doubt, throw it out. Eggs are cheap, and food poisoning isn't.

Stop trying to make conversations happen and start making space for them.

Teens often open up sideways, not face-to-face. Car rides, cooking together, walking the dog, late-night snacks: these low-pressure moments work because there's no eye contact and an easy exit. Be available during them, and resist filling the silence.

When they do talk, listen more than you respond. Hold back the advice, the lecture, and the "I told you so." If you react to small confessions with alarm or judgment, they'll stop sharing big ones. Try "That sounds frustrating" or "What do you think you'll do?" instead.

Ask specific questions rather than "How was your day?" Something like "What was the most annoying thing that happened today?" gets better answers.

Finally, be patient. Pulling back is a normal part of adolescence. Consistency matters more than any single conversation.

Not necessarily. Plenty of people run every day for years without problems, but whether it works for you depends on how hard, how far, and how experienced you are.

The main risk is overuse injury. Running is repetitive, and bones, tendons, and joints adapt more slowly than your heart and lungs. If you jump into daily running too quickly, you're more likely to develop shin splints, stress fractures, or tendon pain. Newer runners usually do better with three or four days a week and rest or cross-training in between.

If you do run daily, vary the effort. Most of your runs should be easy, at a pace where you could hold a conversation. Save hard efforts like intervals or long runs for a couple of days a week, and treat some days as short recovery jogs. Increase your weekly mileage gradually, roughly 10 percent at a time.

Pay attention to warning signs: pain that worsens during a run, lingering soreness, poor sleep, constant fatigue, or declining performance. These suggest you need more rest.

Good shoes, enough sleep, and adequate food matter too. Listen to your body, and daily running can be perfectly healthy.

The short version: a process is a running program with its own memory, and a thread is a path of execution inside a process. Every process has at least one thread, and it can have many.

The difference that matters day to day is memory. Two processes can't see each other's memory, at least not without deliberately setting something up like shared memory, pipes, or sockets. If one crashes, the other usually keeps going. Threads in the same process share everything: the heap, global variables, open files. Each thread gets only its own stack and registers.

That sharing cuts both ways. It makes threads cheap to create and fast to communicate between, since you just read the same variable. It's also why threaded code is hard to get right. Two threads touching the same data at the same time without a lock gives you race conditions, and those bugs show up once a week in production and never on your machine. One thread doing something bad, like a segfault, takes down the whole process.

Processes cost more. Creating one and switching between them is heavier, and passing data means copying or serializing it. In exchange you get isolation, which is why Chrome runs tabs as separate processes: one bad page doesn't kill your whole browser.

Rule of thumb: use threads when you need lots of tightly shared state, and processes when you want things kept apart.

Git says your branch has "diverged" when your local branch and its remote counterpart (e.g. `origin/main`) each have commits the other doesn't. History has split into two paths from a common ancestor.

A typical way this happens:

1. You and the remote both start at commit A.
2. You make commit B locally.
3. Meanwhile, someone else (or you, from another machine) pushes commit C to the remote.
4. You run `git fetch` or `git status`, and Git sees that your branch has B, the remote has C, and neither contains the other.

Git can't simply fast-forward either side, so it reports something like "Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 1 and 1 different commits each."

It also commonly happens after you rewrite history with a rebase, an amend, or a reset on commits you'd already pushed. The old commits still exist on the remote, and your rewritten ones look like entirely different commits.

To fix it, choose how to reconcile the two lines:

- **Merge:** `git pull --no-rebase` creates a merge commit joining both histories.
- **Rebase:** `git pull --rebase` replays your local commits on top of the remote's.
- **Overwrite the remote:** if you intentionally rewrote history and nobody else depends on it, use `git push --force-with-lease`.

If you're unsure, run `git log --oneline --graph --all` to see exactly where the histories split before deciding.

## Features

### Performance
- **High-throughput storage engine**: A log-structured merge-tree (LSM) engine tuned for write-heavy workloads, with B-tree indexes for fast point lookups and range scans.
- **Vectorized query execution**: Batch-oriented processing that makes full use of modern CPU caches and SIMD instructions.
- **Adaptive caching**: An intelligent buffer pool that learns access patterns and keeps hot data in memory.
- **Parallel query processing**: Large queries are split automatically across all available cores.

### Reliability
- **Full ACID transactions**: Serializable isolation by default, with configurable levels down to read committed.
- **Write-ahead logging**: Every committed transaction survives crashes and power loss.
- **Point-in-time recovery**: Restore your database to any moment within your retention window.
- **Online backups**: Take consistent snapshots with no downtime and no locking.

### Scalability
- **Horizontal sharding**: Data is distributed across nodes automatically, with transparent rebalancing.
- **Raft-based replication**: Strongly consistent replicas with automatic leader election and failover.
- **Multi-region deployment**: Data placement can follow latency, compliance, or residency requirements.
- **Elastic scaling**: Nodes can be added or removed without service interruption.

### Developer Experience
- **Standard SQL**: Broad compatibility with ANSI SQL, including CTEs, window functions, and JSON operators.
- **PostgreSQL wire protocol**: Works with existing drivers, ORMs, and tools out of the box.
- **Native JSON and document support**: Store, index, and query semi-structured data alongside relational tables.
- **Built-in full-text search**: Tokenization, ranking, and fuzzy matching without an external search engine.
- **Vector search**: Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes (HNSW) for embedding-based retrieval and AI workloads.

### Security
- **Encryption everywhere**: TLS for data in transit and AES-256 for data at rest.
- **Fine-grained access control**: Role-based permissions down to the row and column level.
- **Audit logging**: Tamper-evident records of every query, login, and schema change.
- **Pluggable authentication**: Supports passwords, certificates, LDAP, and OIDC/SSO.

### Operations
- **Single binary deployment**: No external dependencies. Run it locally, in containers, or on Kubernetes.
- **Observability built in**: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing, and a built-in web dashboard.
- **Online schema changes**: Add columns, create indexes, and alter tables without blocking reads or writes.
- **Kubernetes operator**: Declarative cluster management with automated upgrades and scaling.

### Open Source
- **Apache 2.0 licensed**: Free to use, modify, and distribute, including in commercial products.
- **Community-driven**: Development happens in the open, with public roadmaps and RFCs.
- **Extensible**: Plugin APIs for custom functions, data types, storage backends, and authentication providers.

The trick is to run both hosts in parallel and let DNS do the cutover gradually:

1. **Lower your DNS TTL** a day or two ahead (e.g., to 300 seconds) so the eventual switch propagates quickly.

2. **Build the new environment** completely: same software versions, config, SSL certificates, cron jobs, and environment variables.

3. **Copy files and the database.** Do an initial bulk sync, then test the new server by editing your local hosts file to point the domain at the new IP.

4. **Handle the database carefully.** For dynamic sites, set up replication from old to new, or schedule a brief read-only window for the final sync. This is usually the hardest part.

5. **Do a final incremental sync** (rsync is ideal) right before cutover.

6. **Switch DNS** to the new IP. Keep the old server running. Some clients will hit it for a while due to caching.

7. **Monitor both servers' logs.** Once traffic on the old host drops to zero (give it 24–48 hours), decommission it and raise your TTL back up.

Also watch email (MX records), hardcoded IPs, and firewall allowlists at third-party services.

Short answer: don't store passwords at all. Store a slow, salted hash of them.

**Use a purpose-built password hashing algorithm:**
- **Argon2id** is the current first choice (winner of the Password Hashing Competition, recommended by OWASP).
- **scrypt** or **bcrypt** are solid alternatives if Argon2 isn't available in your stack.
- **PBKDF2** with a high iteration count is acceptable where FIPS compliance is required.

**Never use** plain MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256 for passwords, even with a salt. They're designed to be fast, which is exactly what an attacker with a GPU wants.

**Key practices:**
- Use your language's well-maintained library (e.g., `argon2-cffi`, `bcrypt`, libsodium). Don't roll your own.
- Each password gets a unique random salt. Good libraries handle this automatically and embed it in the hash string.
- Tune the cost parameters so hashing takes roughly 100–500 ms on your hardware, and raise them over time.
- Optionally add a "pepper": a secret key stored outside the database (e.g., in a KMS or secrets manager).
- Rehash on login when you upgrade algorithms or parameters.
- Rate-limit login attempts and support MFA. Hashing only protects you *after* a breach.

Better still, consider delegating auth to a proven identity provider entirely.

Roughly speaking, it means your server is fully busy but not overloaded. Load average is the average number of tasks that are either running or waiting to run, smoothed over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. With 4 cores and a load of 4, on average every core has exactly one task to work on and nothing is stuck waiting in line. Above 4, tasks start queuing; below 4, you have idle capacity.

There are a few caveats. On Linux, load average also counts processes in uninterruptible sleep (D state), which usually means they are waiting on disk or network I/O. So a load of 4 could mean your CPUs are pegged, or it could mean they are mostly idle while processes wait on a slow NFS mount or a struggling disk. Check top or vmstat and look at the us, sy and wa columns to tell which it is.

Hyperthreading also muddies things. If those 4 cores show up as 8 logical CPUs, the kernel counts 8, though real throughput is less than double.

Finally, look at the trend. If the 1 minute value is much higher than the 15 minute value, load is climbing. If it is lower, things are calming down.

# Appointments API

The Appointments API lets you check availability, book time slots, and manage existing bookings from your own app or backend. If you've ever built a "pick a time" screen and then had to wire it up to a calendar on the other end, this is the part we handle for you.

Everything is plain REST over HTTPS. Requests and responses are JSON, and you authenticate with an API key in the `Authorization` header. There's no SDK you have to install, though we do have a few if you'd rather not write the HTTP calls yourself.

Most integrations only touch three resources:

- **Providers**: the people or rooms that can be booked
- **Availability**: open slots for a provider over a date range
- **Appointments**: the bookings themselves, which you can create, reschedule, or cancel

A typical flow looks like this: fetch availability for a provider, show those slots to your user, then create an appointment with the slot they picked. If someone grabs the same slot a second before you do, you'll get a `409 Conflict` back, and you can refetch and try again.

All times are in UTC and use ISO 8601. Convert to local time on your side before showing anything to users. It saves a lot of daylight-saving headaches.

If you just want to see it work, the [Quickstart](#quickstart) gets you from API key to a booked appointment in about ten minutes. If something in these docs is wrong or unclear, let us know. We'd rather fix it than have you guess.
