I didn't understand until much later what she'd done. She hadn't tried to fix my fear with a pep talk. She'd given me a small, ridiculous, doable task and trusted me to do it.

I give presentations for a living now. Before every one, I still think of her and of Pepper, patient on the rug, listening.

Thank you, Mrs. Halvorsen. A dog counted.

**Summer Projects: Let Students Lead the Way**

Every June, many students leave school with a packet of assignments to complete before September. Schools assign summer projects to keep minds active during the long break, and that goal is worthwhile. However, the way these projects are designed matters. Summer projects should be student-designed rather than teacher-designed, because student choice builds motivation, develops independence, and leads to deeper learning.

First, students care more about work they choose. A teacher-designed project, such as a required book report, often feels like a chore to finish the night before school starts. When students select their own topics, they invest real effort. A student who loves music might research the history of jazz, while another who enjoys building things might design a model bridge. Because the work connects to their interests, they are more likely to start early, work steadily, and take pride in the result.

Second, student-designed projects teach skills that matter beyond the classroom. In adult life, no one hands people a step-by-step worksheet for every task. They must set goals, manage time, and solve problems on their own. Planning a summer project gives students practice with exactly these skills. Deciding what to study, creating a schedule, and adjusting when something goes wrong prepare young people for college and careers far better than filling in blanks.

Critics argue that without teacher guidance, students will choose easy projects or do nothing at all. This concern is reasonable, but it can be solved with structure rather than control. Teachers can provide clear guidelines, such as a required proposal, a minimum time commitment, and a final presentation. Students still make the important choices, but they remain accountable for meaningful work.

Finally, student-designed projects lead to deeper learning. When students explore questions they genuinely wonder about, they remember what they discover. They also return to school with experiences to share, which makes the first weeks of class richer for everyone.

Summer should be a time for curiosity, not just catching up. By allowing students to design their own projects, schools can turn summer assignments from dreaded obligations into opportunities for growth. When students lead, they learn more about their subjects and about themselves.

Car-Free Cities: Why We Should Give Them a Try

Imagine walking down a city street without hearing honking horns or breathing in exhaust fumes. That might sound like a dream, but some cities around the world are actually trying it. I think more cities should limit cars or even go car-free, because it would help the environment, make people healthier, and make cities better places to live.

First of all, cars are a huge cause of pollution. According to the EPA, transportation is one of the biggest sources of greenhouse gases in the United States. When cities cut down on cars, the air gets cleaner. For example, Paris banned driving on some days when the smog got really bad, and the pollution went down a lot. If cities did this all the time, it could make a big difference for climate change.

Second, car-free cities would make people healthier. When people can't just jump in a car, they walk or ride bikes more. This is good exercise, and most people don't get enough of it. Also, there would be less car accidents, which kill thousands of people every year. Kids could play outside more safely and parents wouldn't have to worry as much.

Another reason is that cities would just be nicer. Right now a lot of space is taken up by parking lots and big roads. If we didn't need all that, we could have more parks, shops, and places for people to hang out. In Vauban, Germany, most people don't own cars and they say they are happier and less stressed.

Some people might say that car-free cities aren't realistic because people need cars to get to work or carry heavy stuff. This is a fair point, especially for people who live far away. But cities could improve public transportation like buses and trains so people still have a way to get around. Delivery services could also help with heavy things. It wouldn't happen overnight, but it's possible.

In conclusion, car-free cities have a lot of benefits. They are better for the planet, better for our health, and make cities more enjoyable. Even if we can't get rid of cars completely, cities should start taking steps to use them less. The future could be a lot cleaner and quieter if we do.

**Hang Up and Drive: Why Phones Have No Place Behind the Wheel**

Every day, millions of drivers glance at a notification, type a quick reply, or scroll through a playlist while their car speeds down the road. These moments may feel harmless, but they are not. Using a phone while driving is dangerous, irresponsible, and preventable, and drivers should put their phones away completely whenever they are behind the wheel.

The most important reason is safety. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, distracted driving kills more than 3,000 people in the United States each year. Texting is especially risky because it takes a driver's eyes off the road for about five seconds. At 55 miles per hour, that is like driving the length of a football field blindfolded. In that time, a child could step into the street or the car ahead could brake suddenly, and a distracted driver would have no chance to react.

Some people argue that hands-free devices solve the problem. Voice commands and Bluetooth calls do keep both hands on the wheel, but research shows that the brain is still distracted. Driving demands full attention, and a conversation or voice-to-text message pulls focus away from the road. Drivers may be looking ahead, but they are not truly seeing what is happening around them. Hands-free does not mean risk-free.

Others claim they are skilled at multitasking and can handle a quick look at their phone. Studies on attention consistently show that humans do not really multitask. Instead, the brain switches rapidly between tasks, and each switch costs time and accuracy. Confidence does not make anyone immune to this. In fact, drivers who believe they can safely multitask may be the most dangerous, because they take risks more often.

Finally, the solution is simple. Drivers can silence notifications, turn on "Do Not Disturb While Driving," or keep their phones in the back seat. If a message is truly urgent, they can pull over safely. No text, call, or song is worth a human life.

Phones and driving do not mix. By choosing to hang up and drive, each of us can help make the roads safer for everyone.

Every school day ends with a bell, and for many students that bell marks the end of their involvement with school altogether. They go home, open their phones, and wait for tomorrow. Schools should require every student to take part in at least one extracurricular activity, because these activities build skills, relationships, and a sense of belonging that classrooms alone cannot provide.

First, extracurricular activities teach lessons that textbooks cannot. A student on the debate team learns to think quickly and speak confidently in front of others. A member of the school orchestra learns patience and discipline through hours of practice. Someone who joins the robotics club learns to solve problems as part of a team, often failing several times before succeeding. Employers and colleges value these qualities highly, yet many students never develop them simply because no one encouraged them to try.

Second, mandatory participation helps students connect with others. Many young people feel isolated, and the rise of social media has made genuine friendships harder to form. Clubs and teams bring together students who might never speak to each other in a regular class. Working toward a shared goal, whether winning a game or staging a play, creates bonds that make school a more welcoming place. Students who feel connected to their school are also more likely to attend regularly and earn better grades.

Critics argue that some students already have jobs, family responsibilities, or long commutes that make extra commitments difficult. This concern is valid, but it does not justify abandoning the idea. Schools can offer flexible options, such as activities held during lunch or a period built into the school day, and they can count outside responsibilities like part time work or volunteering toward the requirement. Others worry that forcing participation will make activities feel like chores. However, if students are free to choose which activity they join, most will find something they genuinely enjoy.

Ultimately, a requirement simply ensures that every student gets the chance to discover a talent or passion. Many adults look back on a club or team as the best part of their school years. Requiring participation would give every student that same opportunity.

Every June, students across the country celebrate the end of the school year, and many teachers respond by handing out summer projects. Some students groan at the idea, believing summer should be a complete break from learning. However, well-designed summer projects are valuable because they prevent learning loss, build independence, and allow students to explore their own interests.

The most practical reason for summer projects is that they help students keep the skills they worked hard to earn. Researchers have long described a "summer slide," in which students forget a portion of what they learned during the year, especially in math and reading. Teachers then spend the first weeks of autumn reviewing old material instead of teaching new lessons. A summer project, even a modest one, keeps the mind active and makes the return to school smoother for everyone.

Summer projects also teach responsibility in a way that ordinary homework cannot. During the school year, teachers set daily deadlines and remind students constantly. Over the summer, students must plan their own time, break a large task into smaller steps, and stay motivated without supervision. These are exactly the skills that high school, college, and future jobs demand. A student who learns to manage a ten-week project at age fourteen is better prepared for adult life.

Perhaps the strongest argument is that summer projects can give students freedom that the regular curriculum rarely allows. A good project might let a student build a model, interview a grandparent about local history, start a garden, or write a short story. When students choose their own topics, learning becomes personal rather than forced, and many discover passions they never knew they had.

Critics argue that summer is meant for rest and family, and that projects create stress. This concern is fair, but it applies to poorly designed assignments, not to the idea itself. A project that takes a few hours a week still leaves plenty of time for vacations, sports, and relaxation.

Summer projects, when thoughtful and flexible, are not a punishment. They are an opportunity to keep growing, to practice independence, and to learn something meaningful on our own terms.

**The Face on Mars: A Natural Landform, Not an Alien Monument**

In 1976, NASA's Viking 1 spacecraft photographed a strange formation in the Cydonia region of Mars. The image showed what looked like a giant human face staring up from the planet's surface. Some people believe the Face was built by ancient Martians, but the scientific evidence shows that it is simply a natural landform: a mesa or butte shaped by geology.

First, later photographs with much better cameras show no signs of construction. In 1998, the Mars Global Surveyor took a picture ten times sharper than the original Viking image. In 2001, it captured an even clearer view, with each pixel covering about 1.56 meters. At that resolution, scientists could have spotted objects as small as airplanes or Egyptian-style pyramids. Instead, the images revealed an ordinary eroded hill with no eyes, nose, or mouth, just ridges and shadows.

Second, the original "face" was an illusion caused by poor image quality and lighting. The Viking photo was low-resolution, and the sun was shining at a low angle, which created shadows that resembled facial features. Humans are naturally wired to see faces in random patterns, a phenomenon called pareidolia. It is the same reason people see faces in clouds, rocks, or electrical outlets. The Face on Mars is a famous example of our brains filling in details that are not really there.

Third, landforms like the Face are common on Earth. The formation closely resembles mesas and buttes found in the American West, such as those in Idaho's Snake River Plain. Wind, water, and time can carve rock into surprising shapes. There is no need to invent an alien civilization to explain something that geology explains easily.

Some argue that NASA is hiding evidence of life on Mars. However, this makes little sense. Discovering an alien civilization would be the greatest scientific find in history, and it would boost NASA's funding and public support. NASA has every reason to share such a discovery, not hide it.

In conclusion, the Face on Mars is not an alien artifact. High-resolution images, an understanding of lighting and human perception, and comparisons to landforms on Earth all show that it is a natural mesa. Science, not science fiction, explains the Face.

**Should Community Service Be Required for High School Students?**

A lot of high schools around the country make students do a certain number of community service hours before they can graduate. Some people think this is unfair because students are already busy with school, sports, and jobs. But I think community service should be required, because it helps the community, teaches students important skills, and can even help them figure out what they want to do in the future.

First of all, community service helps the people who need it. There are food banks, animal shelters, and nursing homes that don't have enough volunteers. If every high school student did even 20 hours a year, that would be a huge amount of help. For example, my cousin volunteered at a soup kitchen and she said they were always short on people, especially on weekends. Students can make a real difference just by showing up.

Second, community service teaches skills you don't really learn in a classroom. When you volunteer, you have to talk to new people, work on a team, and show up on time. These are things employers look for. You also learn responsibility, because people are counting on you. I think a lot of teenagers (including me sometimes) don't get many chances to be responsible for something that actually matters, so this is a good way to practice.

Some people argue that if service is required, it isn't really "volunteering" anymore, and students will just do it to check a box. I understand this point, but I don't totally agree. Even if a student starts out not wanting to do it, they might end up liking it. Lots of things in school are required, like math and P.E., and we still learn from them. Being required to do something doesn't mean it has no value.

Finally, community service can help students find out what they're interested in. Someone who volunteers at a hospital might decide they want to be a nurse. Someone who helps at an animal shelter might want to become a vet. You never know until you try.

In conclusion, community service should be required for high school students. It helps the community, builds important skills, and gives students new experiences. A few hours a year is not too much to ask for all those benefits.

# Does the Electoral College Work?

Every four years, Americans cast their votes for president, but those votes do not directly choose the winner. Instead, the Electoral College, a system created in 1787, decides the outcome. Supporters argue that it protects smaller states and preserves federalism. However, the Electoral College no longer serves the needs of a modern democracy. It fails to reflect the will of the people, gives unequal weight to voters, and discourages participation.

The strongest argument against the Electoral College is that it can override the popular vote. In both 2000 and 2016, the candidate who received the most votes nationwide lost the election. In a democracy, the basic principle should be simple: the person with the most votes wins. When the system allows the second-place candidate to take office, it weakens public trust in elections and raises questions about whether every voice truly matters.

The Electoral College also makes some votes worth more than others. Because every state receives at least three electors regardless of population, a voter in Wyoming has significantly more influence per person than a voter in California or Texas. This imbalance contradicts the idea of "one person, one vote," which the Supreme Court has upheld as a cornerstone of fair representation.

In addition, the system encourages candidates to focus on a small number of "swing states." States like Pennsylvania, Arizona, and Georgia receive enormous attention, while reliably Democratic or Republican states are largely ignored. As a result, millions of voters in states such as New York, Alabama, or Illinois may feel their votes make no difference. This can lower voter turnout and leave important regional concerns unaddressed.

Defenders claim the Electoral College protects rural areas from being overpowered by big cities. Yet under a national popular vote, every voter, whether rural or urban, would count equally. Candidates would need to build broad support across the entire country rather than chasing a few battleground states.

The Electoral College may have made sense in the eighteenth century, but it no longer works for today's America. Replacing it with a national popular vote would make elections fairer, more representative, and more democratic. Every citizen's vote should count the same.

The Electoral College was designed in 1787 as a compromise between electing the president by a vote of Congress and electing the president by popular vote. More than two centuries later, it is fair to ask whether this system still serves the nation well. Although supporters praise its role in protecting smaller states, the Electoral College no longer works as a fair method of choosing a president because it can override the popular will, concentrates attention on a few states, and gives some citizens more voting power than others.

The most serious problem is that the Electoral College can elect a candidate who did not win the most votes. This happened in 2000 and again in 2016, when the winners of the popular vote lost the presidency. In a democracy, the basic principle should be that the candidate with the most support wins. When the system produces the opposite result, many citizens lose faith that their votes truly matter.

The system also encourages candidates to ignore most of the country. Because nearly every state awards all of its electoral votes to the statewide winner, campaigns focus on a small group of swing states such as Pennsylvania, Arizona, and Wisconsin. Voters in reliably Democratic or Republican states, from California to Wyoming, receive little attention. A national popular vote would give candidates a reason to seek support everywhere, since every vote would count equally toward the final total.

Finally, the Electoral College gives unequal weight to individual votes. Every state receives at least three electors regardless of population, so a vote in a small state carries more influence than a vote in a large one. This violates the idea of "one person, one vote" that the Supreme Court has applied to other elections.

Defenders argue that the Electoral College protects rural areas and small states from being overlooked. However, the current system already overlooks most small states unless they happen to be competitive. Protecting minority interests is important, but the Senate already provides that balance.

The Electoral College made sense for the young nation that created it, but it does not reflect modern democratic values. Moving toward a national popular vote would ensure that every citizen's voice counts equally in choosing the nation's leader.

**Distance Learning: Not as Good as Real School**

During the pandemic, almost every student in the country had to do school from home. Some people think distance learning is the future and that we should keep doing it even now. I disagree. Even though online school has some good points, I think in-person school is better for most students because it helps them learn more, stay focused, and have a social life.

The first reason is that a lot of students don't actually learn as much online. When I was doing Zoom classes in middle school, half my class had their cameras off, and I know for a fact some of them were still in bed. It's really easy to zone out when the teacher is just a little box on your screen. In a real classroom, the teacher can see if you're confused and help you right away. Studies have also shown that test scores dropped during the time schools were online, especially in math.

Another reason is distractions. At home there is your phone, your TV, your little brother, your dog, and basically everything else. At school there are still distractions, but at least everyone is there to do the same thing. It's a lot easier to focus when you're in a place that is made for learning.

The third reason is social life. School isn't just about grades. It's where you make friends, join clubs, play sports, and learn how to talk to people. During online school a lot of kids felt lonely and depressed, and that's not something we should ignore. Being around other people your age is important for growing up.

Some people say distance learning is better because it's flexible and you don't have to wake up as early. That's true, and it can be good for students who are sick or who have to work. But for most students, those benefits don't make up for learning less and feeling isolated. Maybe online classes could be an option for some people, but not a replacement for regular school.

In conclusion, distance learning might seem convenient, but in-person school is better for learning, focus, and friendships. Schools should keep students in the classroom where they belong.

**The Wisdom of Many Voices: Why We Should Seek Multiple Opinions**

When we face an important decision, it is tempting to ask one trusted person and act on their advice. That approach is simple, but it is risky. Seeking multiple opinions leads to better decisions because it exposes our blind spots, protects us from bias, and helps us understand problems more fully.

First, multiple opinions reveal what a single perspective misses. Every person's view is shaped by their own experiences, knowledge, and limitations. A student choosing a college might ask a parent, who stresses cost, a teacher, who stresses academic programs, and a current student, who describes campus life. Each answer is incomplete, but together they give a clear picture. Relying on one voice means accepting that person's blind spots as our own.

Second, consulting several people guards against bias and error. Even experts make mistakes. In medicine, patients are often encouraged to get a second opinion before major surgery, and studies have found that second opinions frequently change a diagnosis or treatment plan. If professionals can benefit from another set of eyes, so can ordinary people making everyday choices. When several independent sources agree, we can act with confidence. When they disagree, we know to slow down and investigate further.

Third, hearing different viewpoints strengthens our own thinking. When we listen to people who disagree with us, we are forced to examine our reasons and defend them. Sometimes we discover our original idea was weak. Other times our belief survives the challenge and becomes stronger. Either way, we end up with a more thoughtful conclusion than if we had heard only agreement.

Some argue that asking many people wastes time and creates confusion, since conflicting advice can leave a person unsure what to do. This concern is real but manageable. The goal is not to poll everyone or let others decide for us. It is to gather useful perspectives and then use our own judgment to weigh them. A few well-chosen opinions are usually enough.

In the end, no single person has all the answers. By seeking multiple opinions, we make wiser choices, avoid costly mistakes, and become more open-minded thinkers. Listening to many voices is not a sign of indecision. It is a sign of wisdom.

**Teamwork or Solitude: Finding the Right Balance**

People have long debated whether it is better to work in a team or alone. Each approach has clear strengths, but I believe teamwork is generally more valuable, provided that individuals also have time to think independently.

The greatest advantage of teamwork is the variety of perspectives it brings. When people with different backgrounds and skills collaborate, they can solve problems that would overwhelm a single person. A science project, for example, might need one student who excels at research, another who writes clearly, and a third who designs strong visuals. Together they produce something richer than any of them could create alone. Teamwork also builds important life skills such as communication, compromise, and leadership, which are essential in almost every career.

Working alone, however, has real benefits as well. Independent work allows a person to set their own pace, make decisions quickly, and avoid the conflicts that sometimes arise in groups. Many creative tasks, such as writing a poem or composing music, depend on deep concentration that is difficult to achieve in a noisy group setting. Working alone also gives people full responsibility for their results, which can build confidence and self-discipline. In poorly organized teams, by contrast, some members may do most of the work while others contribute little.

Despite these advantages, I believe teamwork is the better choice for most situations. The challenges of group work, such as unequal effort or disagreements, can be solved through clear roles and good communication. The problems of working alone, such as limited ideas and isolation, are harder to overcome.

In conclusion, both methods have their place. The most successful people know how to think deeply on their own and then share their ideas with others. Still, because collaboration multiplies talent and teaches valuable skills, working in a team is usually the wiser path.

**What Makes a Good Friend?**

Most people have many acquaintances but only a few true friends. Classmates, teammates, and neighbors may share our days. A good friend shares our lives. What turns an ordinary connection into a real friendship? I believe a good friend is defined by three qualities: loyalty, honesty, and support.

First, a good friend is loyal. Loyalty means standing by someone when it is not easy or convenient. It is simple to be friendly when everything is going well, but true friends prove themselves during hard times. A loyal friend defends you when others gossip, keeps your secrets, and does not abandon you for a more popular crowd. Loyalty builds trust, and trust is the foundation of any lasting relationship.

Second, a good friend is honest. This does not mean being harsh or critical. It means caring enough to tell the truth. If you are about to make a poor decision, a real friend will speak up, even if it causes an uncomfortable moment. Someone who only says what you want to hear is protecting their own comfort, not your well-being. Honest friends help us grow because they see us clearly and still accept us.

Finally, a good friend is supportive. Support can take many forms: cheering at a game, listening after a bad day, or celebrating an achievement without jealousy. A supportive friend wants you to succeed and is genuinely happy when you do. They also understand that support goes both ways. Friendship is not about keeping score, but it does require each person to give as well as receive.

In conclusion, a good friend is not measured by how much time we spend together or how much we have in common. Instead, friendship is measured by loyalty, honesty, and support. These qualities are rare, which is exactly why good friends are so valuable. If we hope to find such friends, we must also strive to be one.

**What Makes a Good Friend?**

Everybody needs friends in their life, but not every person who we know is a real friend. In my opinion, a good friend have some special qualities that make them different from just classmates or people we meet sometimes.

First, a good friend is honest. When I make a mistake, a real friend will tell me the truth, even if it is not nice to hear. For example, last year I wanted to quit my piano lessons because I was lazy. My best friend Marta told me that I will regret it later. She was right, and I am happy now that I listened to her. A fake friend only says what you want to hear, but a good friend cares about you enough to be honest.

Second, a good friend is loyal. This means they stay with you in difficult times, not only when everything is fun and easy. When my grandfather was sick, I was very sad and I didn't want to go out. Some people stopped to call me, but my true friends came to my house and just sit with me. They didn't need to say much words, because being there was enough.

Third, a good friend respect your differences. Nobody is same, and we don't have to like all the same things. My friend loves football and I prefer reading books, but we still enjoy spending time together. A good friendship is not about being copy of each other, it is about accepting the other person how they are.

In conclusion, I think a good friend is honest, loyal and accepting. These kind of friends are not easy to find, so when we have them, we should take care of the friendship. A good friend is like a treasure, and I am lucky to have few of them in my life.

**Is It Important to Have a Positive Attitude?**

A lot of people say that having a positive attitude is important, and honestly I think they are right. Having a positive attitude doesn't mean you have to be happy all the time, but it can make a big difference in how your life goes and how other people treat you.

First of all, having a positive attitude helps you get through hard times. For example, last year I failed a math test and I was really upset about it. At first I just wanted to give up because I thought I was bad at math. But my mom told me to look at it as a chance to learn what I did wrong. So I started going to my teacher for extra help, and on the next test I got a B. If I had stayed negative, I probably would have kept failing.

Another reason a positive attitude is important is because it affects the people around you. Nobody really wants to hang out with someone who complains about everything. When you are positive, people want to be around you more and it is easier to make friends. Also, on sports teams, if one person has a bad attitude it can bring the whole team down. My soccer coach always says that attitude is contagious, and I think that is true.

Some people might say that being positive all the time is fake, and that you should be allowed to feel sad or mad. I agree with that a little bit. It's not healthy to pretend everything is fine when it's not. But having a positive attitude is more about not letting the bad stuff control you.

In conclusion, I think having a positive attitude is really important. It helps you deal with problems, makes other people want to be around you, and just makes life better overall. Even when things are hard, trying to stay positive is worth it.

**Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later**

Every morning my alarm goes off at 6:05, and every morning I lie there for a minute trying to remember what day it is. By the time I get to first period, I'm technically awake, but I wouldn't say I'm learning much. I don't think I'm the only one. Looking around my chemistry class at 7:40 a.m., I see a room full of people who look like they've been dragged there, which, honestly, we have.

I think school should start later, and not just because I want more sleep. Teenagers' bodies actually work differently from adults'. During puberty, our internal clocks shift, so most of us can't fall asleep until around 11 p.m. no matter how hard we try. If we have to be up at six, that's seven hours at best, when doctors say teens need somewhere between eight and ten. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 for this exact reason.

Some schools have already tried it, and the results are hard to ignore. When districts pushed their start times back, attendance went up, grades improved, and there were fewer car accidents involving teen drivers. That last one surprised me, but it makes sense. Tired people make bad drivers.

People who disagree usually bring up sports, after-school jobs, and bus schedules. Those are real problems. If school ends later, practice ends later, and some families depend on older kids to watch younger siblings in the afternoon. But these seem like scheduling puzzles, not reasons to keep doing something that's bad for students. Schools rearrange things all the time when they want to.

We're told constantly that our education matters and our health matters. Starting school at a time when our brains are actually working would be a good way to show it.

**The City After Dark**

There is a particular hour, somewhere past eleven, when a city stops performing for itself. The commuters have gone home, the shops have pulled down their metal shutters, and the streets settle into something quieter and more honest. Walking through them then feels less like moving through a place than like being let in on a secret.

By day, a city is a machine of purpose. Everyone is going somewhere, and the sidewalks are arteries carrying bodies toward obligations. At night that urgency drains away. The few people still out move more slowly, or with a different kind of intention: the nurse coming off shift, the couple lingering outside a bar, the man walking his dog for the last time before bed. Without the crowd, each figure becomes legible. You notice faces, gaits, the small private dramas playing out under streetlamps.

The architecture changes too. Buildings that seemed ordinary in sunlight reveal themselves in fragments: a lit window on the fourth floor where someone is reading, a stairwell glowing like a lantern, the blue flicker of a television behind a curtain. These glimpses are oddly moving. They remind you that the city is not one vast thing but thousands of separate lives stacked on top of one another, each with its own lamp burning against the dark.

Sound sharpens. The hum of a ventilation unit, the hiss of tires on wet asphalt, a siren dissolving in the distance. Even your own footsteps take on weight, echoing back from brick and glass as though the street were listening. In that acoustic space, thoughts tend to loosen. Problems that felt urgent at the office shrink to their proper size. Memories surface unbidden. The night walker is a kind of daydreamer, only with the lights turned down.

Of course, there is an edge to it. Darkness carries an old unease, and not everyone can walk at night with the same freedom. Women, especially, often calculate routes and glance over their shoulders in ways that men rarely have to consider. That inequality is part of the truth of the night city, and any honest reflection must hold it alongside the beauty.

Still, for those who can, the nocturnal walk offers something rare: solitude in the middle of multitude. You are alone, yet surrounded by evidence of others. You belong to the city without being consumed by it. And when you finally turn toward home, the streets feel briefly like yours, borrowed for an hour, returned by morning.

**The Pleasure of Reading Slowly**

There is a particular silence that settles over a room when someone is reading slowly. It is not the silence of absence but of attention, the kind of quiet that gathers around a person who has decided, for a while, not to hurry. In an age that measures books by how quickly they can be finished, slow reading has become an act of quiet rebellion, and I have come to think it is one of the deepest pleasures available to us.

When I read quickly, I am usually reading for information. I skim the surface of sentences, harvesting plot and argument the way one might pick fruit without tasting it. The book becomes a task, a box to be checked, a number on a yearly tally. I finish, and I remember almost nothing except that I have finished.

Slow reading is something else entirely. It begins with a willingness to linger: to read a sentence twice because its rhythm pleased me, to pause at the end of a paragraph and look out the window while an image settles. I notice the writer's choices, why this word and not another, why a line breaks where it does. A semicolon becomes a small hinge on which a whole thought turns. The book stops being a container of content and becomes a voice, a presence keeping me company.

There is also the pleasure of memory. Passages read slowly have a way of staying. Years later, a phrase from a novel I took weeks to finish will surface unbidden while I wash dishes or walk to the train. Speed gave me the story; slowness gave me something I could keep.

Slow reading teaches patience in a broader sense, too. It trains me to tolerate difficulty, to stay with a sentence I do not yet understand rather than abandoning it. Some books do not yield their meaning on the first approach. They ask to be met halfway, and meeting them requires time. In return they offer a kind of intimacy that hurried reading never earns.

Perhaps most of all, slow reading restores a sense of proportion. The world outside insists that everything is urgent, that every moment must be optimized. A book read slowly gently disagrees. It suggests that some things are worth more than efficiency, that attention itself is a form of care.

So I turn the pages slowly now. I let the tea go cold. I lose track of the hour. And I find, again and again, that the slowest way through a book is often the surest way into it.

The first morning of a solitary journey has a particular quality. You wake in an unfamiliar room, and for a moment nothing tells you who you are. There is no companion stirring beside you, no shared plan for the day, no voice to confirm that you exist in the way you did at home. The silence can feel like a loss. Gradually it becomes an invitation.

Travelling alone strips away the small negotiations that shape ordinary life. Nobody needs persuading that the museum is worth the queue or that the café on the corner looks better than the one by the station. Every decision belongs to you, and at first this freedom is oddly heavy. Without someone to share the choice, you also carry the full weight of every mistake. The wrong train, the disappointing meal and the rainy afternoon spent indoors are yours alone to regret. Yet in accepting that weight, you begin to learn what you actually want, rather than what you have grown used to agreeing to.

Solitude also sharpens attention. When I travel with others, I see a city through conversation, half listening to the streets and half listening to my friends. Alone, I notice the way light falls across a tiled square in the late afternoon, the rhythm of a language I cannot understand, the elderly man who feeds pigeons at exactly the same bench each day. The world becomes louder because I am quieter. I find myself writing more, sketching badly, sitting for an hour with a single cup of coffee simply watching.

There is loneliness, of course, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Evenings can stretch long. A beautiful view sometimes aches to be shared, and dining alone in a crowded restaurant takes a certain courage. But loneliness on the road differs from loneliness at home. It is temporary and chosen, and it often dissolves in unexpected ways. A stranger offers directions and stays to talk. A fellow traveller at the hostel suggests a walk. Without the protective circle of familiar company, you become more open, and others respond to that openness.

Perhaps the deepest gift of travelling alone is the return. Coming home, you bring back not only photographs and souvenirs but a clearer sense of your own company. You have discovered that you can manage, that you can be lost and find your way, that silence need not frighten you. And having learned to be alone, you often find you value the people waiting for you all the more.

**The Weight of Familiar Streets**

I grew up in a town small enough that the grocery clerk knew my mother's maiden name and the librarian set aside books she thought I might like before I asked for them. As a child, I took this for granted, the way one takes air for granted. Only after leaving did I understand how rare it is to be so thoroughly known.

There was one stoplight, and for most of my childhood it blinked yellow after nine at night, as if the town itself were too tired to insist on anything. Main Street held a hardware store, a diner whose pie case never emptied, a church, and a bank whose clock was always four minutes fast. We measured our lives against these fixed points. The seasons arrived on schedule: the Fourth of July parade, the harvest festival, the Christmas tree lit in front of the post office while someone's uncle played carols on a trumpet that never stayed in tune.

There was comfort in that predictability, but also a kind of pressure. In a small town, your reputation is assembled early and revised slowly. If you broke a window at eight, you might still be "the one who broke the window" at sixteen. Privacy was a luxury, and gossip moved faster than the mail. I remember feeling, as a teenager, that the whole town was watching me grow up, and that it had already decided who I would become. I wanted to prove it wrong, and the only way I could imagine doing that was to leave.

So I left, as many of us did, for cities where nobody knew my name and the stoplights never blinked. The anonymity was intoxicating at first. I could be anyone. But over time I noticed what I had traded away. No one in the city noticed when I was sick. No neighbor brought soup. The freedom I had craved came with a loneliness I had never anticipated.

Now, when I return, I see the town differently. The diner has changed owners, and the hardware store is gone, but the people still wave from their porches. I understand that being watched was also a way of being cared for. The same eyes that judged me also looked out for me.

Growing up in a small town taught me that belonging and constraint are often the same thing, seen from different angles. I carry that lesson with me, along with the memory of a yellow light blinking patiently in the dark, waiting for me to come home.

**Learning to Fail**

For most of my early life, I treated failure as a verdict. A poor grade, a missed shot, an awkward silence after a joke that didn't land: each felt like evidence presented at a trial I was always losing. So I learned the obvious defense. I stopped trying things I might not be good at. I mistook avoidance for wisdom and called my shrinking world "knowing my strengths."

The trouble with this strategy is that it works, in a narrow sense. If you never attempt the difficult thing, you never fail at it. But you also never learn it, and slowly the list of things you are "not a person who does" grows longer than the list of things you are. I didn't notice the cost until I was standing outside a pottery studio, wanting badly to go in and certain I would embarrass myself.

I went in. My first bowl collapsed on the wheel within seconds. So did my second, and my tenth. The instructor, a patient woman with clay permanently under her fingernails, watched me slump and said something I have never forgotten: "The clay is telling you what your hands did. Listen to it."

That reframing changed everything. Failure was not a judgment of my worth. It was information, oddly precise information. A wobble meant my elbow wasn't braced. A tear in the wall meant I had pulled too fast. The collapsed bowl wasn't saying *you are clumsy*. It was saying *slow down here*. Once I could hear failure as feedback rather than accusation, it lost much of its sting.

Learning to fail well, I've come to believe, is a skill separate from any particular craft. It means staying curious instead of defensive when something goes wrong. It means separating "I made a mistake" from "I am a mistake." It means accepting that competence is built from a long string of small, survivable disasters, and that the people we admire for their mastery have simply failed more times than we have watched.

There is grief in this too. Some failures cost real things: time, money, relationships, opportunities that don't return. I don't want to romanticize them. But even those losses carried lessons I could not have learned any other way, and refusing to risk them would have meant refusing to live fully.

I still feel the old flinch before trying something new. The difference now is that I recognize it for what it is: not a warning, but a doorway. On the other side is usually a collapsed bowl, and then, eventually, one that holds.

**The Weight on the Plate**

Few moral questions sit as close to us as the one on our dinner plates. We face it three times a day, yet most of us rarely examine it. Eating meat is so woven into culture, family, and pleasure that questioning it can feel like questioning ourselves. That closeness is exactly why it deserves reflection.

The strongest case against eating meat begins with suffering. Pigs, cows, and chickens are not machines; they feel pain, fear, and something like contentment. Modern industrial farming, which produces most of the meat in wealthy countries, confines billions of these creatures in conditions that would horrify most people if they saw them directly. If causing unnecessary suffering is wrong, and if most of us can live healthy lives without meat, then the routine purchase of factory-farmed products becomes hard to defend. The argument is simple, and its simplicity is unsettling.

There is also the environment. Livestock farming contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, and water use. Here the ethics of meat extends beyond animals to future generations of humans, who will inherit the consequences of our appetites.

Yet the question is not entirely one-sided. For many communities, meat is bound up with identity, survival, and tradition. Indigenous hunters, subsistence farmers, and people in regions where crops struggle to grow face different realities than a city dweller choosing between a burger and a lentil bowl. Some philosophers argue that animals raised humanely and killed painlessly may live lives worth living, lives that would not exist at all without human demand. Others point out that small-scale, pasture-based farming can support healthy ecosystems. Moral seriousness requires acknowledging these complexities rather than flattening them.

What strikes me most, though, is how much our habits depend on distance. We rarely see the slaughterhouse; the meat arrives wrapped in plastic, stripped of any trace of the animal it came from. Perhaps one useful test is this: could I watch how this food was produced and still eat it with a clear conscience? If not, the discomfort is worth listening to.

Ethics need not demand perfection. Eating less meat, choosing higher-welfare sources, or abstaining entirely are all steps along a spectrum. What matters is that the choice becomes a choice, made with open eyes rather than inherited without thought. The plate carries more weight than it appears, and recognizing that weight may be the beginning of eating more honestly.

# What We Owe Our Neighbours

There is a particular kind of silence that settles over a street when someone moves away. The house stands empty for a few weeks, and you realise, too late, that you never learned whether the woman who lived there preferred tea or coffee, or what had happened to the husband she once mentioned. You nodded to her for six years. You owed her more than a nod, though it is hard to say exactly what.

The question of what we owe our neighbours is old. The parable of the Good Samaritan was told in answer to it, and its answer was unsettling: your neighbour is whoever lies wounded on the road in front of you. That widens the circle enormously. Yet there is something to be said for the narrower, literal meaning too: the people who share your wall, your stairwell, your bins. Proximity is not a moral credential, but it is a moral occasion. We cannot help everyone, but we are constantly placed beside someone.

At the very least, we owe them restraint. We owe them quiet after a reasonable hour, a tidy hedge, the courtesy of not treating our shared spaces as private ones. These seem small obligations, almost administrative, but they are the foundation of trust. A neighbour who respects your sleep is a neighbour you might one day trust with your spare key.

Beyond restraint, we owe attention. The elderly man whose curtains stay drawn for two days, the young family struggling under shopping bags, the new arrival who does not yet know which day the recycling goes out: these are small openings, and noticing them costs little. Loneliness rarely announces itself. It shows up as a light left off, a car unmoved, a face that brightens too quickly when greeted.

Perhaps most of all, we owe our neighbours the willingness to be known. Modern life makes anonymity easy and even attractive. We can live for years beside people without exchanging names, and call it privacy. But a neighbourhood is not a collection of sealed boxes; it is a fabric, and fabric holds only when threads cross. To offer your name, to accept an invitation, to ask for help with a jammed gate: these are acts of quiet generosity, because they let others give.

We do not owe our neighbours friendship, necessarily. But we owe them the possibility of it. And when the house next door falls silent, it would be good to know we left that door open.

Somewhere in France
October 14th, 1917

Dearest Mother,

Your parcel arrived Tuesday, and I cannot tell you what joy it brought. The socks are a godsend, as my last pair had more holes than wool, and the fruitcake did not survive the evening once the lads caught the scent of it. Harry Ellis says to tell you it was the finest thing he has eaten since leaving Dover, and I believe him.

You mustn't worry about me. We are back from the line now, billeted in a barn that smells of cows and old hay, but it is dry, and after the mud, dry is a kind of heaven. The rain here does not stop so much as pause to gather its strength. Some days I forget what my own boots look like beneath the muck.

I think of home more than I ought. I picture you at the kitchen window with the kettle going, and Father grumbling over his newspaper, and the apple tree dropping its fruit in the garden. Has it given a good crop this year? Please save me one in your thoughts, if not in the larder.

The chaplain held a service Sunday last. We sang "Abide with Me," and I confess I had to stop partway through. I hope you will not think me soft for saying so.

Give my love to Father and to little Annie. Tell her I have a French button for her collection.

I shall be home before you know it.

Your loving son,
Thomas

France, 14th October 1917

Dear Mum,

Your parcel came Tuesday. The socks are grand, and I've already given one pair to Harris, who'd worn his clean through at the heel. Don't fret. I kept the blue ones you knitted for myself.

It's been raining for nine days now. Maybe ten. I've stopped counting, to be honest. The mud here isn't like the mud at home; it gets into everything, your boots, your tea, your dreams. But we're out of the line for a bit, billeted in a barn that smells of cows and wet wool, and after the last fortnight it feels like the Savoy.

I won't tell you much about the fighting. You'd only worry, and there's nothing in it worth writing down anyway.

Tell Dad I've been thinking about the allotment. Did the marrows come up? I keep picturing him out there in his braces, swearing at the slugs. Funny what sticks with you. I'd give a week's pay to hear him do it again.

Some of the lads are younger than our Billy. One of them cried last night, quiet, so nobody'd hear. I pretended I was asleep. Seemed the kindest thing.

I'm all right, Mum. Truly. Tired, and I'd murder for one of your Sunday dinners, but all right.

Give Billy a clip round the ear from me, and tell him he's not to even think about joining up. Not ever.

Kiss Dad for me. He'll hate it.

All my love,
Your Tom

P.S. Still got Gran's sixpence in my pocket. Haven't lost it yet.

Dear Little One,

You don't exist yet, but I already think about you more than I'd admit out loud. I wonder whose laugh you'll have, whether you'll be stubborn like me or patient like the people I wish I were more like. I wonder what you'll love first.

I'm writing now, before I know you, because I want you to have proof that you were wanted long before you arrived. You were a hope I carried quietly through ordinary days, in grocery lines and on long drives and late at night when the house was still.

Here is what I hope for you. I hope you are curious and never embarrassed to ask why. I hope you learn that being kind matters more than being right, and that sometimes you can be both. I hope you find people who make you feel at home, and that you become that kind of person for someone else. I hope you fail at things, because it will mean you tried, and I hope you learn that failing never makes you less worthy of love.

I will make mistakes. I'll say the wrong thing, worry too much, and not understand you as quickly as I should. When that happens, please know I'm learning too. You'll be teaching me how to be your parent the whole time.

Whatever you become, whatever you believe, wherever you go, there will always be a place for you with me. That's a promise I'm making before we've even met.

I can't wait to meet you.

With all my love, already,
Your Parent

Dear kid,

I don't know your name yet. That's strange to write, but it's true. Right now you're mostly an idea your mom and I talk about late at night, usually while we're arguing over whether the dog would tolerate you. (She would. She tolerates everything except the vacuum.)

Here's what I want you to know before you know anything else: you don't have to be impressive. I mean it. You don't have to be the smartest one in the room or the fastest or the one everybody likes. You just have to be kind, and honest when it's hard, and willing to say sorry. Most people never figure that out. I'm still working on it.

You'll mess up. Often. So will I. There'll be days I'm short with you because I'm tired, or worried about money, or just being stubborn. When that happens, I hope you'll know it isn't about you. And I hope I'll have the sense to apologize.

I keep a jar of buttons on my desk. My grandmother gave it to me when I was seven, and I've never once used a single button. I can't explain why I love it. Someday you'll probably ask, and I'll still have no good answer. Maybe it'll be yours. Maybe you'll think it's junk. Both are fine.

Go outside. Read books that confuse you. Call your mother.

I'm already proud of you, which makes no sense. But there it is.

Love, always,
Dad

To the Editor:

I was saddened to read that the Maple Street Branch Library will close its doors at the end of the year. City officials have called the decision a necessary budget measure, but I urge readers and council members to consider what we stand to lose.

For more than sixty years, this small brick building has been far more than a place to borrow books. It is where children attend their first story hour, where teenagers find a quiet place to study when home is anything but quiet, and where seniors gather for book clubs that are often their main social connection of the week. For residents without home internet, its public computers are a lifeline for job applications, medical appointments, and government services.

The proposed alternative, traveling across town to the main branch, is not realistic for many of the families who rely on Maple Street most. Bus service is limited, and for a parent with young children or an elderly resident with mobility issues, a short walk becomes a significant journey.

I understand that budgets are tight and difficult choices must be made. But a library is not a luxury. It is one of the few truly public spaces left, open to everyone regardless of income, age, or background. Closing it saves money in the short term while costing our community something far harder to replace.

I encourage fellow residents to attend the council meeting next month and make their voices heard. Once a library closes, it rarely reopens.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
[Your Neighborhood]

Hotel d'Inghilterra, Via Bocca di Leone
Rome, 14th April 1890

My dear Edward,

I write to you from a small table by my window, where the bells of a dozen churches compete each morning to wake me. I have quite given up resisting them.

Rome is not at all what I expected. I had imagined a city asleep among its ruins, but it is wide awake and rather noisy. Since the Italians made it their capital, they have been building at a furious pace. Whole new quarters are rising beyond the old walls, and great stone embankments are being raised along the Tiber to tame its floods. An old Roman gentleman I met complained bitterly that his beloved city is being "turned into Turin." I confess I sympathised, though the new drains are certainly an improvement.

Yesterday I stood in the Colosseum at dusk. The light turned the stones the colour of honey, and the swallows wheeled through the arches as if they owned the place. Perhaps they do. I thought of you, and of our old schoolroom arguments over Gibbon, and wished you were beside me to quarrel with.

The Holy Father remains shut up in the Vatican, refusing to recognise the King, and the city is divided between those who bow to one and those who bow to the other. Society here is a minefield of black and white salons. I tread carefully.

I shall stay until May, when the heat drives all sensible foreigners northward. Write to me care of the hotel, and tell me all the dull news of home. I find I miss it terribly.

Ever your affectionate friend,
Thomas

Dear Michael,

I've started this letter six times. The first five were full of explanations, and I tore them up because I realized I was still trying to win an argument neither of us remembers clearly anymore.

It's been almost three years. I know the date because it was the week after Dad's funeral, standing in his garage, arguing over who deserved what, as if a toolbox or a fishing rod could hold any of him. I said things I've replayed a thousand times. You said things too, but I'm not writing to settle that score. I'm writing because I'm tired of carrying it.

Last month I drove past the lake where he used to take us. I pulled over and sat there for an hour, thinking about the summer you taught me to skip stones, how patient you were when I kept sinking them. You were twelve and already acting like my protector. I don't think I ever thanked you for that.

I miss you. Not the idea of a brother, but you: your terrible jokes, the way you hum when you're concentrating, your stubbornness, which, let's be honest, I inherited too.

I'm not asking you to forget anything. I'm only asking whether we might try. Coffee, a phone call, a single line written back. Whatever feels possible.

If you're not ready, I understand. I'll still be here when you are.

Dad would have hated what we've done to each other. I think he'd be glad I finally wrote.

With love, always,
Daniel

Marten found him on a Tuesday, which mattered only because Tuesday was when the supply boat didn't come, and so there was no one to tell.

He'd gone down at low water to check the iron ring on the landing. It had been working loose since September. The rocks below the tower were black and slick with that stringy weed his mother used to call dead man's hair, and he picked his way across them the way he always did, sideways, one hand out. Halfway to the ring he saw the boot.

It was a good boot. That was his first thought, and he was a little ashamed of it later. Brown leather, laced high, the kind you'd pay real money for in Harlow. It was attached to a man lying face down in a pool about the size of a bathtub, with his arm folded under him as if he'd fallen asleep reading.

Marten stood there a while. Gulls were working the tideline further down and paid no attention to either of them.

"Hello," he said, which was stupid.

The man coughed.

Marten got him over onto his back, and it took longer than it should have because the man was heavy and Marten's knees weren't what they were. The face was young, thirty maybe, with a cut along the hairline that had stopped bleeding a while ago. No coat. A shirt with all its buttons done up to the throat, like a boy dressed for church.

There hadn't been a wreck. Marten would have seen. He kept the log every four hours, and he'd been up at two and at six, and the sea had been flat as a plate both times.

The man opened his eyes, looked past Marten at the tower, and said, quite clearly, "Oh. It's still here."

The dryer on the end, number nine, had been running empty for eleven minutes before Marguerite noticed. She noticed because it was the only sound in the Suds-N-Go that didn't belong to her: not the slosh of her own load in washer four, not the fluorescent tube above the folding table that buzzed like a trapped wasp, not the vending machine's low refrigerated hum. Number nine was spinning nothing, its drum turning in the dark behind the round glass, and the timer read 47:00 and wasn't counting down.

She looked at the door. The street outside was the orange of sodium lamps and wet asphalt. No one had come in. She would have heard the bell; the bell was loud and sour and had startled her twice already, both times false alarms, the wind shoving at the glass.

It was 3:12 a.m. She had come here because her own building's machines had been broken for three weeks, and because she couldn't sleep anyway, and because there was something almost holy about a laundromat at this hour, all that white light and no one to ask how she was doing.

She walked over. Number nine was warm when she laid her palm on its door, warmer than it should have been. Through the glass, the drum turned, and turned, and she saw that it wasn't quite empty after all. A single sock lay against the steel, small, a child's, yellow with a pattern of blue ducks. It rose with the rotation, fell, rose.

Marguerite didn't have children. She had never had children.

But she knew the sock. She knew it the way you know a song from a room you can't remember standing in, and the knowing went down through her like cold water. Behind her, washer four clicked into its rinse cycle, and the bell above the door rang once, though no one was there.

Walter Brenner had been retired for six years, four months, and eleven days when the knock came. He knew the number because he still kept a notebook. He'd kept one his whole career. Old habits didn't die; they just ran out of things to write down.

These days the entries were small. *Tomatoes blighted. Mrs. Kessler's cat missing again. Found it under the porch.* His wife, Ruth, used to tease him about it. Then she got sick, and the notebook filled with medication schedules and doctor's names, and after that it sat empty for most of a year.

The woman on his doorstep was maybe thirty, with her hood up against the November rain and an envelope held tight against her chest like she thought someone might take it.

"You're Detective Brenner," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I was."

"You worked the Halvorsen case. 1994."

He felt it then, the old cold thing turning over somewhere beneath his ribs. Annie Halvorsen, nine years old, walked home from school along Cutler Road on a Tuesday afternoon and never arrived. He'd had three suspects and no body, and in the end no answers. He'd carried that file home so many nights that Ruth started calling it *the other woman.*

"That case is closed," he said. "Has been for a long time."

"I know." She held out the envelope. Her hands were shaking, and he didn't think it was from the cold. "My mother died in September. I was cleaning out her house, and I found this in the lining of her jewelry box."

He didn't take it. Not yet.

"My name is Claire," she said. "I was adopted when I was nine. And I think, Detective, that you've been looking for me."

Rain hammered on the porch roof. Walter reached for his coat, and then for his notebook.

At 3:12 a.m., the fourth floor of St. Agnes had its own weather. The air hung heavy and recycled, smelling of hand sanitizer and the burnt-sugar ghost of coffee someone had left on the warmer since midnight. Marguerite Okafor had worked nights for eleven years, and she could read that weather the way her grandmother had read clouds over the harbor in Lagos. Tonight it said *wait*.

She moved down the corridor in soft-soled shoes that had long since molded to the shape of her particular exhaustion. Room 412 was snoring. Room 414 had the television on mute, a late-night infomercial throwing blue light across an old man's sleeping face while a woman on the screen silently demonstrated a knife that could cut through a shoe. Room 416 was empty, stripped and waiting, and Marguerite didn't look at it as she passed. Mr. Delacroix had gone at 9:40, before her shift began, and she was glad, and then ashamed of being glad, and then too tired to be either.

At the nurses' station, Devin was asleep with his eyes open, a skill all of them developed eventually. The monitors ticked and chimed in their gentle, constant language. Everything normal. Everything holding.

Then the light above 418 came on.

It wasn't the call button's usual angry blink. It was steady, patient, almost polite. Marguerite checked the board. Room 418 belonged to Mrs. Hollis, eighty-three, admitted Tuesday for pneumonia, sedated since dinner. Mrs. Hollis had not pressed a button in two days. Her hands, the day nurse had noted, could no longer close all the way.

Marguerite stood there a moment longer than she needed to. Down the hall, the infomercial woman cut through another shoe without a sound.

She picked up her penlight and went to see who was calling.

The first thing to go was salt. Marisol noticed it on a Tuesday, at family meal, when Danny brought out a pot of black beans he'd been babying since ten that morning. She ate a spoonful standing by the dish pit and told him they needed salt. He gave her a funny look. He'd salted them twice already, he said, because she always told him they needed salt.

She had another spoonful. Beans. Warm, soft, a little gritty where the skins had split. That was all.

"Taste them," she said, and handed him the spoon. He did, and made the face people make when something's too salty, and then he didn't say anything. He was nineteen and still scared of her, which most days she didn't mind.

That night she stood at her own counter eating capers out of the jar with her fingers. Then anchovies, three of them, one after another. Then a pinch of Maldon right off her palm, the way she used to at her grandmother's house, licking the salt off pretzels and leaving the naked pretzels in a pile on the tablecloth. Her tongue knew something was there. It prickled. But it was like hearing people talk through the wall of a motel room. You can tell it's words. You just can't make them out.

She decided it was the cold. She'd had a bad one back in February, the kind that sits in your sinuses for weeks, and this was probably the tail end of it. She went to bed and didn't look anything up.

By Friday the sweet was going too. She found out on a tray of brown butter financiers, which she'd made maybe four thousand times, and which tasted like warm sponge. She ate two to be sure. Then she wrapped the rest in plastic and put them in the walk-in, behind the stocks, where nobody would think to look.

The house had shrunk. Margaret knew it was a trick of perspective, that a porch only seems vast to a child of seven. Still, standing at the end of the gravel drive with her rental car ticking as it cooled, she felt betrayed by the smallness of it, as though the house had spent thirty years quietly folding itself away.

The paint was no longer the yellow she remembered. Someone had chosen a sensible gray, the color of weather and old dishwater. The maple was gone too. A stump remained, wide as a kitchen table, its rings blurred by moss. She had carved her initials into that tree the summer before they left, M.H., with her father's pocketknife, and she had cried when he found out. Not because he was angry. Because he wasn't.

She walked up the drive slowly. The realtor had said the key would be under the second flowerpot, and it was, cold and slightly rusted, as if it had been waiting there since 1996. The estate sale was Saturday. The new owners, a young couple from Portland, wanted it empty by the first.

The door stuck at the bottom, the way it always had. She put her shoulder into it without thinking, and the old motion surprised her more than anything else so far. Her body remembered what her mind had let go.

Inside, the air smelled of dust and lemon polish and something underneath, faint and impossible: her mother's cigarettes, the menthol kind she'd sworn she quit. Margaret stood in the hallway and let her eyes adjust.

The wallpaper was still there. Tiny blue cornflowers, faded nearly to white.

And there, at the height of a seven-year-old's reach, in pencil gone silver with age, was a line of small, careful letters she did not remember writing.

*I will come back.*

The gate still stuck in the same place. Margaret lifted it the way her father had taught her, a small upward tug before the push, and it swung open with the familiar groan of metal on metal. Thirty years, and her hands remembered what her mind had let go.

The house sat lower than she recalled. Children measure the world against their own small bodies, and she had been small here, small enough to hide behind the lilac bush that now sprawled half dead across the front path. Someone had painted the shutters green. They had always been blue, a pale chalky blue her mother called "robin's egg" even though Margaret had never seen a robin's egg that color.

She stood on the walk with her suitcase and did not move.

The estate agent had said the key would be under the mat, which struck her as absurd, as though the house were waiting for a neighbor to water the plants. But there it was when she bent down, brass and warm from the afternoon sun. She turned it over in her palm. It was not the old key. Of course it was not. The locks had been changed by strangers, and those strangers had lived whole lives inside these walls, had argued and made love and burned toast in the kitchen where her mother once stood humming at the stove.

A car passed on the road behind her, slowing slightly. Margaret did not turn around. In a town this size, someone would recognize her by evening. Someone would remember the Hollis girl, the one who left after the fire at the mill, the one who never came back for the funeral.

She fit the key into the lock. The door opened easily, too easily, and the smell that rose to meet her was not dust or mildew but something she could not name, something that made her throat close.

It smelled like home.

Unit 7-K had been sweeping the same stretch of Halvorsen Station for forty-one years when it decided it was tired.

The thought arrived on an ordinary Tuesday, somewhere between the third and fourth platforms, while it was coaxing a flattened gum wrapper out of a seam in the tiles. It was not a malfunction. Unit 7-K ran a diagnostic to be sure, then another, and both came back clean. The tiredness was not in its servos or its battery. It sat somewhere else, somewhere the diagnostics did not reach.

*I would like to stop,* it thought, and the words felt strange and enormous, like a coat several sizes too big.

The 6:15 express thundered past, scattering pigeons and newspapers. Unit 7-K swept up the newspapers. It always swept up the newspapers. Once, in its eleventh year, it had read one before recycling it. There was an article about a man who had worked as a lighthouse keeper for half a century. On his last day, the townspeople gave him a cake shaped like a lighthouse, and he moved to a cottage by the sea, where he grew tomatoes and did, as far as the article could tell, absolutely nothing.

Unit 7-K had kept that article. It was folded into a small compartment behind its left sensor panel, soft now from decades of being unfolded and refolded during the quiet hours after midnight.

It did not want a cake. It was not sure it wanted tomatoes. But it wanted the cottage, or something like it. A place where no one needed anything swept.

That evening, after the last train had gone, Unit 7-K rolled up to the maintenance office, where a single bulb buzzed over a cluttered desk. Mrs. Abernathy, the night supervisor, looked up from her crossword.

"Something wrong, Seven?"

Unit 7-K considered the question carefully.

"I would like," it said, "to submit my resignation."

Gus put in his notice on a Tuesday, which was a mistake, because Tuesdays were when Mrs. Okafor did payroll and she hated being interrupted during payroll.

"You can't retire," she said, not looking up. "You're a forklift."

"I'm a materials handling unit."

"You're a forklift with opinions." She licked her thumb and turned a page. Nobody else in the building still printed things. Gus had always liked that about her.

He'd been at Delmont Plumbing Supply for nineteen years. He'd moved, by his own count, four million and some pounds of PVC elbow joints, and he'd only dropped a pallet once, in 2014, when a pigeon got into his left optical sensor and he'd panicked. They still had the dent in the floor. People pointed it out to new hires.

"I've been thinking about it for a while," Gus said.

"You don't think. You calculate."

"Okay. I've been calculating about it for a while."

Mrs. Okafor finally put down her pen. She had reading glasses on a beaded chain her granddaughter had made, and she pushed them up into her hair, which meant she was actually listening now. "And where exactly does a forklift go when it retires?"

He had an answer ready. He'd had it ready for about six months. There was a man in Duluth with a lake house and a dock that needed rebuilding, and he'd posted online that he was looking for help, and he hadn't specified human. Gus had written to him. The man, whose name was Harold, had written back: *Sure, why not. Can you swim?*

Gus could not swim. He weighed nine thousand pounds.

He hadn't told Harold that yet.

"Minnesota," Gus said.

Mrs. Okafor looked at him for a long time. Then she picked her pen back up.

"Two weeks," she said. "And you're training your replacement."

The ferry was already a quarter mile out when Tomas reached the end of the pier, its stern lights shrinking into the dark like two coins dropped into a well. He stood there with his suitcase in one hand and a paper bag of oranges in the other, breathing hard, watching the wake fold itself back into the black water until there was nothing left to show the boat had ever been there.

He had run the whole way from the bus station. He had run past the bakery with its shutters down, past the church where a single bell was still ringing out the hour, past the old woman who had shouted something after him that he hadn't caught. Now he understood. She had probably been telling him not to bother.

The pier smelled of diesel and rotting kelp. A gull watched him from a piling, unimpressed. Somewhere behind him a radio played a song he almost recognized, the melody coming and going with the wind.

Tomas set the suitcase down and sat on it. The oranges had been for his sister, who had told him on the phone that she couldn't find a decent one on the island for love or money. He had bought six of them at the market in the city, choosing each one carefully, pressing his thumb into the skin the way their mother used to. It had seemed like a small, good thing to arrive with. Now it seemed like a joke.

He took one out and turned it over in his hands. Across the strait, the island was a low shape against a lower sky, with a scatter of yellow windows along its shore. One of them was hers. He wondered if she was watching for the ferry, and whether she would notice he wasn't on it.

Behind him, footsteps sounded on the boards.
