"Roll up your sleeve."

"Mom."

"Roll it up, Jess. I saw you wincing when you hugged me."

Jess sighed and pushed the fabric past her elbow. A sparrow, small and fine-lined, still pink at the edges, sat on the inside of her forearm.

Her mother stared. "When?"

"Saturday."

"Saturday. And you didn't think to mention it."

"I'm twenty-two. I don't need a permission slip."

"I didn't say you did. I said you didn't *mention* it." She set down the dish towel. "That's permanent, you know. You'll be sixty with that on your arm."

"That's kind of the point."

"The point of what? Looking like you lost a bet?"

"It's a sparrow, not a skull."

"I can see it's a sparrow."

"Do you know *why* it's a sparrow?"

Her mother opened her mouth, then closed it.

"Grandma's kitchen window," Jess said quietly. "The feeder. She used to make me count them while she did the crossword. Every morning, every summer."

The kitchen went still. Her mother reached out, hesitated, then touched the skin just beside the ink, careful of the soreness.

"She called them her little gossips," she said.

"I know."

"She'd have hated this, you realize. Absolutely hated it."

"I know." Jess almost smiled. "She'd have told me I ruined a perfectly good arm."

"And then she'd have asked to see it again." Her mother's voice cracked on the last word. She cleared her throat and picked up the towel. "Put some lotion on it. It looks dry."

"Is that a yes?"

"It's a *put lotion on it*."

Gate 14 was crowded, so Maya took the only open seat, beside a man hunched over a crossword.

"Seven letters," he muttered. "'Long-lost companion.'"

She glanced at the page, then at his face. "Theo?"

He looked up. The pen slipped from his fingers. "Maya Brennan. You're joking."

"I'm not. What are you doing in Denver?"

"Layover. Four hours. You?"

"Delayed. Three." She laughed. "Twenty years, and we run into each other at a gate that smells like cinnamon pretzels."

"Twenty-two," he said. "Your going-away party. You cried into the punch bowl."

"I did not."

"You absolutely did. Danny had to pour it out."

She shook her head, smiling. "How is Danny?"

Theo's face changed, just slightly. "He passed. Three years ago. Heart."

"Oh, Theo. I didn't know."

"How could you? We all scattered." He picked up the pen and turned it over. "He talked about you, you know. Said you were the only one of us who actually left."

"Leaving isn't the same as going somewhere."

"Did you? Go somewhere?"

She thought about it. "Lisbon for a while. Then Toronto. Two kids. A divorce. A garden I'm terrible at."

"Sounds like somewhere to me."

The intercom crackled. *Flight 2210 to Toronto, now boarding.*

"That's me," she said, but didn't stand.

Theo tore the corner off his newspaper, wrote a number, and handed it to her. "Don't make it twenty-two more."

She tucked it into her pocket. "Seven letters. 'Long-lost companion.'"

He grinned. "I'll figure it out."

"I'm just saying, I found the listing."

"You found it on a site I sent you."

Gabe was standing in the doorway of the big room with his arms out, like he could measure it with his wingspan. He couldn't. It had a radiator under the window that clanked every few minutes for no reason.

"Okay, but I called the guy," he said.

"You called him once. I went to the viewing."

"I was at work."

"You were at Kyle's."

He didn't argue with that. Tom set the box he was holding on the floor of the hallway, which was where most of their stuff still was.

"Rock paper scissors," Gabe said.

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because you always do rock first and you know I know that, so you'll do paper, and then it's just this whole thing."

"So what, then? Coin?"

"I don't have a coin. Who has a coin."

Gabe dug in his pocket and came up with a hair tie and a receipt from the Shell station. He looked at both like one of them might help.

"Fine," Tom said. "You take it. But you pay sixty more."

"Sixty?"

"It's like a third bigger."

"It is not a third bigger."

"It has a closet, Gabe. Mine has a hook."

Gabe looked back into the room. The radiator clanked.

"Forty," he said.

"Fifty, and you deal with the landlord. Every time."

"Even the toilet thing?"

"Especially the toilet thing."

Gabe sighed and dragged his mattress in sideways, knocking the light switch off on his way through.

"We passed that cow already," Dana said.

"All cows look the same."

"This one has a spot shaped like Ohio, Mark. We've seen Ohio three times."

Mark gripped the wheel tighter. "The GPS said turn left at the fork."

"The GPS also said 'recalculating' for forty minutes and then died."

"It didn't die. It's resting."

"It's a phone, not a golden retriever."

The road narrowed. Corn pressed in on both sides like a crowd at a parade nobody wanted to attend.

"We could ask someone," Dana offered.

"Who? The cow?"

"She seems to know the area."

Mark laughed despite himself, then caught it and tried to look stern. "I had a plan. Scenic route. Romantic. You said you wanted adventure."

"I said I wanted a waffle."

"Adventure waffle. That was the plan."

"Where's the waffle, Mark?"

"Somewhere," he said, gesturing vaguely at the horizon, "in that direction. Probably."

She reached over and turned on the radio. Static, then a fiddle, then a man's voice announcing the Harvest Festival in a town neither of them had heard of.

"Pancake breakfast," Dana repeated slowly. "Eight to noon."

They looked at each other.

"Pancakes are just flat waffles," Mark said.

"That's not even a little bit true."

"Do you want to argue, or do you want pancakes?"

She considered it. Outside, the cow watched them idle at the fork.

"Left," she said. "And if we see Ohio again, I'm driving."

Mr. Kowalczyk held the water bottle up to the window like he was checking it for fish.

"Molar mass of sodium chloride," he said. "Fifty-eight point four four. That's very good, Tyler."

"That's not mine."

"It's got your name on the cap."

"My mom writes my name on everything. That doesn't mean anything."

"Your mom wrote the molar mass of sodium chloride on the inside of the label."

Tyler looked at the floor. Somebody's gum was stuck near the leg of the desk, gray and flattened out, and he looked at that instead.

"You peeled it back and wrote on the paper side," Kowalczyk said. "That's actually kind of clever. Took me a second."

"So can I go?"

"No."

"Lunch is in like four minutes."

"I know when lunch is." He set the bottle down. It was still half full and it sloshed. "You want to know what gets me? You had Avogadro's number on there too. Spelled wrong. We haven't even done that yet."

"I didn't know what'd be on it."

"So you wrote everything."

"Kind of."

"How long did that take?"

Tyler shrugged. "Like an hour."

"The quiz was ten questions. You could've just studied for an hour."

"That's different."

"How?"

Tyler opened his mouth and closed it. A bell went off somewhere down the hall, the early one for the freshman wing.

"I'm calling your mom," Kowalczyk said.

"Okay."

"You can retake it Thursday. No bottle."

"Can I have it back, though? It's a good bottle."

Kowalczyk looked at it for a while. "Thursday," he said.

**Hartwell's Bakery Celebrates a Century of Fresh Bread on Main Street**

When Elsie Hartwell first opened her bakery doors on Main Street in 1926, a loaf of bread cost nine cents. On Saturday, her great-grandson Daniel Hartwell marked the shop's 100th anniversary by handing out free cinnamon rolls to a line of customers that wrapped around the block.

"People ask what the secret is," said Daniel, 44, who took over the business from his father in 2012. "Honestly, it's showing up at four in the morning, every morning, for a hundred years."

The bakery has weathered the Great Depression, wartime sugar rationing, and the arrival of two supermarket chains on the edge of town. Through it all, the Hartwells have kept the same sourdough starter alive. Family legend holds that Elsie brought it from her mother's kitchen in Ohio.

Longtime customer Margaret Olsen, 87, remembers buying jelly doughnuts there as a girl. "I came here with my mother, then with my children, and now my grandchildren drag me in," she said, laughing. "The doughnuts taste exactly the same."

The celebration drew Mayor Tom Reyes, who presented the family with a plaque recognizing the bakery as the town's oldest continuously operating business. The local high school band played outside, and a display of black-and-white photographs showed the storefront through the decades.

Daniel's teenage daughter, Lily, now works weekend shifts behind the counter. Asked whether she might one day run the bakery herself, she smiled.

"Maybe," she said. "Somebody has to keep the starter going."

Hartwell Bakery Celebrates a Century on Main Street

When Margaret Hartwell first opened the doors of her small bakery on Main Street in 1926, a loaf of bread cost nine cents and the ovens were fired with coal. One hundred years later, the shop still smells of warm rye and cinnamon, and the line still stretches out the door on Saturday mornings.

Hartwell Bakery marked its centennial this weekend with a celebration that drew hundreds of residents. Families lined up for free slices of anniversary cake, and longtime customers shared stories of birthdays, weddings and holidays made sweeter by the bakery's famous almond kringle.

The business is now run by Margaret's great-grandson, Daniel Hartwell, who started sweeping floors there at age twelve. "My great-grandmother wrote her recipes on index cards, and we still use most of them," he said. "Some of the cards are so stained with butter you can barely read them, but we know them by heart."

The bakery has weathered the Great Depression, wartime rationing and the arrival of supermarket chains. Daniel credits loyal neighbors for its survival. "People here kept coming back, even when times were hard. That's the only reason we're still standing."

Eighty-seven-year-old Ruth Callahan has been a customer since childhood. "I bought my first cinnamon roll here with a nickel my father gave me," she said. "It tastes exactly the same today."

To honor the milestone, the bakery will offer a different vintage recipe each week through the end of the year. Hartwell Bakery is open Tuesday through Sunday, starting at 6 a.m.

**Thousands Left Without Power After Overnight Fault**

Around 4,000 homes were left without electricity on Tuesday evening after a fault at a local substation plunged several neighbourhoods into darkness.

The outage began shortly after 7pm, affecting households across the town's northern and eastern districts. Residents reported lights flickering before failing completely, with streetlights, traffic signals and some shops also losing power.

The regional network operator said engineers were dispatched within the hour and traced the problem to a damaged underground cable feeding the Millbrook Road substation. Power was gradually restored in stages, with most customers reconnected by midnight. A small number of homes remained affected until around 3am.

"We understand how disruptive a power cut can be, especially on a cold November evening," a spokesperson for the operator said. "Our teams worked through the night to get everyone back on supply as quickly and safely as possible. We apologise for the inconvenience."

Local resident Margaret Hollis, 72, said she spent the evening wrapped in blankets by candlelight. "It came on so suddenly. My neighbour checked in on me, which was kind, but it was a long few hours," she said.

Police were called to manage traffic at two junctions where signals had failed, and no serious incidents were reported.

The operator has advised affected customers who were without power for more than 12 hours that they may be eligible for compensation. Vulnerable residents are encouraged to join the Priority Services Register to receive extra support during future outages.

The cause of the cable damage is still under investigation.

Thousands left without power after cable fault in Ashford

Around 4,000 homes across Ashford and the surrounding villages lost power on Tuesday evening after an underground cable failed near the Kingsnorth substation.

The outage began shortly after 6.15pm, just as many families were sitting down to dinner. Streets in Kingsnorth, Park Farm and parts of Willesborough went dark, and traffic lights on the A2070 stopped working for a time, causing queues heading into town.

UK Power Networks said engineers were sent out within half an hour. By 9pm supply had been restored to about 2,600 properties by rerouting power through other parts of the network. The remaining homes were back on just before 1am.

A spokesman for the company said: "We're sorry to everyone affected. The fault was on an underground cable and our teams worked through the night to find it and get people's power back on."

Sue Halden, 67, of Brookfield Road, said she had been halfway through cooking when the lights went out. "I had a pan of potatoes on and that was that," she said. "We got the candles out and sat it out. You just have to, don't you?"

Others were less patient. Several residents complained online that the company's outage map wasn't updated for over an hour.

Customers who were without power for more than 12 hours may be entitled to compensation. Anyone vulnerable or relying on medical equipment can sign up to the Priority Services Register by calling 105.

The company said repairs to the damaged cable would carry on through the week.

**Students Squeezed as Rents Climb Again Near Campus**

By Dana Kowalczyk, Staff Writer

Maya Herrera thought she'd found a deal last spring: a two-bedroom on Locust Street, $1,150 a month, split with a friend from her chemistry lab. When the lease came up for renewal in August, the landlord wanted $1,425.

"I just kind of stared at the email for a while," said Herrera, a junior at Bellmont State. "We signed it anyway. Where else were we going to go?"

She's far from alone. Average rent for a one-bedroom within a mile of campus hit $1,040 this fall, up about 11 percent from last year, according to figures the city housing office released Monday. Two years ago, the same unit went for around $860.

Part of the problem is simple math. Enrollment at Bellmont State grew by roughly 1,400 students since 2023, while the university added just one new dorm, which opened with 310 beds. Everyone else is competing for the same old houses on the north side.

Longtime residents are feeling it too. Gerald Pruitt, 71, has rented the same duplex on Elm Avenue for 19 years. His rent went up $200 in October.

"They know some kid's parents will pay it," Pruitt said. "I'm on a fixed income. I can't."

City Councilmember Ruth Ahn said she plans to bring a proposal to the council next month that would push the university to build more student housing. Rent control, she added, isn't on the table under state law.

The council meets Dec. 9 at 7 p.m. at City Hall.

The Millbrook River Bridge on Route 9 will close to all traffic beginning Monday, December 1, as crews start a six month repair project that officials say is long overdue.

The 62 year old steel truss bridge, which carries roughly 11,000 vehicles a day between downtown Harlow and the residential neighborhoods of East Ridge, was flagged during a state inspection last spring. Engineers found corrosion in several support beams and deterioration in the concrete deck.

"The bridge is not unsafe today, but it will be if we wait," said Dana Whitfield, the county's director of public works. "This is the responsible time to act."

The $4.3 million project will replace the deck, reinforce the main supports and install new railings and lighting. Funding comes from a combination of state infrastructure grants and the county's capital budget. Contractor Delaney & Sons is expected to finish the work by early June, weather permitting.

During the closure, drivers will be detoured to the Oak Street crossing about two miles north. County officials warn that commutes could increase by 10 to 15 minutes during peak hours. Additional traffic signals and signage will be added along the detour route.

Pedestrians and cyclists will also lose access, though the county is arranging a free shuttle between both sides of the river on weekdays.

Some business owners near the bridge expressed concern. "We rely on people passing through," said Marcy Lunde, who owns a bakery on Front Street. "Six months is a long time."

Residents can find detour maps and project updates on the county website.

**Hartwell Museum sends carved figures home to Ghana**

Four wooden figures that sat in a glass case at the Hartwell Museum for nearly ninety years were packed into crates on Tuesday and driven to the airport, bound for Kumasi.

The carvings, which depict Asante court officials, were brought to the town in 1937 by Reginald Askew, a former colonial administrator who left most of his collection to the museum when he died. Records show he bought two of them from a trader. Nobody is sure how he got the other two.

"That's really the problem," said Claire Medway, the museum's director. "When you can't say how something left a country, you have to ask whether it should be here at all."

The museum began talking with Ghana's National Museum in 2023 after a researcher from the University of Ghana got in touch about the pieces. Medway said the board voted unanimously last spring to return them.

Not everyone in town is happy. Dennis Royle, 71, who said he had visited the figures since he was a boy, called the decision "a shame for local kids who'll never see them now."

Others were more relaxed about it. "They were never ours to begin with," said Priya Shah, who was visiting the museum with her two children on Saturday. "I'd rather they go back."

Two curators from Accra will hold a public talk at the museum on December 4 about the carvings and the families they were made for. Entry is free, though Medway suggested arriving early, as the lecture room only holds about sixty people.

The empty case will stay where it is for now, with a note explaining what happened.

Students at Maple Ridge High School will have to keep their phones out of sight during lessons starting next month, after the school board voted 5 to 2 on Tuesday evening to approve a new classroom device policy.

Under the rule, students must place their phones in lockers or in sealed pouches at the start of each class. Phones may still be used before school, at lunch and after the final bell. Teachers will be allowed to make exceptions for medical needs or approved learning activities.

Principal Dana Whitfield said the decision followed a year of complaints from staff about distraction and declining focus. "Our teachers were spending too much time policing screens instead of teaching," she said. "We want classrooms to be places where students can really pay attention to each other and to the material."

A survey conducted by the school last spring found that nearly 70 percent of teachers believed phones were harming student learning. About half of parents who responded supported a ban.

Not everyone is convinced. Several parents spoke at the meeting, raising concerns about reaching their children during emergencies. Board member Tom Reyes, who voted against the policy, said he worried the rule would be difficult to enforce fairly. "I understand the goal, but I think we need a clearer plan," he said.

Some students were also skeptical. Junior Priya Shah said she uses her phone to check assignments and calendars. "It feels like we are being punished for something only some people do," she said.

The school plans to review the policy at the end of the academic year.

# How to Apply for a Residential Parking Permit

Residential parking permits let eligible residents park on streets in designated permit zones without time limits. This page explains who can apply and how.

## Who Is Eligible

You may apply if:

- You live at an address within a designated permit zone
- The vehicle is registered to you at that address
- Your vehicle registration and insurance are current

Each household may hold up to two resident permits. Visitor permits are available separately.

## What You Will Need

Before you start, gather the following:

- **Proof of residency** dated within the last 60 days, such as a utility bill, lease agreement, or council tax statement
- **Vehicle registration document** showing your name and current address
- **Valid driver's licence**
- **Payment** by debit or credit card

## How to Apply

1. **Online:** Visit our Parking Services portal, create an account, and upload your documents. This is the fastest method.
2. **In person:** Bring your documents to any Customer Service Centre, Monday to Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
3. **By post:** Download and complete Form PP-1, then mail it with copies of your documents and a cheque to Parking Services.

## Fees and Processing Times

The annual permit fee is £45. Online applications are usually processed within five working days. Postal applications may take up to 15 working days.

## After You Apply

Most permits are digital and linked to your registration number, so no window display is required. Permits must be renewed every 12 months. We will send a reminder 30 days before expiry.

## Need Help?

Contact Parking Services at 0300 123 4567 or visit our website for further information.

**Household Recycling: What You Need to Know**

*Department of Environmental Services – Public Guidance*

Recycling correctly helps reduce landfill waste, conserve natural resources, and keep collection costs down for everyone. Please follow these rules when preparing your household recycling.

**What Goes in Your Recycling Bin**

- Paper and cardboard: newspapers, magazines, office paper, cereal boxes, and flattened cardboard boxes
- Plastic bottles and containers marked with recycling codes 1, 2, and 5
- Metal cans: aluminum drink cans, steel food tins, and clean aluminum foil
- Glass bottles and jars (clear, green, and brown)

**What Does Not Belong**

- Plastic bags and film wrap (return these to participating retail drop-off points)
- Food waste, greasy pizza boxes, and soiled paper
- Polystyrene foam, ceramics, and window glass
- Batteries, electronics, light bulbs, and paint. These require special disposal at designated collection sites.

**Preparation Tips**

1. **Rinse containers.** Remove food and liquid residue. Items do not need to be spotless.
2. **Keep items loose.** Do not bag your recyclables.
3. **Flatten cardboard** to save space in your bin.
4. **When in doubt, leave it out.** Contaminated loads may be sent to landfill.

**Collection Schedule**

Recycling is collected every other week on your regular trash day. Place your bin at the curb by 6:00 a.m. with the lid closed and handles facing the street.

**Need More Help?**

Visit our website or call the Recycling Information Line during business hours. Residents may also request a free replacement bin or a printed collection calendar.

*Thank you for helping keep our community clean and sustainable.*

# What to Do If You Lose Your Job

Losing your job can be stressful, but help is available. Taking a few steps early can protect your income and make your search for new work easier.

## 1. Apply for Unemployment Benefits

File a claim as soon as possible after your last day of work. Delays may reduce the benefits you receive. You can apply online or by phone. Have these ready:

- Your Social Security number
- Names and addresses of employers from the past 18 months
- Dates of employment and reason for separation
- Bank details for direct deposit

## 2. Review Your Health Coverage

If you had health insurance through your employer, you may be able to keep it for a limited time. You may also qualify for coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace or Medicaid. Losing job-based coverage opens a special enrollment period, usually lasting 60 days.

## 3. Check Your Final Pay

Your employer must pay all wages owed by the deadline set in state law. Ask about unused vacation pay, severance, and retirement accounts.

## 4. Get Help Finding Work

Local career centers offer free services, including:

- Job listings and referrals
- Resume and interview workshops
- Training programs for new skills
- Computer and internet access

## 5. Plan Your Budget

Contact lenders, landlords, and utility companies if you expect trouble paying bills. Many offer hardship programs.

## Need Help?

Call our helpline Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., or visit your nearest career center. Services are free and available in multiple languages.

# Getting a Fishing Licence

If you are aged 13 or over and want to fish for freshwater species in rivers, lakes, canals or reservoirs, you need a valid fishing licence. Licences help fund the protection of fish stocks, the improvement of habitats and the enforcement of fishing laws.

## Who needs a licence

You must have a licence if you fish with a rod and line in inland waters. Children under 13 do not need one. Licences for those aged 13 to 16 are free, but you must still register for one. Sea fishing from the shore or a boat does not usually require a licence, although local rules may apply.

## Types of licence

You can choose from:

- **1-day licence**: suitable for occasional fishing
- **8-day licence**: ideal for holidays
- **12-month licence**: the best value for regular anglers

Discounts are available for people aged 66 and over and for those receiving certain disability benefits.

## How to apply

The quickest way to apply is online through our licensing service. You will need your personal details and a payment card. You can also apply by phone or at participating Post Office branches.

Your licence is valid from the date and time you choose. Keep it with you while fishing, either in print or on your phone.

## Permission to fish

A licence does not give you the right to fish anywhere. You must also have permission from the landowner or the club that controls the fishing rights.

## Penalties

Fishing without a licence is an offence. You could be fined up to £2,500.

For more information, contact our customer helpline.

# School Admissions: Key Deadlines for Families

Applying for a school place is an important step for your child. This guidance explains the main deadlines and what you need to do to apply on time.

## Who needs to apply

You must apply if your child is:

- starting primary school for the first time
- moving from primary to secondary school
- changing schools outside the normal admissions round

## Main deadlines

**Secondary school places:** Applications must be submitted by **31 October**. Offers are sent on **1 March**.

**Primary school places:** Applications must be submitted by **15 January**. Offers are sent on **16 April**.

Applications received after these dates will be treated as late. Late applications are considered only after all on-time applications, which may reduce your chances of getting your preferred school.

## How to apply

Apply online through your local council's admissions portal. You can list up to six preferred schools, in order of preference. Make sure you:

- provide accurate address details
- include any supporting evidence, such as proof of sibling links or medical needs
- keep a copy of your confirmation email

## If you miss the deadline

Contact your local council's admissions team as soon as possible. In some cases, late applications may be accepted if there is a good reason, such as moving into the area recently.

## Appealing a decision

If your child is not offered a place at a school you applied for, you have the right to appeal. Appeals must usually be lodged within 20 school days of receiving your offer.

## Get help

For further support, contact your local council's admissions team.

# Keeping Warm and Safe in Cold Weather

Cold weather can be dangerous, especially for older adults, young children, and people with long-term health conditions. Following a few simple steps can help protect you and your family this winter.

## Heat Your Home Safely

- Keep the main living area at about 18°C (64°F), and warmer if you are older or unwell.
- Close curtains at dusk and keep doors closed to hold in heat.
- Never use gas ovens, outdoor grills, or generators indoors to heat your home. They can produce deadly carbon monoxide.
- Test your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms each month.

## Dress for the Weather

- Wear several thin layers rather than one thick layer.
- Cover your head, hands, and feet when you go outside.
- Change out of wet clothing as soon as possible.

## Eat and Stay Active

- Eat regular hot meals and have warm drinks throughout the day.
- Try to move around at least once an hour. Staying active helps your body make heat.

## Know the Warning Signs

Seek medical help right away if someone shows signs of **hypothermia**, such as shivering, confusion, slurred speech, or drowsiness. Signs of **frostbite** include numbness and pale, hard, or waxy skin, often on the fingers, toes, nose, or ears.

## Look Out for Others

Check on elderly neighbours, relatives, and anyone living alone. A quick phone call or visit can make a real difference.

## Get Support

If you are struggling with heating costs, you may be eligible for financial help. Contact your local council or visit our website to find out more.

**In an emergency, always call 999.**

Close curtains at dusk and keep internal doors shut to hold in warmth. # Quill 2.0 Is Here

**November 18, 2026**

After eighteen months of development, more than 2,400 merged pull requests, and contributions from 312 people around the world, we're proud to announce **Quill 2.0**, the biggest release in the project's history.

Quill started as a weekend experiment: a fast, keyboard-first editor that didn't ask you to choose between simplicity and power. Version 2.0 keeps that promise while rebuilding nearly everything underneath it.

## What's New

### A Rewritten Core
The text engine has been rebuilt on a rope data structure with incremental parsing. In practice:

- **Files over 1 GB open in under two seconds** on typical hardware.
- **Typing latency is consistently below 4 ms**, even with dozens of plugins active.
- **Memory usage is down roughly 40%** compared to 1.x on large projects.

### Native Language Server Support
LSP support is now built in, so you no longer need a plugin for it. Quill detects installed language servers automatically and gives you completions, go-to-definition, inline diagnostics, rename refactoring, and code actions with no configuration. Over 60 languages work out of the box.

### Collaborative Editing
Real-time collaboration has been our most requested feature for years, and it's finally here. Share a session with a single command, see your collaborators' cursors live, and keep working offline. Changes merge automatically using CRDTs. Sessions are end-to-end encrypted, and you can self-host the relay server.

### Tree-sitter Everywhere
Syntax highlighting, code folding, and structural selection now run on Tree-sitter grammars. Highlighting is more accurate and faster. You can also expand a selection to the enclosing function, block, or argument with a single keystroke.

### A New Plugin API
The 2.0 plugin API is built on WebAssembly, so you can write extensions in Rust, Go, Zig, C, or any language that compiles to Wasm. Plugins run sandboxed with explicit permissions, so an extension can't touch your filesystem or network unless you allow it.

### Refreshed Interface
- A redesigned command palette with fuzzy search across commands, files, symbols, and settings
- Split panes that can be dragged, docked, and saved as named layouts
- A new default theme, **Lantern**, in light and dark variants with WCAG AA contrast throughout
- Full screen reader support on Linux, macOS, and Windows

### Smaller Improvements
- Multi-cursor editing with regex-based cursor placement
- Built-in Git gutter, blame view, and inline diff
- An integrated terminal with shell integration
- Settings sync through any Git remote you control
- Startup time reduced to under 80 ms

## Breaking Changes

Because this is a major release, some things have changed:

- **1.x plugins are not compatible with 2.0.** A compatibility shim covers the most common APIs, and our [migration guide](https://quilleditor.org/docs/migrating-to-2) walks plugin authors through porting. The 40 most popular plugins have already been updated.
- **The configuration format has moved from INI to TOML.** Quill converts your existing config automatically the first time you launch it and keeps a backup of the original.
- **Some keybindings have changed** to resolve long-standing conflicts. Run `quill --keymap legacy` to restore the 1.x defaults.

## Get Quill 2.0

Quill 2.0 is available now for Linux, macOS, Windows, and FreeBSD.

- **Download:** [quilleditor.org/download](https://quilleditor.org/download)
- **Homebrew:** `brew install quill`
- **Cargo:** `cargo install quill-editor`
- **Flatpak:** `flatpak install org.quilleditor.Quill`
- **Arch Linux:** `pacman -S quill`

Version 1.x will receive security fixes until June 2027.

## Thank You

Quill is and always will be free, open-source software under the MIT license. It exists because of the people who write code, report bugs, translate the interface, improve the documentation, and answer questions in our forums. Special thanks to our 47 first-time contributors this cycle, and to our sponsors, whose support funds two full-time maintainers.

If you'd like to get involved, check out our [contributing guide](https://quilleditor.org/contribute), join the conversation on [Matrix](https://matrix.to/#/#quill:matrix.org), or pick up an issue tagged `good-first-issue` on GitHub.

Happy editing.

**The Quill Team**

**Introducing Privacy Mode: Your Work, Untouched by AI**

Today we're launching Privacy Mode, a new workspace setting that gives you complete control over how your data is handled. When Privacy Mode is on, no AI features process your content. None.

**Why we built it**

Many of you have told us the same thing: AI features are useful, but sometimes they aren't welcome. Maybe you handle client contracts under strict confidentiality agreements. Maybe your industry has compliance requirements that haven't caught up with machine learning. Or maybe you simply prefer that your work stays yours. We heard you, and we think that choice should be easy to make.

**What Privacy Mode does**

- **Disables all AI features** across your workspace, including smart suggestions, auto-summaries, writing assistance, and search ranking powered by machine learning.
- **Excludes your data from model training and evaluation.** Nothing you create, upload, or share while Privacy Mode is active is used to improve AI systems, ours or anyone else's.
- **Blocks third-party AI processing.** Your content is never sent to external AI providers.
- **Applies retroactively on request.** Admins can request that previously processed data be purged from any AI-related caches or logs.

**What stays the same**

Everything else. Your documents, projects, integrations, permissions, and workflows all work exactly as before. Standard search, templates, automations, and collaboration tools remain fully available.

**How to turn it on**

Workspace admins can enable Privacy Mode under **Settings → Security & Privacy → Privacy Mode**. It takes effect immediately for every member of the workspace. Individual users on personal plans can find the same toggle in their account settings.

**Available today**

Privacy Mode is free and available now on every plan. We don't believe privacy should be a premium feature.

**Our commitment**

We'll keep building AI tools for the people who want them, and we'll keep building ways to opt out for the people who don't. Both are worth doing well.

Questions? Visit our Help Center or reach out to our support team. We're glad to walk you through it.

*The Product Team*

Introducing Privacy Mode: Your Work, Untouched by AI

Today we are launching Privacy Mode, a new setting that lets you use our platform with every AI feature switched off and every piece of your data kept out of AI systems entirely.

Over the past year, we have added a number of AI-powered tools to help you write faster, summarize information, and automate routine tasks. Many of you have found them useful. We have also heard from a growing number of customers who want something different. Legal teams handling privileged documents, healthcare organizations bound by strict compliance rules, journalists protecting sources, and plenty of individuals who simply prefer to keep their work private have asked us for a clear, reliable way to opt out. Privacy Mode is our answer.

When you turn on Privacy Mode, all AI features disappear from your workspace. There are no suggestions, no auto-generated summaries, and no smart assistants running in the background. More importantly, your content is never sent to any AI model, whether ours or a third party's. Your documents, messages, files, and metadata are not used for training, not used for inference, and not processed by any machine learning system. What you create stays exactly where you put it.

We built Privacy Mode to be simple to understand and easy to verify. Administrators can enable it for an entire organization with a single toggle in the security settings, and they can lock it so individual users cannot turn it off. Every change to the setting is recorded in your audit log, giving compliance teams a clear record they can point to. We have also updated our data processing agreement and published a technical overview explaining exactly how data flows are isolated when Privacy Mode is active.

Choosing Privacy Mode does not mean giving up the features you rely on every day. Search, collaboration, version history, integrations, permissions, and everything else that makes our platform work will continue to function just as they always have. The only difference is that nothing touches an AI system along the way.

Privacy Mode is available starting today on all plans at no additional cost. We believe the ability to keep your data away from AI should be a basic right, not a premium upgrade.

To get started, visit Settings, open the Privacy and Security tab, and select Privacy Mode. If you have questions or want help rolling it out across your organization, our support team is ready to assist.

Thank you for trusting us with your work. We will keep building tools that give you more control, not less.

A few things to work through, roughly in order:

**1. Is time sync actually running?** Most drift complaints come down to NTP not working. Check whether chrony, ntpd, or systemd-timesyncd is active, and confirm it's reaching its upstream servers. `timedatectl` or `chronyc tracking` will tell you quickly. Make sure only one sync daemon is running, since two fighting each other causes weird behavior.

**2. Can it reach NTP servers?** Firewalls often block outbound UDP 123. Check that your configured servers resolve and respond.

**3. Is it a VM?** Virtual machines are notorious for drift, especially after host load spikes, live migration, or suspend/resume. Use the hypervisor's recommended clock source (e.g., kvm-clock) and either guest tools time sync *or* NTP, not both.

**4. Clock source and hardware.** Check the current clocksource in `/sys/devices/system/clock/clocksource/`. An unstable TSC can cause trouble. On bare metal, a dying CMOS battery or bad RTC can cause drift across reboots.

**5. Logs.** Look for "clocksource unstable" or large-step messages in the kernel log and your sync daemon's log.

Chrony generally handles intermittent connectivity and VMs better than classic ntpd.

Done this a bunch of times. The trick is mostly DNS prep and not rushing.

1. **Lower your DNS TTL a day or two ahead.** Drop it to 300 seconds or so. If it's sitting at 86400, resolvers will cache the old IP for a full day after you switch, and that's where most "downtime" comes from.

2. **Build the new server completely before touching DNS.** Copy files, import the database, set up SSL. Test by editing your local hosts file to point the domain at the new IP. Click around, log in, submit a form, check that the cert is valid.

3. **Handle the database carefully.** For a static site this is a non-issue. If people are writing data (comments, orders, whatever), either put the old site in read-only/maintenance mode for a few minutes during the final sync, or set up replication so both stay current.

4. **Do a final rsync and DB dump right before cutover**, then flip the A record.

5. **Leave the old server running for a few days.** Some resolvers ignore TTLs. Check the old box's access logs, and once traffic drops to nothing, shut it down.

Once the dust settles, put the TTL back up.

Almost always it's one of three things: distance/obstacles, interference, or a weak spot in your router's coverage.

**Obstacles:** Wi-Fi hates certain materials. Brick, concrete, plaster with metal lath, mirrors, aquariums, refrigerators, and foil-backed insulation can kill signal. One extra wall in the path can halve your throughput, especially on 5 GHz, which has less range than 2.4 GHz.

**Interference:** Microwaves, cordless phones, baby monitors, and Bluetooth gear all crowd 2.4 GHz. If that room is near the kitchen or a neighbor's router, try switching channels (1, 6, or 11 on 2.4 GHz) or forcing that device onto 5 GHz.

**Antenna placement:** Routers tucked in a cabinet, on the floor, or in a corner radiate poorly. Move it higher and more central, and point antennas both vertically and horizontally.

**To diagnose:** Use a Wi-Fi analyzer app to check signal strength (anything below about -70 dBm is poor) and channel congestion in that room versus elsewhere.

**Fixes, cheapest first:** relocate the router, change channels, add a wired access point or a mesh node near the problem room. Avoid cheap repeaters; they often halve bandwidth.

Start with the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy offsite. For a small office, that usually means the live data, a local backup (NAS or external drive), and a cloud copy.

Then answer a few questions:

- **What matters?** Inventory file shares, email, accounting databases, line-of-business apps, and laptops. Don't forget SaaS data. Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace aren't true backups by default.
- **How much can you lose?** Your RPO (recovery point objective) decides frequency. If losing a day of work is unacceptable, back up hourly or continuously.
- **How fast must you recover?** Your RTO (recovery time objective) decides method. Local image backups restore quickly. Cloud-only restores of large datasets can take days.
- **Ransomware protection:** Keep at least one copy immutable or offline. Backups reachable from a compromised admin account will get encrypted too.
- **Budget and skills:** Pick something someone will actually maintain. Managed tools like Veeam, Synology Active Backup, Backblaze, or Acronis beat clever scripts nobody monitors.

Most importantly, test restores regularly. An untested backup is a hope, not a strategy. Set up alerts for failed jobs and do a restore drill quarterly.

Start by figuring out what you actually can't afford to lose and how long you can be down. For most small offices that's the accounting data, shared drive, and email. If losing a day of work is annoying but survivable, nightly backups are fine. If it's not, you need something more frequent.

Then follow 3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one offsite. In practice that's usually a NAS in the closet (Synology is popular for a reason) plus a cloud target like Backblaze B2 or Wasabi. Don't count a USB drive someone "takes home on Fridays." That works for about three Fridays.

Make sure at least one copy is immutable or versioned so ransomware can't encrypt your backups along with everything else. This is the part people skip, and it's the part that matters most now.

If you're on Microsoft 365, back that up separately. Their retention isn't a backup, no matter what the sales rep implied.

Most important of all: test restores. Pick a random file every month and actually restore it. Once a year, try restoring a whole machine. A backup you've never restored from is a guess.

Keep it simple enough that whoever replaces you can understand it.

Hard to say without details, but slow builds almost always come down to a handful of usual suspects. Before guessing, measure: most build tools can show per-step timing (verbose or profiling flags, or your CI's step durations). Find where the minutes actually go.

Common culprits:

- **No caching.** Dependencies re-downloaded every run, or a Docker layer order that invalidates the cache early (copying source before installing deps is the classic mistake).
- **Full rebuilds instead of incremental ones.** A `clean` step in your script, timestamps getting touched, or generated files that always look "changed."
- **Serial execution.** Not using parallel jobs (`-j`, worker settings) even though you have cores available.
- **Tests bundled into the build.** Slow integration tests or tests that sleep or hit the network.
- **Underpowered or cold CI runners.** Low RAM leading to swapping, or fresh VMs with empty caches every time.
- **Heavy optimization or linking.** Release-mode LTO, huge static binaries, or type-checking a massive codebase in one pass.
- **Antivirus or file watchers** scanning thousands of small files (especially on Windows or in `node_modules`).

If you share your stack, build tool, and where it runs (local vs CI), people can give much more specific advice.

Background data drain usually comes from a handful of culprits:

1. **Sync and refresh.** Email, cloud storage (Photos, Drive, OneDrive), and social apps poll servers or upload content when you're not looking. Auto-backup of photos and videos is often the biggest offender.

2. **Push notifications and keep-alive connections.** Messaging apps hold persistent connections. Each ping is small, but they add up, especially with many apps.

3. **Prefetching.** News, video, and social apps preload content so it appears instantly when you open them.

4. **Updates.** App store auto-updates and OS updates may run over cellular if allowed.

5. **Analytics and ads.** SDKs bundled in apps send telemetry and fetch ad content.

6. **Retry loops.** A buggy app on a flaky connection can repeatedly fail and retry, burning data.

**How to find and fix it:**
- Check per-app usage: *Settings > Network > Data usage* (Android) or *Settings > Cellular* (iOS).
- Restrict background data per app (Android) or disable Background App Refresh (iOS).
- Set backups and updates to Wi-Fi only.
- Enable Data Saver / Low Data Mode.

If one app looks abnormal, clear its cache, update it, or reinstall it.

Usually it's one of a handful of things, and which one depends on whether it's your app or someone else's.

If it's an app you're building, check your sync logic first. A lot of devs set up periodic refresh with WorkManager or BackgroundFetch and forget the backoff, so a failed request retries constantly. Also look for analytics and crash-reporting SDKs. Some of them batch uploads aggressively, and ad SDKs are even worse because they prefetch creatives.

Push notifications that trigger a full data pull, instead of just the delta, will also add up fast.

If it's an app you're just using, the usual suspects are:
- Auto-play video or preloading in social apps
- Photo/cloud backup set to sync over cellular
- Podcast or music apps downloading new episodes
- Maps caching tiles

To find the culprit, go to Settings > Network (or Cellular on iOS) and check per-app usage. Both platforms let you restrict background data per app. On Android, Data Saver mode kills most of it outright.

If you want to see exactly what's being sent, put a proxy like mitmproxy or Charles in front of the device. It's eye-opening how chatty some apps are.

First, confirm it's actually a leak. Graph the process's RSS (or heap size, if your runtime exposes it) over hours or days. Steady growth that never plateaus, even after garbage collection, points to a leak. Growth that levels off is often just caches warming up or allocator fragmentation.

Next, correlate the growth with load. Does memory climb with request count, specific endpoints, scheduled jobs, or reconnections? That narrows down which code path is responsible.

Then compare heap snapshots. Take one early, let the service run under load, and take another later. Most runtimes have tooling for this: pprof for Go, heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools for Node, tracemalloc or memray for Python, jcmd/Eclipse MAT for the JVM, and Valgrind massif or heaptrack for C/C++. Diff the snapshots and look for object types whose counts keep growing.

The usual culprits:
- Unbounded caches or maps keyed by user, session, or request
- Event listeners or callbacks that are registered but never removed
- Goroutines, threads, or promises that never finish
- Connections, file handles, or buffers that aren't closed
- Global collections that only ever get appended to

If you can reproduce it locally with a load generator, iterating is much faster than poking at production.

As a stopgap, scheduled restarts or memory limits keep you alive, but they don't fix anything.

Version 2.4.0 (2026-11-18)

This release adds first-class TypeScript support. The package now ships its own type declarations, so you no longer need to install a separate @types package or write your own ambient module definitions. Types are generated from the source and published alongside the compiled JavaScript, which keeps them in sync with every future release.

All public functions, classes, and configuration objects are fully typed, including overloads for methods that accept multiple argument shapes. Generic parameters are used where the return type depends on the input, so editors can now infer accurate result types without manual annotations. Option objects are exported as named interfaces, making it easy to build typed wrappers or extend the defaults in your own code.

The declarations target TypeScript 4.7 and later and work with both the "node16" and "bundler" module resolution modes. The package.json exports map now includes a "types" condition for each entry point, so ESM and CommonJS consumers both resolve the correct files.

If you were previously using the community-maintained @types package, you can safely uninstall it. A few type names differ from that package; see the migration notes in the documentation for a full mapping. There are no runtime changes in this release, and existing JavaScript users are unaffected.

## Getting started

You'll need Node 18 or newer. Install it globally with `npm install -g quill-ssg`, then run `quill new my-site` to scaffold a project. That gives you a `content/` folder for your Markdown files, a `templates/` folder with a plain default layout, and a `quill.config.js` you can mostly ignore for now. Run `quill serve` inside the project and open http://localhost:4000. The page reloads whenever you save a file, so it's easiest to keep the browser and your editor side by side while you poke around. When you're happy with it, `quill build` writes the finished site to `dist/`, and you can upload that folder to pretty much any host. If something breaks, run the command again with `--verbose`. The error is usually a typo in a template's front matter.

Search is one of the most frequently used features in our product, and its performance has degraded to the point where it now harms user experience and business outcomes. Over the past two quarters, median search latency has risen from roughly 300 milliseconds to over 1.2 seconds, and the 95th percentile now regularly exceeds 4 seconds during peak traffic. Users notice these delays. Session recordings show people retyping queries, abandoning searches midway, or leaving the page before results appear. Support tickets mentioning slow or unresponsive search have tripled over the same period.

The impact goes beyond frustration. Search is the primary entry point for product discovery, and internal analytics show a clear relationship between latency and conversion. When results take longer than two seconds to load, the likelihood that a user clicks a result drops by about 35 percent, and downstream purchases fall accordingly. Because search traffic makes up a large share of total sessions, even modest slowdowns translate into meaningful lost revenue and reduced engagement.

Several factors appear to contribute to the problem, though none has been confirmed as the dominant cause. The search index has grown nearly fourfold as the catalog has expanded, but the underlying infrastructure and query patterns have not changed to match. Recent features such as personalized ranking and faceted filtering add computation to every request, and some of that work runs serially when it could run in parallel. Caching is inconsistent across services, and cache hit rates have dropped as query diversity has increased. We also lack fine-grained observability into the search pipeline, which makes it difficult to determine where time is actually spent for a given request.

This lack of visibility is itself part of the problem. Engineers investigating latency spikes currently rely on aggregate dashboards that cannot distinguish between time spent in query parsing, retrieval, ranking, and response serialization. As a result, past optimization efforts have been reactive and narrowly scoped, producing short-term improvements that eroded as traffic and data volume continued to grow.

The goal of this effort is to understand the root causes of search latency and to bring performance back to an acceptable and sustainable level. Specifically, we aim to return median latency to under 400 milliseconds and keep 95th percentile latency under one second at projected peak load for the next eighteen months. Any solution must preserve the relevance quality of current results, avoid significant increases in infrastructure cost, and remain maintainable by the existing search team. This document does not propose a redesign of the ranking model or changes to the search user interface, although findings from this work may inform those efforts later.
